answer: Check in order: (1) HEAD position: git log -1 / rev-parse HEAD on both machines: same branch name does not imply same commit (yours may be pre-fetch); git fetch + git status shows ahead/behind truth; (2) untracked-but-ignored divergence: git status is clean yet node_modules/.cache, .env.local, or a generated routes file differ (menu config from a codegen step not yet run locally after pull): compare git clean -ndx and rerun documented generate steps; (3) submodule pointer mismatch: git submodule status (the - prefix means not updated): a UI package inside a submodule pinned older explains 'same branch, fewer menus'; (4) LFS smudge state: pointer files instead of content (config JSON stored via LFS not pulled: git lfs pull); (5) runtime cache from before the pull (dev server holding old bundle). Each hypothesis maps to a command that distinguishes it; run those before touching code. Conclusion: clean status only covers tracked files at HEAD: verify commit identity, ignored/generated files, submodule/LFS state first.

instruction: A script reports 'branch feature-x is merged' but git log shows the feature commits are NOT ancestors of main; a merge commit exists titled 'Merge feature-x' that brought in an older state. How can a merge commit exist without bringing the tip commits, and how do you verify what a merge actually introduced?
reasoning: Merge commits record parents, not content guarantees. Merges of pre-divergence points, botched conflict resolutions (kept 'ours'), or rebased-then-remerged branches produce merges that omit later commits. Verification is ancestry (merge-base --is-ancestor) plus content diff (diff of merge result vs branch tip), never the merge title.
answer: Explanations: (1) someone merged feature-x at commit A, then feature-x gained more commits (the tip you checked): the merge honestly merged A, not the tip; (2) the merge was executed with --strategy=ours or conflicts resolved by discarding their hunks: content never arrived though ancestry says it did; (3) the branch was rebased after merging (new SHAs of the same work): original commits unmerged while equivalents exist: cherry (git cherry main feature-x) reveals patch-equivalence. Verify properly: (a) git merge-base --is-ancestor <feature-tip> main && echo truly merged (fast boolean); (b) content check: git diff main...feature-x: empty means main contains all changes (semantically merged even if SHAs differ); (c) for the title-only suspicion: git show the merge commit's second parent and diff the merge tree against both parents to see what it introduced. Act on (b)'s answer: if nonempty, the branch has unintegrated content regardless of merge titles. Conclusion: trust ancestry booleans and content diffs; merge commit messages are labels, not evidence.

instruction: Someone ran git clean -fdx in the monorepo root 'to fix a build issue' and now all .env.local files, IDE settings, and untracked migration drafts are gone; worse, a nested node_modules broke the runner cache. What's the blast-radius understanding of clean with -x in a working repo, and what habits limit damage?
reasoning: -x deletes ignored files too. Env files, local certs, editor state, build caches, and untracked drafts vanish with no undo (they were never in git). Habit. Dry-run first (git clean -ndx), scope to a subdirectory, and treat ignored local config as precious, re-creatable only via documented bootstrap.
answer: Blast radius: git clean -fdx removes anything untracked INCLUDING ignored paths: the -x is what nuked .env.local (gitignored by design) and caches: none of it recoverable via git (reflog doesn't know untracked files); local-only artifacts (draft SQL, scratch notebooks) are the true losses: some may be regenerable (npm ci rebuilds node_modules, caches refill at time cost), but env.local values must be re-obtained per machine (team shared vault entry, platform dashboard pulls). Damage-limit habits: (1) always preview: git clean -ndx lists victims first (tilt it at the subdir you meant: clean -fdx packages/web); (2) safer alternative for build issues: remove specific cache dirs (rm -rf dist .turbo) name-known rather than scorched-earth; (3) team insurance: keep a bootstrap script that regenerates .env.example → prompts/seeds .env.local, and document where real values live (vault), so clean events are inconveniences; (4) stash-instead habit: when wanting a pristine tree, git stash -u keeps an undo path. Report the incident to recover shared drafts from colleagues' machines (their untracked copies may survive). Conclusion: -x converts cache-clearing into local-state deletion: dry-run, scope narrowly, and ensure local-only state has a regeneration path.

instruction: PR review comment: 'drop these merge commits from your branch before I approve'. The team uses squash merges; the feature branch contains 4 merge commits from main. What's the legitimate request here, and what rewrite considerations apply if the branch was already pushed and reviewed by others?
reasoning: With squash-merge convention, intermediate merge-back commits only pollute the final diff/approval. Rebasing the feature branch onto main linearizes it. But rewriting published history invalidates reviewers' local copies and open comments. Coordinate timing, force-push-with-lease, and notify.
answer: Legitimacy: the merges create noise in the PR file view (already-on-main changes shown as branch changes in some UIs) and, post-squash, carry no meaning: a rebase --onto main (or interactive rebase dropping merge lines, which rebase does by default flattening) gives a clean single-lineahead diff. Rewrite protocol for a pushed, reviewed branch: (1) agree to do it at a sync point (right after a review round, not mid-typing by another contributor); (2) fetch fresh, rebase onto origin/main, resolve conflicts once (rebase replays branch commits, merge-back conflicts reappear but final states equal); (3) verify equivalence: diff the rebased branch against the pre-rebase tree (range-diff or plain diff working trees) to prove no content change; (4) push --force-with-lease (fails if someone else pushed meanwhile: the lease checks your assumption of the remote ref); (5) comment in the PR that history was rebased (review tools show a force-push event; prior inline comments may remap or orphan: reviewers re-fetch). If the branch were SHARED by multiple authors, prefer merge-back instead of rebase regardless of aesthetics. Conclusion: rebase-to-clean is right for solo feature branches pre-merge; wrap it in lease-protected pushes, equivalence verification, and reviewer notification.

instruction: Main broke in CI yesterday; git bisect lands on a merge commit with a 60-file diff, and the team asks 'so who broke it: the merge?' Why is a bisect landing on a merge commit ambiguous, and what's the technique to isolate the true fault within?
reasoning: A merge combines two histories. The break can be semantic conflict (each side passes alone) or carried-in fault. Bisect into the merge by testing both parents, then continue bisection on the guilty parent. 'merge commit' as culprit usually means interaction, not authorship.
answer: Disambiguation technique: (1) checkout each parent of the merge and run the failing test: outcomes: (a) both parents pass → the breakage is an INTERACTION (semantic conflict: e.g., branch A renamed a column while branch B added a query using the old name; both green alone, broken together): the fault belongs to the missing cross-team integration test, not a single author; fix on main directly (post-merge integration) or add contract coverage; (b) one parent fails → the fault was carried in from that branch; continue bisecting along THAT parent (git bisect supports following first-parent boundaries; manual: bisect good <good-parent> bad <merge> continues automatically) until the introducing commit appears; (2) also consider the merge RESOLUTION content: diff merge tree vs auto-merge result (git show merge vs what rerere/ours modifications reveal): hand-resolutions can inject faults neither branch had. Assign blame to process, not just people: result typically yields 'we need the integration test X' as the durable fix. Conclusion: test both merge parents: passing parents mean a semantic-conflict class bug (interaction/missing integration test), failing parents continue bisection into that branch.

instruction: You find 30 stale local branches; some were force-pushed/rewritten upstream so git branch --merged lies about their state. Propose a branch-hygiene sweep that distinguishes merged, abandoned, and diverged-but-valuable work without deleting anyone's half-finished spike.
reasoning: --merged checks commit ancestry, which rebases/squash-merges invalidate for identical content. Hygiene must use patch-equivalence (git cherry / cherry-pick detection), remote PR status (merged PRs have closed refs), age, and author pings before any deletion, with recovery via reflog.
answer: Sweep protocol: (1) sync facts: git fetch --prune to drop dead remote refs; for each local branch gather: upstream delta (rev-list --left-right --count), PR status via gh pr list --head (a MERGED squash merge means content is integrated despite non-ancestry), last-commit date/author; (2) classify: (a) squash-merged equivalents: verify with git cherry main <branch> (empty output = all patches equivalent upstream): safe-delete class, still announce first; (b) ahead-with-PR-still-open or recent: keep; (c) ahead, ancient, no PR: candidate archive: rename with prefix (spike/name-date) or push a backup ref (refs/archive/) then delete local; (d) behind-main-only branches (pure stale copies of main): delete freely; (3) acts: delete with git branch -D only after the archive ref exists; record the sweep list shared in chat for a week of protests; (4) recovery note: reflog + archive refs make every deletion cheap to undo: say so, to reduce deletion fear; (5) policy forward: delete remote branches at merge (GitHub auto-delete), monthly sweep cadence. Conclusion: squash-era hygiene = patch-equivalence plus PR state plus archival backups; ancestry alone convicts innocent branches.

instruction: A teammate 'lost' 3 commits after git reset --hard HEAD~3 while experimenting; no branch/tag points at them. They force-quit their terminal already. Walk the recovery reasoning: what does reflog know, and what's the careful sequence to restore without compounding?
reasoning: reset --hard moves refs but objects persist via reflog entries for weeks. Recovery is reflog archaeology plus re-anchoring the found tip to a new branch. Sequence matters because any new writes/reflog churn and destructive flags (gc, prune) shorten the window.
answer: Recovery sequence: (1) DO NOTHING destructive: no gc, no further resets, avoid checkout churn that floods reflog (each operation adds entries, but doesn't delete old ones: time is fine, panic isn't); (2) git reflog (or reflog show <branch>) and read top-down: find the line where HEAD sat at the pre-reset tip: entries like 'commit: add X' followed later by 'reset: moving to HEAD~3': the SHA before reset is your target (also -g flag shows timestamps); (3) verify identity of the found SHA before re-anchoring: git show <sha> (message/stats), and git log <sha> --oneline -5 matches the lost trio; (4) anchor immediately: git branch recovery/lost-work <sha> (never reset the current branch onto it as first move: branch creation is non-destructive; only after confirming, merge/cherry-pick or reset from a safe state); (5) scan for stash losses similarly (git stash list, and fsck --unreachable for stash-shaped commits if previously dropped). Teach the near-miss: reset --hard is delete-shaped; reset --soft/--keep or committing WIP to a throwaway branch first preserves doors. Conclusion: objects survive ref moves; reflog finds the orphaned tip, verify-then-branch restores, and disciplined anchoring beats heroic resets.

instruction: Deploy pipeline checks out tag v2.4.0 (immutable release tags). A hotfix was committed to main but no new tag exists; on-call 'redeployed' expecting the fix and declared victory though prod still runs old code. Why did redeploy do nothing, and what tag discipline + verification closes the loop?
reasoning: Tag-deployed systems rebuild from the tag's immutable commit. Commits on main are invisible until a new tag moves the pointer semantics (a NEW tag, not a moved one). Loop closure = release process creating v2.4.1 plus post-deploy verification of running SHA, not assumption.
answer: Mechanics: the pipeline resolves REF v2.4.0 → commit SHA at tag creation: immutable by convention: redeploy checks out the same SHA every time; 'redeploy' re-ran packaging of identical bits: victory was declared over a receipt, not behavior. Additionally moved tags (force-reattach v2.4.0) would be a worse sin: breaks cache identity and provenance (two artifacts claim one tag). Discipline: (1) hotfix path = patch release flow: cherry-pick the fix onto a release/hotfix branch from the tag if main has diverged (don't ship unrelated main commits in a firedrill), tag v2.4.1, pipeline naturally builds new; (2) verification never assumed: post-deploy check compares RUNNING artifact identity (GET /version returning build SHA, which must equal the tag SHA) and a functional smoke asserting the fixed behavior: 'deployed' = observed, not reported; (3) dashboards/alerts record release tags so 'prod at v2.4.0 while fix is on main' is visible in one glance during incidents. Communicate back to on-call curriculums: 'redeploy is re-run, not refresh: pointers decide'. Conclusion: tag-based deploys are pointer-frozen: fixes travel only through new tags, and victory requires observed running-SHA + behavioral smoke.

instruction: git log --follow on config/prod.yaml shows only one commit ('initial'), yet production clearly evolved alongside it for two years. The file's history 'vanished'. Enumerate the git-level reasons history appears lost (renames without -M, filter-branch, renames beyond thresholds) and the archaeology commands that recover the true lineage.
reasoning: Per-file history depends on rename detection, path restructures, and past history rewrites; --follow tracks one path only across simple renames. Archaeology. History with rename thresholds, --full-history across restructures, directory-level log, and forge-level blame, before concluding information is gone.
answer: Vanish causes: (1) renames: 'initial' likely isn't the true start: the file was moved from config/environments/production.yaml or similar with content changes exceeding similarity threshold in the same commit (-M50% default misses heavily-edited renames): log --follow bails; (2) path restructures: repo re-orgs (config/ → infra/config) split history into segments; (3) rewrites: a past filter-branch/git-filter-repo/squash-of-repo-history (monorepo merge!) rewrote every SHA with flattened ancestry: 'initial' is the post-rewrite epoch; original history may live in an archived repo or refs/original; (4) shallow clone depth cutting history locally (CI clones --depth=1 make everything look one-commit). Recovery commands: git log --follow --find-renames=20% --full-history -- <path>; walk parent directories (git log --oneline -- config/ and infer moves by commit titles like 'reorganize'); git log -S 'distinctiveOldKey' --all to catch pre-rename content; check remote for orphan branches/tags predating rewrite; check the forge UI (PR history references SHAs even though rewritten: wayback for configs). If truly rewritten: document the archived-repo location in README as the historical source. Conclusion: 'lost file history' is usually rename-threshold or restructure segmentation: escalate thresholds, search by content, and hunt pre-rewrite archives.

instruction: A shared repo has .gitattributes with text=auto. A Windows contributor's checkout converts LF→CRLF in shell scripts; executed inside Linux containers via bind mount they fail with '/bin/bash^M: bad interpreter'. Why does attribute-level line-ending policy fail this topology, and what configuration fixes the class (not the file)?
reasoning: text=auto normalizes on COMMIT but writes platform-native endings on checkout. Linux containers running Windows checkouts inherit CRLF. The class fix pins checkout behavior per file-type (*.sh eol=lf) and enforces via attributes, not per-developer core.autocrlf folklore, plus shebang-aware CI linting.
answer: Mechanics: text=auto stores LF in the repo but checkout honors host convention (core.eol/crlf defaults on Windows produce CRLF working trees): bind-mounted into Linux, bash sees CR bytes in the shebang line: the 'bad interpreter' with caret-M provenance. Per-developer fixes (set core.autocrlf=input on your machine) don't scale: every new Windows dev re-hits it. Class fix: (1) .gitattributes policy that controls CHECKOUT bytes regardless of checkout OS: '*.sh text eol=lf' plus 'Makefile text eol=lf', and binary markers for images/fonts ('*.png binary') to stop conversion accidents; critical: renormalize the existing tree once (git add --renormalize .) and commit the resulting byte-changes, or policy lands only on future edits; (2) CI guard: lint stage failing on CRLF in scripts (file check or dos2unix detector) catches lapses from tooling that ignores attributes (some IDEs write directly); (3) alternative topology: build inside WSL/native Linux checkout for container work (document). Communicate: this attribute commit changes byte-level content teamwide: land it alone (not mixed into a feature PR) to keep blame usable. Conclusion: cross-OS container consumption needs checkout-level eol pinning via attributes + renormalization commit + CI lint: host conventions can't govern shared bind-mounts.

instruction: Two long-lived branches, main and release/2023-lts (customers pinned), both receive fixes; a race-condition patch went to main only six months ago, and LTS users still report the bug. No process says what backports. What dual-maintenance state discipline does a repo with live release branches require?
reasoning: Long-lived release lines create N active truths. Fixes silently land in the newest only unless backport bookkeeping (labels, cherry-pick tasks, per-line trackers) is institutional. The repo must encode which lines are alive and route each fix through a 'lines affected' decision.
answer: Discipline required: (1) declare living lines: SUPPORT.md (or repo bot config) listing supported branch lines with EOL dates: 'release/2023-lts until 2025-06': support questions default to 'which lines are affected'; (2) decision workflow: every bugfix PR template includes 'Backport needed to:' checkboxes with automation: GitHub Action/bot reading labels creates cherry-pick PRs per line (or instructs manual when conflicts): unmerged-backport tracking stays visible (a project board or label query 'backport-pending'); (3) divergence strategy helpers: cherry-pick -x records source SHA (traceability), and where lines diverged enough, per-line patches get authored with mainline cross-reference in message; (4) verification per line: CI matrix runs the suite on each living branch (LTS CI can't rot or backports land blind); (5) audit queries for the PMO: 'fixes on main since <date> lacking backport-merged label' catches leaks like the six-month race fix; (6) sunset grammar: EOL announcements actively downgrade backport pressure as lines die. Handling this case now: audit the incident: reproduce on LTS branch, backport the patch (cherry-pick -x, resolving conflicts from divergence), add the tracking-label retroactively, run the audit query for other missed fixes. Conclusion: multiple living branches need declared lifespans + label-driven backport routing + per-line CI + audit queries, else 'fixed' is per-line fiction.

instruction: CI's versioning step runs git describe --tags to stamp artifacts; after switching the workflow to actions/checkout shallow fetch (depth=1 for speed), versions become '0.0.0-dev-g<sha>'. Why does shallow history mutate version computation, and what fetch-depth policy pairs speed with tag availability?
reasoning: git describe walks ancestry to the nearest tag. Depth=1 erases ancestry. So describe falls back to defaults or fails. Fix. Fetch tags with sufficient depth (fetch-depth: 0), or fetch-tags plus targeted deepening, or compute the version bearer in a dedicated job while build jobs stay shallow.
answer: Mechanics: describe needs the commit's ancestors until it meets a tag object; a depth-1 clone fabricates a grafted boundary so traversal stops immediately: no tag reachable → the fallback identity you see (some flows even tag versions wrong and publish artifacts labeled dev). Policies in order of preference: (1) full history only for the version-emitting job (actions/checkout fetch-depth: 0 with fetch-tags: true) that computes the version once, stores it as artifact/env, downstream build/test jobs keep depth=1 speed and consume the stamped value: best of both; (2) depth compromise: fetch-depth N where N comfortably exceeds commits-per-release cycle (fragile under hotfix storms: prefer (1)); (3) explicit tag hydration: fetch specific tag objects + partial deep (git fetch --unshallow --tags) when monorepo size punishes full clones. Related landmines in shallow clones: changelog generation (needs range), semantic-release (needs history), merge-base computations for affected-detection (nx affected needs base SHA history: similarly broken by depth=1: same fix pattern). Add a CI assertion: computed version must NOT match dev fallback pattern, failing loudly rather than publishing mislabeled artifacts. Conclusion: history-derived versions require fetched history: hydrate fully in one version job and fan out the stamp, else describe degenerates silently.

instruction: git blame on api/routes.ts attributes every line to a single 'big refactor' commit from a year ago (mechanical reformat + move). Team claims blame is 'useless' on this file for finding original intent. What blame-attribution preservation/recovery techniques apply when mass-mechanical commits poison line history?
reasoning: Mechanical rewrites steal authorship per line but not information. Blame -w/-C (ignore whitespace, detect moved lines), hyper-blame ignore-revs files, and archaeology through the refactor commit's parents restore intent-finding. Instituting .git-blame-ignore-revs makes the next rewrite zero-cost to history users.
answer: Recovery techniques: (1) blame with ignore options: git blame -w (whitespace-insensitive) collapses pure-reformat attribution back to prior authors; -C -C tracks lines moved/copied across files (the 'move' part): often enough to reattribute 80% of lines; (2) skip the poison commit explicitly: git blame --ignore-rev <sha>, better institutionalized as .git-blame-ignore-revs listing mechanical commits (GitHub and modern git honor blame.ignoreRevsFile: configure once, every future blame is clean); (3) archaeology past the commit: blame the PARENT version (git blame <sha>^ -- path-at-that-time) then map lines forward: slower but exact for intent questions; (4) range-diff/log -L for specific functions (git log -L :functionName:file tracks a function across history, immune to file moves). Prevention rituals: mechanical changes travel alone (no semantic edits in reformat commits: mixed commits permanently blur), the ignore-revs file gets a line in the same PR as the mass-change (template checkbox), and formatting enforcement lands in pre-commit so stray future reformats don't need bulk events. Conclusion: blame-poisoning is recoverable via -w/-C/--ignore-rev tooling and a committed ignore-revs manifest; keep mechanical diffs pure and registered so intent archaeology stays cheap.

instruction: A release process uses annotated tags carrying changelog notes; someone created a LIGHTWEIGHT tag for v2.5.0. Downstream tooling (release notes generator, SBOM attestation) silently skipped it. Why do tag types have distinct consumer semantics, and what's the repo-guard that fixes, not just repairs, the mistake?
reasoning: Annotated tags are objects with metadata+identity (verifiable, listable via for-each-ref of tag type), lightweight tags are bare refs. Tooling filtering tag objects or verifying signatures skips them silently. Guards. CI validation on tag refs (type annotation check), protected tag patterns, and a scripted release entry that never hands humans raw git tag.
answer: Semantics: an annotated tag object stores tagger/date/message (your changelog notes + signature for attestation chains); tooling that enumerates 'tag objects' (git for-each-ref refs/tags --format with objecttype filter, or sigstore/GPG verification in SBOM flows) sees nothing for a bare ref pointing straight at a commit: the release looked absent, hence 'silent skip' rather than error: the worst shape. Repair: create an annotated tag on the same commit (tag -a -m or -s, force-move the ref: because lightweight v2.5.0 already propagated, coordinate: force-moving tags breaks clones that fetched it: pick v2.5.0-post or accept a forced retag window with comms; purge caches). Repo-guard fixes: (1) release script is the ONLY tagging path (make release): it errors on pre-existing refs, signs, pushes, and verifies remotely after push (object type check); (2) CI gate on tag events: workflow asserts github ref is an annotated tag (git cat-file -t) before notes/SBOM stages, failing LOUD rather than skipping; (3) server-side protection: tag ref rules restricting who can push tags (forge features) so bypassing the script is visible; (4) docs near the release runbook explaining the why (silent consumers breed repeat mistakes). Conclusion: tag type is a consumer-facing contract: retag annotated, script the path, and make pipelines fail loudly on bare refs.

instruction: A PR shows +0/-0 files changed on the platform but 'cannot merge: conflicts' simultaneously; locally the branch merges cleanly into a fresh main clone. Explain the checkout-version-dependent conflict and the steps to reproduce the platform's exact evaluation before 'resolving' blindly.
reasoning: Forges evaluate merges against THEIR merge state (possibly newer main than your local, different rename/similarity handling, or RMS of rerere/mode bits); 'clean locally' can be an older or differently-configured evaluation. Reproduce by syncing to the same base and using the forge's merge-ref if exposed, then resolve against that state only.
answer: Divergence sources: (1) stale local main: platform main moved since your last fetch: new conflicting edits landed there today; always reproduce against origin/main pulled NOW; (2) merge strategy/flags differ: platform uses merge-tree (ort) with rename detection while your config sets diff.renames=false (or threshold differences), so a rename+edit pair conflicts remotely only; (3) mode/attribute bits: executable bit or symlinks treated differently across OS checkouts (core.fileMode) generating phantom conflicts in forge evaluations; (4) the +0/-0 anomaly suggests a last-reverted diff (your branch adds and reverts same change) where the merge base computation still intersects on touched hunks: ort flags it while recursive ignores: version-tied behavior. Reproduction path: fetch --all; git merge-tree $(merge-base) / git merge --no-commit origin/main locally after matching configs; if offered, fetch the forge's ephemeral merge ref (refs/pull/N/merge on GitHub) and inspect its conflict state exactly; resolve ONLY in a branch synced to that base (#3 suspects: inspect file modes in the diff: chmod corrections belong in their own commit with explanation). Then push and recheck platform state, which re-evaluates deterministically. Conclusion: platform conflicts are evaluated on platform state with platform settings: sync base, match rename/mode configs, reproduce with merge-tree or the PR merge ref, then resolve.

instruction: Someone committed their local .env (with live credentials) two weeks ago, then deleted it in the next commit. The fix branch 'removes the secret from history' via interactive rebase of only the last 20 commits. Why is that insufficient, and write the complete secret-remediation reasoning including rotation and rewrite scoping.
reasoning: Deletion commits never erase history. Secrets propagate through every clone/fork/CI cache and via any ref pointing at pre-deletion commits. Remediation = credential rotation FIRST (assume compromised), then history rewrite across ALL refs (filter-repo, not 20-commit rebase), coordination for re-clone, and cache purges. Scan for recurrence.
answer: Insufficiency anatomy: (1) a rebase over 20 commits rewrites only commits on that branch range: the secret persists in any other branch/tag containing the original commits, in remote refs (PR refs, release tags), in every existing clone and fork (propagation happened at clone time: assume harvested), CI build caches, and archived bundles; (2) deletion-in-next-commit means the leaked value lived in a pushed commit for an unknown exposure window: secrets in git are considered PUBLIC regardless of rewrite: rotation is the primary remediation, history surgery is hygiene. Complete sequence: (1) ROTATE immediately (new keys, revoke old: do it before any rewriting; rewriting without rotating leaves valid keys in the world); (2) inventory exposure: which branches/tags contain the blob (git log -S / rev-list --objects | grep blob), plus provider access logs around the window (was the key already used?); (3) rewrite ALL refs with git filter-repo --invert-paths/--replace-text (handles blobs across refs, not rebase), force-push everything, coordinate: all clones invalidated (everyone re-clones; stale forks deleted/re-pushed); (4) purge caches: forge support request for dangling PR refs if the platform requires it (GitHub PR refs need support/ticket), CI caches cleared; (5) prevent: secret-scanning pre-commit (gitleaks) + push-protection server-side + move env handling to .env.example+vault docs. Conclusion: rotation first (compromise assumed), filter-repo across every ref second, clone/cache coordination third, scanning fourth: rebase-20 is a cosmetic subset of the problem.

instruction: An engineer's commits show 'Co-authored-by' trailer lines crediting a former employee on 40 new commits; audit asks if copy-paste of trailers is gaming attribution stats. Separately, you notice the committed code matches a rejected PR from months ago. What does trailer forensics + provenance comparison tell you, and how do you proceed professionally?
reasoning: Trailers are self-asserted metadata, easily replicated. Attribution questions need content-provenance evidence. Similarity to the rejected PR's diff, review-comment incorporation patterns, and author-domain knowledge signals. Proceed by documenting evidence neutrally and routing to owners/maintainers, not accusations.
answer: Forensics available: (1) content provenance: git range-diff between the new commits and the rejected PR's branch (or GitHub's compare across forks): high patch-ID overlap identifies copy-through even if rewritten (range-diff handles message/base changes); literal diff hash matches for files are stronger; (2) trailer mechanics: Co-authored-by is free text added by committer: anyone can add anyone (no consent protocol): statistical anomalies (40 commits, zero reciprocal credit, trailer added via alias script in git config: inspect committer vs trailer consistency) suggest bulk templating; (3) review-context comparison: did the new PR incorporate the REJECTED PR's review fixes (the rejected one's unresolved comments all 'addressed' identically is a provenance trail); (4) falsifiability of contribution claims: issue assignments, design doc authorship, branch push times vs PR creation. Professional handling: collect this as a neutral fact pack (commands + outputs) routed to the repo owners/HR channel designated for conduct questions: do NOT litigate in PR comments (that's escalation without process); maintainers may add attribution corrections via revert-reapply with proper credit or update governance requiring DCO sign-offs; remember legitimate explanations exist (pairing leftovers in git templates: commit --reset-author hygiene lapses are the common innocent cause of trailer drift). Conclusion: treat trailers as claims, diffs as evidence: range-diff similarity + review-trail analysis packaged neutrally to maintainers beats public accusation, with innocent-template failure modes kept on the table.

instruction: git log shows an impossible ordering: commit B (child, later timestamp) appears BELOW commit A in --graph output while dates say A is older than its grandparent. A chronological report built on commit dates produced nonsense. Why are commit timestamps unreliable ordering, and what ordering semantics should audit/reporting use?
reasoning: Committer dates are author-machine claims (clock skew, rebases preserving author dates, amended times). Topology (parent-child edges) is the only authoritative sequence. Reports must order by topo/date hybrid (git log --date-order/--topo-order) and treat timestamps as approximate metadata, especially across forks/timezones.
answer: Unreliability sources: (1) author vs committer dates distinct (a commit authored last year, rebased yesterday carries BOTH: naive parsers often read author date and misplace it in 'recent activity' reports); (2) skew: contributor machines with wrong clocks produce future/past timestamps skewing sort-by-date; (3) rebase/cherry-pick produce new SHAs whose committer date is 'now' while content+author date is old (the classic 'old commit appears new'); (4) merges interleave parallel branches: there IS no total chronological truth for concurrent work regardless of timestamps. Correct reporting semantics: (1) topology-first: --topo-order (children never precede parents) for anything dependency/causality-flavored ('what changes did release X contain': use tag-differing rev-lists, not dates: git log A..B is THE definition of 'in B not A'); (2) dates only as display metadata with timezone + source labeled (committer date for 'when integrated', author date for 'when written': the distinction itself answers many audit questions: backports show old author/new committer); (3) for 'what happened in week W' use first-parent + committer-date windows on the integration branch (approximation disclosed); avoid author-date windows for compliance material. Teach the audit consumer: a report claiming order from timestamps alone is fabrication-grade. Conclusion: ordering = graph topology; dates are authored metadata with skew classes: reports must pick topo/rev-list semantics and label which date flavor they display.

instruction: Team uses git worktree for parallel branches; a dev deleted a worktree directory with rm -rf instead of git worktree remove. Now branch hotfix/x can't be checked out ('already used by worktree') and .git/worktrees metadata is stale. Explain the administrative residue model and the repair commands plus the workflow lesson.
reasoning: Worktrees register administrative state inside the main .git dir. Filesystem deletion leaves registrations pointing at ghosts, blocking ref checkouts. Repair. Git worktree prune (after confirming work is disposable) or repair the registration. Lesson. Lifecycle ops go through git commands so metadata stays consistent.
answer: Residue model: creating a worktree writes .git/worktrees/<name>/ with HEAD/commondir metadata plus a lock on that worktree's checked-out branch; rm -rf removes the files only: the registration survives, so git enforces 'branch in use' (a protection feature working as designed against phantom state). Additional residue: the worktree's own index and any uncommitted changes are truly gone with the directory (fs deletion is not recoverable via git: confirm nothing valuable lived there first: ask the dev, check their editor backups, then proceed). Repair: (1) confirm the work is gone/unnecessary; (2) git worktree list (shows stale path), git worktree prune to drop registrations whose directories vanished (prune respects locks: --expire now if needed); (3) verify: git worktree list clean, branch checkable; alternates: if the directory was MOVED instead of deleted, git worktree move/repair relinks instead of pruning; (4) repeat offender-proofing: document 'delete = git worktree remove <path>' (which also refuses dirty trees unless --force: a safety your rm bypassed) in the team git cheatsheet; wrapper alias optional. Conclusion: worktrees are metadata-managed views: delete via git worktree remove/prune so registrations die with directories, and treat rm -rf of registered state as an administrative-inconsistency event needing prune cleanup.

instruction: Pull requests from a FORK arrive with commits whose author email belongs to 'github-actions[bot]' but content is a feature; the fork owner copied commits from an internal mirror to contribute back. Questions arise: do bot-authored copied commits break CLA/DCO sign-off and attribution, and how should upstream handle provenance-clean contribution?
reasoning: Copy-commits transport changes without original authorship/DCO context. License sign-offs and attribution attach to arbitrary identities, undermining the legal chain the DCO exists to create. Uptream should request original-branch PRs or cherry-picked commits with preserved authors and added sign-offs.
answer: Chain-of-custody problem: DCO's Signed-off-by asserts the CONTRIBUTOR's right to submit under license: a copy bearing 'github-actions[bot]' as author means (a) real authorship erased (copyright attribution wrong: IP hygiene issue), (b) any sign-off line present belonged to a different submission context (internal mirror's bot): upstream cannot treat it as the human's declaration, (c) CLA bots evaluating the PR check the fork owner's identity while code comes from N real authors none of whom consented in this channel. Clean-contribution patterns: (1) contribute from the ORIGINAL branches (internal contributors open PRs directly from feature branches to upstream fork-less or via organization forks): authorship and existing sign-offs ride along; (2) if copying is unavoidable (mirror isolation), re-create provenance: cherry-pick preserving --author info (cherry-pick keeps Author, new Committer) + append 'Signed-off-by' by the ORIGINAL authors (obtainable via the internal repo's sign-offs: they did sign internally) and the submitting human adds their own sign-off attesting transport; document this in PR body; (3) policy: reject bot-authored bulk copies absent per-commit author restoration (MAINTAINERS file entry: provenance rules); (4) tooling: require DCO + verify trailer authors match commit authors (dco-check apps support flags). Conclusion: copied commits sever the legal/attribution chain DCO exists to maintain: preserve authors on transport and demand human sign-offs per change, or route contributions through original branches.

instruction: git bisect run ./test.sh aborts midway: some commits fail to BUILD (broken build at those revisions), test.sh exits 125 randomly because the build doesn't produce the binary. The team reverts to manual bisect with 'skip' and loses days. What's the bisect-protocol design for repos where not every commit builds, including untestable-commit handling?
reasoning: Bisect assumes testability at each step. Real repos interleave build-broken commits. Protocol. Exit 125 ONLY for provable-untestable (build failure), never for product failures. Make builds hermetic per checkout (isolated node_modules/build dirs). Pre-verify the script at endpoints. Consider --first-parent to reduce broken-tree density.
answer: Protocol design: (1) script contract: exit 0 = good, 1-124 = bad, 125 = skip: UNTESTABLE RESERVED for missing artifacts only: write the script to distinguish (build failure → 125; binary exists but test fails → 1): the 'random 125' happens when build artifacts from the PREVIOUS bisect step leak (stale dist/ from an adjacent commit masking breakage: clean between steps or hash-verify the artifact matches the checkout); (2) hermetic steps: each iteration: clean tree state (skip node_modules reinstall via cached store but wipe build outputs), fail fast on any build error before tests; document time budget per step; (3) skip clustering: when too many consecutive 125s appear, bisect's skip wanders: help it: narrow range (--first-parent skips feature-branch interiors where broken commits concentrate, testing merge states on main only: denser testability), or pick an alternate test approach (build-tolerant test: unit-level instead of binary-run for the offending era); (4) post-analysis: bisect run with logging (log each tested SHA): after finding the boundary, re-verify by hand: the found commit's parent passes, commit fails, repeat twice: automation without verification has bitten teams (a flaky test.sh marking false-bad shifts boundaries silently: make the test deterministic first: statistical flakiness needs repeated runs per step inside script or manual mode); (5) chronic prevention: CI must keep every main commit buildable (that's what bisect eats): the underlying hygiene. Conclusion: reserve 125 for true untestability with hermetic-per-step builds, prefer first-parent topology, log everything, and re-verify boundaries manually.

instruction: A new hire git pulls, runs tests: 200 failures mention missing table 'audit_events'. Migration exists on a feature branch merged via squash, but on main the migration file number COLLIDES with another merged branch's migration (both teams took '0047'). DBs apply only one. How do migration-number collisions sneak through git-level merges, and what repo-level guards apply?
reasoning: Sequential migration filenames collide across parallel branches. Git merges content cleanly (different 0047_* names), leaving the migration tool to apply one by ledger. Guards. CI generating fresh migrations only on main-order, uniqueness checks across dirs, and rebase-before-merge policies for migration PRs.
answer: Sneak path: branch A creates 0047_add_x.sql, branch B creates 0047_add_y.sql in parallel: git sees distinct filenames with disjoint content: merge succeeds, both files land; the migration runner's ledger keys on the VERSION component (0047): whichever runs first claims the number; the second is skipped or errors depending on tool strictness (your new hire's DB applied the loser: missing audit_events since the winner occupied 0047): environment-dependent schema drift from a clean git merge. Guard set: (1) uniqueness lint in CI: script checks no duplicate version prefixes across the migrations dir (post-merge simulation: run on PR), fails loud: minimum viable guard; (2) merge-time rebasing policy: migrations must regenerate against latest main before merge (bot command /rebase-migrations renumbers the branch's migration to a free head): many frameworks (rails/django docs) institutionalize this; (3) tool migration to collision-proof schemes: long-form names (timestamped at generation plus author) or hash-based ordering (some tools apply-by-ledger-id not number): if the framework allows, switch; (4) repair path for THIS instance: two deployed worlds exist: some DBs applied A, some B: converge via a NEW migration that applies the loser's content idempotently (IF NOT EXISTS), and reconcile ledgers per tool's 'mark as applied' mechanism on environments that have it: then delete or keep per documentation with a README beside the collision recounting the event; (5) awareness: any 'works locally, fails fresh clone' with migrations involved → suspect version conflicts FIRST. Conclusion: parallel sequential IDs are merge-blind: add CI uniqueness checks + rebase-regenerate policy, converge existing splits via forward idempotent migrations with ledger reconciliation.

instruction: The repo's main branch history is LINEAR (rebase-only merges per policy), yet blame reveals features landing out of PR order judgded by issue numbers; a release-notes generator assuming PR-order landed items got sequencing wrong. What does linear-history + landing-order actually mean, and how should release tooling map issues to history positions?
reasoning: Linear history preserves A sequence of integration events, not the sequence of PR numbers nor author dates. Landing order = merge/rebase completion time, which queue systems reorder. Release tooling must anchor on merge-queue events or landed-commit timestamps per PR, not issue/PR ordinals.
answer: Meaning precisely: linear main = each PR's commits replayed on top of the previous landed state: position in history says 'integration happened after all below it': that's the ONLY ordering history legitimately encodes. PR-42 landing before PR-40 despite numbers means queue timing (approvals/CI durations) reordered them: normal; issue numbers say nothing about landing. Tooling corrections: (1) source sequence from the merge event stream: git rev-list --first-parent main gives landed commits in landing order (with squash, each first-parent commit IS a PR): generate notes by walking first-parent between release tags, mapping each to its PR via trailer/'(#N)' in title or forge API by SHA: (2) never sort by PR number or created_at: order per landing sequence (or group by category explicitly if notes should be topical: then say 'grouped by area' and stop implying chronology); (3) merge-queue users: the queue's OWN event log (platform API) is even more precise for 'when the decision to land happened' vs 'when commit objects finalized': pick git-landed order as the canonical one (it matches deployed content exactly: SR-answerability: 'was fix in build N?' = is SHA ancestor of that release tag); (4) backfill check: verify each mapped SHA-to-PR before publishing notes (API misses happen with cross-fork PRs). Conclusion: in linear histories, integration order is rev-list order: release notes must derive sequence and inclusion from first-parent traversal and SHA-to-PR mapping, never PR/issue ordinals.

instruction: A repo has 15MB of committed test fixture binaries added before LFS was adopted; new clones crawl. Team debates: migrate history to LFS vs leave it. What does the size-forever property of git history imply for each option, and what decision inputs settle it?
reasoning: Committed blobs live in history forever. Deleting them from HEAD shrinks no clone. History rewrite migrates them at the cost of rewriting every SHA (coordination chaos, broken forks/PRs/CI caches). Decide from clone pain metrics, churn rate of binaries, SHA-stability dependencies, and team coordination windows.
answer: Implications per option: (1) leave as-is: current 15MB remains in every clone forever; if binaries are frozen (fixtures rarely edited), growth stops: pain is a one-time clone cost (shallow or partial clones mitigate: --filter=blob:none plus filter on those extensions gives near-full benefit WITHOUT rewrite); CI caches absorb most repeated cost: often the right call for stable fixture sets; (2) migrate history to LFS (git lfs migrate import --include): every affected commit rewritten (all descendant SHAs change): existing open PRs/forks desync (must rebase), CI caches busted, signed commits invalidated, mirrored repos need force-re-syncing: real coordination cost, pays off when binaries churn (every edit adds full blob copies forever: growth compounding) or clone time blocks onboarding/CI minutes meaningfully. Decision inputs: measure (clone wall-time in target environments, monthly repo growth curve from fixture edits: git rev-list --objects --all | sizes), churn history of the fixture dir (edits/year), SHA-stability consumers (signed releases, compliance archives, cited SHAs in docs/issues rewrite breaks those), and a coordination window (freeze period available?). Middle path shipped most often: LFS for NEW binaries + lazy-clone guidance, history untouched. If rewrite wins: announce freeze, run migrate import with --include-ref all refs, force-push, everyone re-clones, audit external references. Conclusion: history-size is append-forever: migrating buys future growth control at rewrite chaos; frozen binaries favor mitigations (partial clone) over surgery.

instruction: Pre-push hooks pass locally; remote rejects the push: 'protected branch, PR required'. The dev's local branch was created WEEKS ago named 'main' but tracking origin/main... they actually committed 6 commits directly onto local main. What's the rescue choreography that preserves work without any force-push or history damage?
reasoning: Commits on the wrong local branch aren't lost work. Rescue = branch the tip into a feature branch, then reset local main to the true upstream (fetch first, reset --hard origin/main is SAFE here because the work is anchored elsewhere), open the PR. No remote history is touched at any point.
answer: Choreography: (1) anchor the work FIRST: git branch feature/my-work (creates the branch at current tip holding all 6 commits: now nothing can be lost regardless of what follows: also note the tip SHA on paper/reflog as cheap insurance); (2) sync truth: git fetch origin: update the remote-tracking ref (their local origin/main may be equally stale); (3) rebase for currency (recommended): git switch feature/my-work && git rebase origin/main: their 6 commits replay onto fresh main (resolving conflicts against two weeks of drift NOW, locally, before reviewers see it); (4) repair local main: git switch main && git reset --hard origin/main: destructive flags are fine here because commits are anchored on the feature branch: result: local main pristine, feature branch contains the work, nothing force-pushed anywhere; (5) push the feature branch (normal, permitted), open PR; (6) habit-layer afterwards: an unprotected LOCAL main is the trap: suggest 'git config branch.autoSetupRebase' or a pre-commit hook refusing direct commits on main (client-side guard: server protected branch already did its job for the remote half), plus visual indicators (prompt shows branch). Conclusion: mis-branched work is 100% recoverable by branch-then-reset with upstream refresh: anchor first, rebase to drift, reset the misused local line, push normally: zero history damage required.

instruction: Release tooling generates release/* branches with signed commits from CI, but a recent SOX-style audit requires 'human approver unambiguously bound to release commit'. Currently signatures are CI-bot keys. What does binding accountability into git objects require, and how do you design the attestation without making humans bottlenecks for routine builds?
reasoning: Signatures bind to keys, and keys sit with holders. CI-bot signing authenticates the PIPELINE, not a human decision. Accountability design. Human-verified approval events merged into the object chain (signed tag by release captain referencing CI attestation, or sigstore identity-bound signing via OIDC to the approver), applied at release boundaries only.
answer: Requirement reading: the audit needs provable 'this human authorized THIS content': (a) bot keys in CI cannot express it (any pipeline run signs anything it builds), (b) author/committer text fields are self-asserted (not binding), (c) platform 'PR approvals' live outside git (forge export needed for auditors, fragile evidence). Design: (1) human-signed release TAG (annotated, GPG/sigstore): the release captain runs a script that fetches the release branch head, prints its CI attestation bundle (build provenance, test attestation links), and signs the tag naming bot+run-id: object chain: signed tag → exact commit (bot-signed for pipeline integrity) → CI attestations: 'human bound' achieved at release granularity, zero routine-friction (only releases need captain sign-off: key on hardware token or sigstore with identity OIDC binding their SSO account: no shared keyring); (2) alternative: sigstore/gitsign-style OIDC signing where the CI approval ACTION itself (approved environment gate) mints a signature bound to the approver's identity via short-lived certs: fully automated yet human-attributed: depends on your forge+sigstore maturity; (3) record-keeping: signatures + Fulcio/Rekor transparency log references exported into the compliance evidence store per release. Scope explicitly: routine CI builds keep bot signatures (pipeline integrity), release objects carry human attestation: auditors get the binding at the boundary where meaningful. Conclusion: bind humans by signing release-scoped objects (tags or approval-attestations via OIDC-bound keys), chaining over bot-signed commits, so accountability lands at human pace only where audits require it.

instruction: After a botched merge, history on main contains a revert of the merge of branch-x immediately followed by 'Merge branch x (attempt 2)'. Months later, fixes from branch x appear MISSING on main even though attempt-2 shows in history. What's the revert-of-merge trap, and how do you diagnose + verify the missing content before re-merging anything?
reasoning: Reverting a merge reverses its CONTENT but keeps its ANCESTRY. Git now treats x's commits as merged. So re-merging x brings nothing new. Content stays reverted. Diagnose with ancestry+content comparison. The fix is reverting the REVERT (or recreating branch commits), then carefully re-merging.
answer: Trap mechanics: merge M brought x's commits into ancestry; revert-of-M undid every line change but left x's commits ancestors of main; attempt-2 merge therefore found 'nothing new' (all x commits already ancestors) and introduced zero content: history LOOKS integrated, content says otherwise: exactly why fixes 'show in history' yet are missing at HEAD. Diagnosis: (1) content truth: git diff main...x (or a fresh branch from x's tip) shows all the missing changes: non-empty diff = missed content despite ancestry; (2) ancestry truth: git merge-base --is-ancestor <x-tip> main = true: confirms the trap precisely; (3) blame sampling: files in question blame to the revert commit lines (evidence the reversal is what's live). Cure: (1) restore content by REVERTING THE REVERT (git revert <revert-of-merge-sha>): simplest, keeps ancestry honest; then future merges of x-family branches behave (new commits on x merge normally); (2) if the want is a REDONE merge (x needed more fixes): revert-the-revert first, then merge x normally with its new commits; (3) alternative when revert is impractical (conflicted context evolved): re-create x's changes as fresh commits (rebase x onto main producing NEW SHAs: ancestry resets because SHAs differ) and merge that: heavier, rewrites x: coordinate owners; (4) verify post-cure: diff main vs expected content on the previously-missing files (empty = restored), run integration tests of the feature; write the incident note because revert-of-merge scars confuse every future archaeologist. Conclusion: ancestry is not content after merge-reverts: diagnose with is-ancestor + diff, cure by reverting the revert (or fresh-SHA rebase), verify content-level restoration.

instruction: An intern ran git commit --amend on a commit that was ALREADY in a reviewed PR, then force-pushed casually; review approvals were dismissed by the platform and comment threads orphaned from their code lines. Team wants rules. What are the amend/force-push semantics on reviewed branches, and what collaborative rewrite rules balance cleanliness with review integrity?
reasoning: Amend rewrites the tip SHA. On reviewed branches that severs comment anchoring and resets review state. Sometimes desired (addressing final nits), sometimes destructive (mid-review rewrites of deeper history). Rules. Amend only the latest commit before review-approval, no rebase mid-review, squash via merge-time squash, and force-push-with-lease + announcement when rewriting anything shared.
answer: Semantics: amend creates a NEW SHA replacing the tip: any platform keying on SHAs (review approvals bound to head OID on GitHub: 'dismiss stale approvals' setting) invalidates; inline comments anchor to positions in specific SHAs: rewritten history orphans them into 'outdated' folds; force-push events also erase the easy before/after per-iteration diff reviewers use ('show changes since last review' becomes full re-review). Collaborative rules that work: (1) during active review iteration: regular commits only ('fixup review comments' commits welcome): reviewers track deltas cheaply; cleanliness is restored at merge time via squash-merge (the platform does it: no local heroics needed); (2) amend/force-push acceptable when: PR unopened (draft), or after EXPLICIT maintainer ask ('squash these then I'll approve'), or before any review began; announce in-thread when done so watchers re-fetch (and always --force-with-lease: refuses to clobber someone else's push: mutual protection on shared feature branches); (3) deeper history surgery mid-review (interactive rebase back 15 commits) is what orphaned those threads: ban by norm unless agreed; (4) institutional switches: enable 'dismiss stale approvals' [already bit them] + required linear/squash merge so the cleanup-not-amend path is the default; publish the rule table in CONTRIBUTING with the why (comment anchoring), or rules read as cargo-cult. Conclusion: amend on reviewed work invalidates review state and anchors: iterate plainly, squash at merge, rewrite only with lease-push + communication.

instruction: Two repos claim one canonical library: org/utils (active, versioned, published) and a FORK org-legacy/utils-old diverged 3 years ago, still referenced as git+ssh dependency by two services with '#4.2' branch pins. Upstream CVE patch was applied to org/utils 5.x; the fork's 4.x line never got it. What fork-pinning liability map do you build, and what remediation ladder applies?
reasoning: Git-URL dependencies bypass registry/versioning discipline. They pin SHA/branch states that security tooling and dependents' update flows ignore. Map consumers+pin semantics first, then ladder. Patch the fork line (if it must live short-term), migrate consumers to the canonical line, finally retire the fork with import-blocking guards.
answer: Liability map per consumer: (1) pin semantics: 'git+ssh://...utils-old#4.2': does '#4.2' name a branch (FLOATING: installs follow stealth changes: supply-chain and drift risk multiples) or a tag/commit (pinned but frozen: never sees fixes): inspect package-lock/resolved entries to know which reality each service lives; (2) code delta: how far is 4.x-fork from canonical 5.x (changelog + API surface used by those services: usage inventory via grep of import sites and called functions: maybe 5 functions: maybe 50); (3) vulnerability reachability: the CVE's vulnerable function: used via the fork in those services? (npm ls won't attribute CVEs to git-deps normally: scanners skip them: manual mapping required: write it down in the risk register so the knowledge persists). Remediation ladder: (1) immediate: if reachable: apply the CVE patch onto the fork's 4.2 line (backport: fork owner signs off: tag 4.2.1-fork) so exposure closes regardless of migration pace; freeze branch pins to exact SHAs meanwhile (kill the floating); (2) migrate: port each service's imports to org/utils (current version), with compat shim if APIs shifted (adapter exposing 4.x signatures over 5.x implementation: reduces port risk per service), one service at a time with their maintainers owning merge+release; (3) retire: when zero consumers (verify via code search across the org + dependency-tree crawls in CI inventory), ARCHIVE the fork (read-only) with README redirect; add dependency-review CI rule forbidding git+ssh deps (registry-only policy with exceptions list) to stop regrowth. Conclusion: git-pinned forks are invisible to security machinery: inventory pins/reachability, backport-patch the fork, migrate behind shims, then archive + policy-block.

instruction: apps/web uses the shared package @org/ui; your fix in packages/ui doesn't appear when web runs. Both live in the same monorepo. What are the candidate broken links between source edit and consuming app?
reasoning: Dependency graph is not execution graph. The app may consume a built artifact of the package (stale dist), a published registry version instead of the workspace copy, or a cache layer (bundler/turbo) keyed without the new inputs. Enumerate resolution and build-order evidence before editing more code.
answer: Candidate links in order: (1) resolution mode: does apps/web package.json depend on ui via workspace protocol (workspace:* / file:../) or a pinned published version (1.4.2)? Registry pins ignore your local edits entirely; check node_modules/@org/ui: is it a symlink into packages/ui (pnpm/yarn workspaces style) or a copied/installed artifact? (2) built-output staleness: if apps resolve dist/ (package.json main/exports point to dist), editing src changes nothing until the ui package's build runs (watch mode dead / build not in dependency chain for dev: turbo run dev --filter=web may not build deps first: check dependsOn); (3) cache: turbo/vite caches keyed without ui src inputs serve pre-change bundles (clear and retry to confirm); (4) multiple copies (hoisting or second nested node_modules) shadowing the intended one (npm ls @org/ui to enumerate). Diagnosis command: import the built artifact and inspect for your edit; fix the specific broken link (workspace protocol, run-dependency wiring, cache key inputs, or dedupe). Conclusion: trace edit → resolution → build input → cache: the symptom lives at exactly one broken link.

instruction: pnpm workspace: apps/api leaks process-env secrets into a shared package's error messages, which apps/web (public SPA) also bundles. Where does package-boundary reasoning replace codebase-wide reasoning for data sensitivity?
reasoning: Monorepos create the illusion of one codebase, but publish/bundle boundaries are real security perimeters. Code in shared packages fans out to every consumer, including ones with opposite trust domains (public client bundles). Sensitivity analysis must track consumer topology, not repo proximity.
answer: Boundary reasoning: (1) map exposure by consumer: a shared packages/core util imported by api (Node, secret-bearing env) and web (browser bundle) means anything it can READ may ship to browsers; env access inside shared code is the hazard: Node process.env in web builds may be statically inlined by bundlers at build time (DefinePlugin/replacement of process.env.X), freezing secrets into public artifacts; (2) grep the shared package for env reads and process references; treat each as a public-API leak vector until proven server-restricted; (3) restructure: inject config into shared packages (constructor params/ factories) from the consuming app, keeping env reads at app edges only (apps/*/config.ts); shared packages declare what they need as parameters: the boundary becomes explicit and testable; (4) enforce: lint rules banning process.env outside apps/*/config (eslint no-restricted-globals per package), plus CI test that builds the web bundle and greps the artifact for secret-shaped patterns; (5) verify current bundle NOW for leaked values (grep dist assets for known secret values/patterns): if found, rotate those secrets. Conclusion: in monorepos, trust domains are per-consumer: keep environment access at app edges and make shared packages config-injected pure code.

instruction: A rename of packages/logger to packages/observability passed CI (green builds) but broke production deploy for one service: its Dockerfile copies packages/logger (hardcoded path) which no longer exists. What does selective build/test coverage hide in monorepo refactors?
reasoning: TypeScript/bundler references are only some of the references to a path. Dockerfiles, CI YAML, deploy scripts, tsconfig paths, CODEOWNERS, docs, and tooling configs reference directories textually. Affected-graph CI compiles the graph but doesn't grep the repo-text universe for the old string.
answer: Hidden-reference classes: (1) infra text: Dockerfile COPY paths, .dockerignore, CI workflow paths-filters and cache key globs, deploy manifests (k8s volume paths), release tooling (changesets config base), nx/turbo project globs and named inputs; (2) repo config: tsconfig references/paths (they'd fail builds: usually caught), eslint override globs, jest projects, CODEOWNERS (review routing silently dies: no error, just no owners); (3) external: README links (broken docs), Grafana dashboards filtering by path label, incident runbooks. Sweep method for renames: before merging, rg the OLD STRING across the whole repo minus node_modules (--hidden to catch CI), then classify each hit: must-update (infra) vs cosmetic (docs) vs historical (CHANGELOG entries: leave); then run the deployment path for affected services (at least docker build of each consumer image), not just typecheck/tests: CI 'green' meant graph-green, deploy was unexercised. Institutional: renames get a checklist attached (paths-filters, docker, deploy, dashboards); monorepos often add integration 'repo-lint' CI that validates config cross-references. Conclusion: code compiles prove graph references, not textual references: sweep the string, classify hits, and exercise deploy surfaces before landing renames.

instruction: Two apps in the monorepo need different major versions of React; the shared packages/components library declares react as a regular dependency. What failure shape does this force, and what dependency-declaration pattern fits shared UI libraries?
reasoning: A regular dependency on React makes the library drag ONE concrete copy, conflicting with differing app-level versions. Duplicate React copies (hooks break, context splits) or blocked upgrades. Shared UI code must declare react as peerDependency (with devDependency for its own tests), letting each app supply its own.
answer: Failure shape: package manager installs components' react under its own node_modules path while the app hoists another: two React instances in one bundle: useState errors ('Invalid hook call'), contexts from one copy unseeable by the other (theme/providers vanish), and duplicated kilobytes; alternatively pnpm strictness refuses coexistence and blocks install: either apps get pinned to the library's choice (upgrade hostage) or installs break. Pattern: in packages/components: peerDependencies: {react: '>=17 || >=18'} documents the contract; devDependencies pin a version for the library's own tests/storybook; optionally peerDependenciesMeta for optional peers. Bundlers then resolve react from the consuming app only: one copy per app. Watchouts: (1) publish flow must not rewrite peers incorrectly (changesets handles ranges); (2) library code must avoid APIs beyond the declared peer range (runtime feature-detection or bump the floor); (3) shared non-React deps (lodash) may stay regular deps: dedupe managed per app; (4) tests should run against BOTH React majors (matrix) since the library claims both. Conclusion: shared component libs declare framework peers, apps own concrete versions: never ship react as a regular dep from reusable packages.

instruction: nx affected --target=test returns 'no projects affected' after your change to libs/shared/types even though three apps import it. CI celebrates green fast. What configuration layers determine affected-graph accuracy, and how do you audit a false-negative?
reasoning: Affected detection composes. Base SHA computation, dependency graph construction (implicit vs explicit imports), and target input definitions. False negatives come from shallow CI checkouts (bad merge-base), type-only imports not parsed, or projects excluded from the graph. Audit each layer with nx graph introspection.
answer: Audit the three layers: (1) base/head computation: CI uses origin/main~1 vs correct merge-base; shallow clones (fetch-depth 1) invent boundaries: nx report shows computed SHAs: compare against git merge-base origin/main HEAD; wrong base = arbitrary affected sets, including empty; (2) graph completeness: nx graph (or print-affected --select=graph) between libs/shared/types and the apps: if edges are absent: causes: imports via path aliases not mapped in tsconfig that nx parses, lazy dynamic imports (string ones), or project.json not registered (implicitDependencies missing for non-import relationships like i18n json consumers): edges must exist for affected to propagate; add explicit project references or nx project graph plugins; type-only imports ARE parsed normally, but path-mapping misalignment hides them; (3) target inputs: test target's inputs exclude {projectRoot}/**? then type changes don't invalidate: check nx.json targetDefaults/namedInputs include source of dependencies (^prefix). Fix whichever layer lied, then add a CI canary: a deliberately-touched shared lib PR must produce non-empty affected (periodic graph-health test). Conclusion: affected accuracy = correct base × complete graph × honest inputs: audit each before trusting 'no projects affected'.

instruction: A developer moves services/auth from packages/auth to apps/auth (promotion from library to service). Imports updated, tests pass. Six weeks later a shared .github/workflows/reusable.yml referencing packages/auth triggers deploys incorrectly. What promotion-checklist items do location changes demand beyond imports?
reasoning: Import updates cover the code graph. Location changes also rewrite identity in every textual config and automation dimension. CI globs, deploy selectors, CODEOWNERS, release/changeset scopes, package name semantics, and boundary rule category (library rules no longer apply). Promotion needs a textual sweep plus automation rerouting.
answer: Checklist for package→app (or reverse): (1) identity/config: package.json name change semantics (@org/auth becoming an app: should it remain publishable? strip publishConfig/version: stop accidental publishes); private: true for apps; (2) workspace globs: ensure the new path is still matched by pnpm-workspace/nx project inclusions (a silently unregistered project breaks CI discovery without errors: verify it appears in project lists); (3) automation text: CI path filters, reusable workflow callers (your failure), deploy selectors (--filter), CODEOWNERS (owner routing reroutes silently otherwise), dependabot configs keyed by directory; (4) boundary rules: nx module-boundaries tags (library constraints like 'cannot depend on apps' flip sense: eslint boundaries config per tag must be updated); (5) caches/artifacts: turbo outputs paths, Dockerfile context assumptions, PR-labeler path maps; (6) communication: teammates' in-flight branches reference old paths (merge churn: announce during low-churn window). Sweep pattern: rg 'packages/auth' everywhere pre-merge and disposition each hit; the bug you found is the pattern: an unchecked automation string grenading six weeks later. Conclusion: location changes = graph updates + textual-identity updates + boundary reclassification; sweep the old string across all config kinds.

instruction: Both apps/web and apps/admin fetch via a shared lib/api-client. A backend breaking change ships; you update lib/api-client; web deploys immediately, admin redeploys only next sprint (it pins its builds weekly). Users of admin see broken UI. What does versioned-consumption of shared code imply for deploy sequencing in monorepos?
reasoning: Sharing code doesn't synchronize deployments. Each app re-bundles shared libs at its own deploy time. So library fixes land staggered. Breaking-change management must version the CONTRACT (API), not just the client, and deploy consumers within the compatibility window the contract guarantees.
answer: Sequencing reality: monorepo libs build into each app's artifact: 'the fix is merged' is not 'the fix is live everywhere'; artifact time-to-live per consumer governs exposure. Discipline layers: (1) contract-first thinking: the backend breaking change needed compatibility staging: deploy backend supporting BOTH shapes (accept old field, emit both) for one window; clients migrate at leisure; contract drops old shape only after telemetry shows consumers current (version headers per app reveal laggards: instrument X-Client-Version on api-client requests, dashboard by app: this is how you KNOW admin is stale instead of tentatively remembering); (2) when a truly atomic change is unavoidable, deploy orchestration must couple: one pipeline that builds+deploys ALL consumers of changed libs (nxAffected --target=deploy) regardless of team calendar: fleet-wide cadence for atomicity; (3) async tolerance for admin-style apps: if staging lag is organizational reality (weekly releases), enforce that lag in the contract window (window > slowest consumer cadence + margin); (4) incident traceability: tag artifacts with lib/api-client version (sourcemaps/buildinfo) so error reports answer 'which client shipped this stack'. Immediate fix: redeploy admin (unblock), then implement client-version telemetry + compat-window rule. Conclusion: shared code multiplies artifact lag per consumer: manage the API contract window to exceed the slowest consumer, or couple deployments onto one affected-driven pipeline.

instruction: circleci config runs ALL tests on every PR; monorepo grows, PR latency hits 70 minutes. A migration to affected-based CI is proposed. What does the graph model trade away for speed, and what hybrid keeps correctness while gaining most of the win?
reasoning: Affected-scoping trades completeness for relevance. Failures outside the computed graph (cross-package integration bugs, infra changes, graph blind spots) defer to main-branch discovery. Hybrid. Affected per-PR + scheduled full runs + global-input change detection that force-runs everything.
answer: Trade-offs to name: (1) semantic conflicts: A renames a column, B adds a query; both PRs affected-scope-pass independently; merge of both breaks main (no single PR was 'failing'): mitigation: merge queue with affected-scope on the QUEUE's combined state (or full tests on main post-merge as net); (2) graph blind spots: textual coupling (i18n keys, env var names, docker paths) escapes import graphs: declare implicitDependencies / global inputs for those files so edits blow scope up deliberately; (3) flake surface reduction is a bonus (70min suites invite green-check trust erosion). Hybrid design: (a) PRs: affected with strict base computation (merge-base, not HEAD~1) + always-run set (lint typecheck across repo is cheap: keep global; install/lockfile/pipeline-file changes force FULL suite via affected 'all' trigger patterns: config globs like .github/**, package-lock.json map to everything); (b) main: full suite per merge or timeboxed (every N merges/2h) with failure paging: catches semantic conflicts within the window; (c) nightly: full + slow suites (e2e matrix) + cache-prime; (d) observability: track affected-hitrate and escapes-per-week: tune inputs when escapes cluster. Result: PR latency ~10-15min typical, correctness bounded by main-window detection. Conclusion: scope per-PR, complete on main, force-full on global inputs, and measure escapes to tune the graph.

instruction: The monorepo uses changesets for publishing; a PR adds a feature to packages/form but forgets the .changeset file. The release cut goes out with the code merged but no version bump: consumers never see the feature via npm. What does intent-declaration versioning require beyond 'tests passed'?
reasoning: Changesets move version bumps from human memory to PR artifacts. Forgetting the file merges intent silently. Release tooling has no signal. Guard. CI checks requiring changesets on package-touching PRs (or explicit no-release labels), because merged code without declaration is unpublished code.
answer: Requirement: in intent-declaration versioning (changesets), the unit of release is: code + changeset describing semver impact: CI green proves code validity, not release-readiness: release PRs (changesets version) compute bumps ONLY from pending .changeset files, so your feature published nothing: packages/form stayed 1.2.0 with new code in repo. Guards: (1) CI changeset-check (changesets/action includes status check; or custom script): fail PR if files under publishable packages changed and no .changeset added: with escape hatch label 'skip-changeset' for docs/tests-only edits (label must be deliberate); (2) reviewer norm: reviewbots comment the computed bump preview ('this PR will release form@minor') so humans see nothing-to-release cases; (3) recover here: add the missing changeset as a new PR ('chore: add missing changeset for #123'), let the next release cut pick it up: the feature then publishes; confirm no consumer pinned-exact versions that block uptake; (4) for coopting sloppiness long-term: some teams generate default changesets via commit-convention tooling (semantic-release style) instead: choose ONE declaration model: mixed models leak releases through the seam between them. Conclusion: declaration-based releases need declaration-checks in CI: code merge is necessary-not-sufficient, and recovery is a follow-up changeset PR.

instruction: A junior asks: 'Why does packages/tsconfig.base.json exist AND every package re-declare the same compilerOptions?' Inspection shows 60 packages, most overriding identically, some overriding slightly differently with no comment. What base-vs-override configuration economics apply here?
reasoning: Base configs amortize policy. Copy-pasted overrides freeze yesterday's default and hide intentional divergence among accidental drift. Economics. Reduce override surface aggressively (extends with true deltas only), comment the remaining deliberate divergences, and robot-check drift to stop re-fragmentation.
answer: Economics: (1) each copy-pasted compilerOptions block is a freeze-frame of the base at copy time: base improvements (new strict flags, lib updates) never propagate: 60 packages age at 60 speeds; the team then believes standards exist that reality abandoned; (2) undifferentiated deltas: some overrides exist for real reasons (DOM lib in web packages, decorators in the DI server, isolatedModules for the vite package): without comments, deliberate and accidental divergences are indistinguishable: nobody dares clean. Program: (1) inventory diffs mechanically (script each tsconfig vs base: classify into 'identical to base' (delete override, extends only), 'delta X cluster' (same delta in N packages: promote to a variant base like tsconfig.node.json/tsconfig.dom.json), and 'unique deltas' (require comment justification or removal)); (2) codify: each surviving override gains a one-line comment 'why'; add renovate/lint check proposing extends-adoption in PRs when new configs appear; (3) behavioral verification per consolidated package before merge (typecheck outputs identical: capture pre-change diagnostics as baseline: error count and codes must match exactly); run in small batches (5-10 packages/PR) to keep review tractable. Conclusion: base-plus-labeled-delta beats base-plus-copies: cluster common deltas into variant bases, comment survivors, and gate against re-drift.

instruction: You must add a lint rule forbidding server-only imports (fs, db clients) in client-bundled packages. The monorepo has 6 apps, 40 packages, two module-boundary conventions (nx tags on some, folder naming on others). Where does boundary enforcement live so it survives convention pluralism?
reasoning: Enforcement must attach to facts every package shares (dependency direction, build outputs) rather than optional conventions. Declare zones (client/server/shared) per package manifest, lint import statements by zone rules, and ratchet violations instead of big-bang, since conventions vary across generations of code.
