instruction: A nightly billing job failed on Feb 29 with 'invalid date: Feb 30' generating invoices for billing period +1 month from Jan 30. Naive date math: new Date(y, m+1, 30). Which calendar-arithmetic classes must date code handle, and what's the test matrix?
reasoning: Period arithmetic with fixed day-of-month crashes or drifts at month-length mismatches (29/30/31, February), DST transitions (midnight doesn't exist), and leap years. Libraries with clamp-vs-throw semantics differ. Billing needs explicit period semantics (clamp to month end? error?) rather than runtime defaults.
answer: Classes: (1) month-length clamping: +1 month from Jan 31 (and from Mar 31 → Apr 30, May 31 → Jun 30): libraries clamp (Feb 28/29) or roll over (Mar 2/3: moment:add(1,'month') clamps in modern versions: older code may roll: know YOURS); business semantics: billing cycle '30th monthly' should clamp to month end explicitly (day = Math.min(day, daysIn(nextMonth))) or define 'last day' cycles properly; (2) February leap logic: Feb 29→non-leap years: clamp Feb 28 vs shift Mar 1: contract decision; (3) DST: midnight-targeted jobs on 2024-03-10 02:30 America/New_York (nonexistent local time: libraries resolve differently: forward vs throw): choose UTC execution or validate local-time existence (luxon invalid reasons detect these); (4) year boundaries + week-based periods (Dec→Jan, week 53); (5) timezone preservation: 'a month later' in user's billing timezone vs UTC vs server. Test matrix: unit-test cycle-advance from: Jan 28/29/30/31 (each), Mar 31, May 31, Oct 31; Dec 31 (year roll); Feb 29 input in leap→non-leap; plus 00:30 during DST-forward gap and 01:30 during DST-backward duplicated hour for relevant zones; run the actual scheduler dry-run across a 14-month simulated window asserting all generated dates valid (fuzz the cron by feeding each day: great coverage per effort). Also assert idempotence of re-generated periods. Deployment note: this class demands TZ-pinned environments (TZ=UTC) or explicit zone libraries: never ambient. Conclusion: date code must declare clamp/DST/year semantics explicitly with month-edge and DST-gap matrix tests: never trust default arithmetic across February.

instruction: Import pipeline created 4x duplicates of products after a user clicked 'Import', closed the laptop, reopened, clicked again. The import runs as a background job; starts have no idempotency; the UI disables the button only after clicking. Give the full defense-in-depth design for 'exactly-one effect' for user-triggered jobs.
reasoning: Button disabling is presentation, not protection. Defense layers are. Client request-token, API idempotency window keyed by user+intent, server single-flight lock across job creation, job-level unique constraints (natural keys), and final-write idempotent upserts. Each layer catches what the above misses.
answer: Layered design: (1) client: on click generate idempotency token (uuid) attached to the request; the button disable covers same-tab double-click only: tokens survive closes/retries enabling server dedupe; (2) API: idempotency-key semantics (header): store (key → job id/result) for a window (24h): second call with same key returns the SAME job (safe retry posture: network blips safe); different key same user+file-hash currently running: 409 'import already in progress' (policy decision: allow queueing a second import afterward or reject: pick and document); (3) job creation: single-flight distributed lock per natural scope (user_id+file_checksum: SET NX EX): prevents two racing creations even under parallel requests/submit-spam; grant user-visible state ('import running: started 3m ago') instead of errors; (4) data layer: natural unique constraints (products dedupe key e.g. (tenant, external_sku)) + job writes as upserts (ON CONFLICT UPDATE): even a fully-escaped duplicated job converges data (your 4x = identity columns not enforced: note that upserting fixes identity but also hides double-runs: keep metrics); (5) job runner: at-least-once execution assumed: handlers idempotent by construction (checkpoint progress: resume not restart: partial-rerun-safe: stage counters); (6) observability: import lifecycle events (started/duplicate-suppressed/completed rows in-out) user-visible: converts confusion ('did it run?') into state. Regression pack: double-click test, close-reopen click test, retry-storm test: each expects exactly one job and one row-set: in CI. Conclusion: exactly-one effect = request tokens + idempotency ledger + create locks + natural-key upserts + idempotent handlers: disable-buttons is only the UX skin.

instruction: 'use client' boundary bug: a Next.js app router page randomly renders day-old blog content; only on the blog listing route. Investigation hint: route is statically rendered; data updates hourly in CMS; no revalidate export; someone 'fixed freshness' by forcing client-side fetch but the dynamic fetch happens only client-side... Explain the render-mode confusion and the config decision record needed.
reasoning: Static-by-default app-router routes cache at build. Without revalidate they never refresh. Client-patching hides staleness on navigation but served HTML remains stale for first loads. The 'fix' was cosmetic. Decision. Choose render semantics per route (SSG+ISR / dynamic / client) with data-freshness SLO recorded.
answer: Mode confusion: the route resolved to static (no dynamic APIs used, fetch cached): HTML baked at build = day-old after deploys; revalidate absent means 'until next deploy': the client-side 'fix' fetches fresh in browser: returning visitors/hydration see fresh, first-load bots/slow-JS see stale (inconsistent experiences and SEO staleness: explains 'random' reports: actually population-split by path/JS-speed!). Decision record per route (write it down in a table): (1) data freshness SLO (blog index tolerates 1h staleness per CMS cadence); (2) mechanism chosen: here: SSG + ISR (export const revalidate = 3600: statically regenerates hourly, keeps CDN-speed for 99% hits); alternates documented: force-dynamic + cache-control (SSR per request: correctness-first at compute cost for admin-y routes), client-fetch with loading skeletons (for user-personal data only: public content shouldn't depend on client JS); (3) explicit rendering contract in code: the export annotation IS the contract, and route-layout forcing unintentional dynamism (reading cookies() at layout level) must be caught (surprise: many teams think SSG while layout cookies()/headers() made it dynamic: know the full disqualifier list); (4) cache-invalidation interplay: if CMS has webhooks, on-demand revalidateTag('blog') beats time-based: register the hook in CMS (revalidate API route secured); (5) verification canary: a CI smoke that deploys, touches CMS, waits revalidate-window, asserts served HTML shows the update: the regression you missed; plus logging rendered-at timestamp into HTML comments for support triage. Conclusion: rendering modes are freshness contracts declared per route with SLOs: ISR revalidation (or on-demand tags) for rate-limited content beats client-side freshness cosmetics.

instruction: A long-running regex over user-supplied input (catastrophic backtracking) periodically pins the event loop of the Node API for seconds; observability shows 'event loop lag' spikes matching specific payloads. What containment and prevention pattern applies to regex execution on untrusted input?
reasoning: ReDoS classes. Nested quantifiers over ambiguous subpatterns blow up on crafted near-matches. Containment. Audit/replace patterns, timebox execution (safe-regex libs, worker threads with timeouts, or RE2-class engines without backtracking), and add payload-shape tests that recreate the polynomial blowup.
answer: Pattern program: (1) audit: inventory regexes processing request-bound strings (grep new RegExp, /literal/ usages near req bodies/headers; don't forget library features: some validators take patterns from config); run a static scanner (safe-regex, redos-detector) as first-pass; for each survivor, check engine semantics manually (the detector has false negatives for some forms); (2) fixes per case: rewrite ambiguous constructs (eliminate nested quantifiers like (a+)+ and (a|aa)+ via possessive-equivalent restructuring or indexed lookups), anchor and bound input length upfront (cheap pre-validation: length and charset checks reduce the blast class), prefer string/parse operations where expressivity isn't required; (3) engine options: RE2 (linear-time guarantees: no backreferences: port patterns that fit; node-re2 bindings) for high-risk surfaces; (4) containment for unavoidable dynamic patterns: run in worker_threads with hard timeouts (terminate: be careful: worker termination is sudden: isolate per-tenant damage) or child sandbox with CPU limits; main-loop stays responsive — log+drop offending payload to a quarantine store for analysis; (5) observability + regression: event-loop lag metrics already exist: alert thresholds; tests: polynomial-blowup payloads in CI asserting the route's latency stays <N ms (generation: append chars to the near-matching prefix until blowup manifests pre-fix, then keep as regression); red-team review for highest-risk desks (auth email validators are classic). Conclusion: treat regexes on untrusted data as potentially-unbounded compute: audit, rewrite or engine-swap, sandbox+timebox what can't be proven, and pin blowup payloads in CI.

instruction: An on-call sees DB CPU at 100% with the SAME parameterized query flooding pg_stat_statements: SELECT ... WHERE token = $1 (sessions table, 900 executions/sec). Sessions table has 200M rows, no index on token. Deploy yesterday 'moved session validation from Redis to DB for consistency'. Postmortem the architectural miss.
reasoning: Hot-path key-value lookups need O(1)-ish read structures. A per-request unindexed scan (200M rows full scan per request × 900 rps) is instant saturation. The migration traded the cache's semantics (fail-closed sessions? acceptable latency?) without the access-pattern math. Indexes are not the lesson, access-pattern engineering is.
answer: Miss anatomy: session validation executes per authenticated request (the hottest read in the system); Redis provides O(1) reads at trivial cost; Postgres does it with a b-tree IF INDEXED (idx on token: absent here: each read = seq scan: seconds each × 900/s). Even with the index, Postgres-per-request reads cost ~0.5-1ms+ and connection pool headroom: at 900 rps sustainable only with careful pool sizing and read replicas: was that modeled? The deploy likely said 'for consistency' (Redis lost sessions on evictions? TTL vs session length drift?): the symptom that MOTIVATED the switch should have shaped the design: e.g., write-through sessions (Redis as primary read + PG as durable backing: read-your-write guaranteed post-login) instead of swap-over. Postmortem fixes: (1) IMMEDIATE: add CONCURRENTLY the index (pg: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids table locks: at 200M rows it still takes minutes+io: pick window: revert deploy if safer); (2) revert to Redis-validation with PG as warm fallback + invalidation discipline (on session mutation: write PG committed, then Redis set/delete: operations order documented; on Redis miss: single-flight DB read repopulate: DB sees only cold misses: query volume back to noise); (3) load-test per-request paths pre-release with production-shaped traffic (this class is ALWAYS catchable: 900rps validation endpoints with 10-minute canary analysis would have paged before global rollout); (4) review gate: any PR touching per-request infra paths requires capacity math in the description (reads/s expected, index presence, pool budgets): reviewer checklist item. Conclusion: session-read patterns demand KV-class reads with PG as durable backing and cold-miss fallback: hot-path migrations need arithmetic, indexes are table stakes, and canary analysis catches the rest.

instruction: QA: 'sometimes two users assigned the same seat on the seating chart' in a ticketing flow. Reserve endpoint: SELECT seat FOR UPDATE skipped silently when seat not 'available'... but check-then-update happens in two queries under READ COMMITTED with concurrent buyers. Walk the serialization gap and the lock-correct implementation.
reasoning: Check-then-act under READ COMMITTED has a race window between SELECT (sees available) and UPDATE. Two transactions both see availability. Correct. Atomic conditional UPDATE (WHERE status='available') with rowcount check, or SELECT FOR UPDATE in the same transaction, or database-enforced allocation via unique partial index.
answer: Gap walk: Tx A: SELECT status='available' (true) → thinks → UPDATE... Tx B same interleave: both write: whoever commits last defines owner; the 'FOR UPDATE skipped when not available' note reveals attempt at locking that didn't cover the actual UPDATE decision path (or lock taken on the wrong row/outer join producing NULL row: skips). Three correct implementation levels: (1) conditional single statement: UPDATE seats SET owner=$u, status='sold' WHERE id=$s AND status='available' RETURNING id: database serializes row lock during update: second tx blocks then re-evaluates predicate (0 rows): app maps 0 rows → 409 seat-taken: simplest and robust; (2) explicit locking: BEGIN; SELECT ... WHERE id=$s FOR UPDATE (blocks concurrrent lock seekers); recheck status post-lock; UPDATE; COMMIT: correct if lock actually row-locks the seat (mind outer-join 'FOR UPDATE cannot lock nullable side' gotchas); (3) schema-level: partial unique index (sold seats: UNIQUE(event_id, seat_id) WHERE status='sold'): makes duplicates IMPOSSIBLE at data level (defense-in-depth even if app races: violation error mapped to conflict response): always add this regardless of code pattern chosen: bugs become exceptions not double-sells. Verification inventory: every code path mutating seat status (refunds/cancellations/admins) must respect the same predicate discipline (cancellation: WHERE status='sold' AND owner=$x). Tests: concurrency harness (N threads racing same seat asserting exactly one success) in CI, plus checking rowcount-driven conflict responses UX ('seat taken, choose another'). Conclusion: reservation = serialized write predicate, not read-then-decide: conditional UPDATE or FOR UPDATE in-txn plus partial unique index as seat-of-the-pants-proof backstop.

instruction: Support ticket: 'dark mode flashes light then dark on every page load, only for logged-in users'. Theme from user profile (server-known), injected cookie 'theme=dark'; _document adds class at first paint... except the cookie is read client-side after hydration, so SSR emits light first. What's the flash-of-theme class fix, done right?
reasoning: FOUC-theme = decision data not available to the first paint path on the server (hydration-time application is always too late). Fix. Transmit the theme choice to the server render path (cookie read server-side at request time, class on <html> in SSR HTML) with inline-boot script as the layer that eliminates any paint gap between HTML parse and script.
answer: Class mechanics: first paint uses SSR HTML; if SSR doesn't know theme (cookie read only in client JS), initial HTML is light-styled; hydration JS applies dark: repaint flash. Anon users' absence (saved via localStorage on their side? different symptom) narrows it: logged-in users with cookie present still flash because the SERVER didn't read it: the cookie exists but rendering ignores it. Right fix chain: (1) SSR reads the theme cookie per request (server component/middleware/_document getInitialProps style: framework-dependent seam: Next app router: cookies() at layout/root server component: sets <html class='dark' data-theme> accordingly: must mark route dynamic or accept per-request evaluation: document the SSG-vs-dynamic tradeoff for marketing pages: static anonymous shells should choose classless boot); (2) inline blocking boot script for client-override cases (user toggles w/o cookie sync yet? or anonymous localStorage): a tiny synchronous inline <script> in <head> reading resolveTheme() (cookie > localStorage > media) and setting the class BEFORE CSS applies body paint: standard pattern: must run early enough (before stylesheet application: place first in head, parser-blocking and tiny); (3) hydration consistency: ensure SSR-class matches boot-resolve (same algorithm both sides: single shared resolve function used by server and inline script: drift here reintroduces flash or hydration mismatch warnings); (4) preference source hygiene: when logged-in preference changes, API writes profile AND updates cookie (same response: single source next request), and system-media-following mode ('auto') resolves via media query at boot script only (documented asymmetry: server can't know media, so auto resolves client-side pre-paint: dark-flash impossible, but SSR can't pre-choose: that's fine because boot script handles). Conclusion: theme must reach the first-paint HTML via server cookie render and/or parser-blocking boot script with shared resolver semantics: hydration-time application guarantees the flash.

instruction: Metrics pipeline: daily active users dipped 20% overnight exactly when app released; product panics; data says API traffic flat. Release notes: analytics batch queue now flushes on pagehide instead of beforeunload. Compose: instrumentation-vs-reality analysis for telemetry regressions after releases.
reasoning: Telemetry pipelines change with releases. Delivery semantics (pagehide reliability API vs legacy), batching thresholds, ad-blocker interactions, sampling, and SDK versions all shift COUNTS without behavior change. Analysis must compare independent truth (server-side API events) against client-reported metrics before declaring user movement.
answer: Analysis steps: (1) parallel truth: API-level event counters (server sees per-user activity: sessions created, key API calls): flat traffic + dipping client events = pipeline artifact hypothesis favored STRONGLY (user behavior rarely changes overnight globally at exactly release time; telemetry changes exactly then); (2) enumerate the release's pipeline diffs: the beforeunload→pagehide move (pagehide is the RELIABLE one actually: beforeunload drops on mobile especially: real change should raise counts... unless the implementation has a bug: reading: 'flushes on pagehide' but maybe flush became async and died with the page in some browsers (sync sendBeacon vs fetch: fetch dies on unload; sendBeacon survives: WHICH transport did they switch to? if they moved from sync XHR-hack (awful but working) to fetch-on-pagehide, mobile Safari kills it: counts DROP: classic); also check batch size changes (queue never reaching threshold before navigation on short sessions: flush logic on pagehide requires flush-to-fire: empty-intervals), and SDK init timing under the new router: events fire before analytics ready → dropped silently (add dropped-event counters!); (3) cohort reruns: replay the old build side-by-side internally (staff cohort on old SDK): metric by cohort vs build isolates pipeline causation; (4) dashboards hygiene going forward: client-sdk version split on every telemetry chart (mixed-version windows annotated) + release markers; a 'pipeline self-test' beacon on init (1 in N clients sends synthetic event: its rate validates ingestion health independently of user behavior); (5) product communication: annotate the metric series as pipeline-corrupted in the window (doctored observability is how companies chase ghosts for quarters); (6) fix transport semantics (sendBeacon), awaiting-beacon or visibility-based robust flushing with keepalive fetch on modern browsers, deploy, verify recovery vs parallel truth. Conclusion: release-adjacent metric shifts demand parallel-truth comparison and pipeline-diff enumeration before behavioral conclusions: annotate corrupted windows explicitly.

instruction: A prod-only slowdown: p95 API latency doubles every ~14 days then a restart fixes it; heap grows slowly unbounded; profiler shows increasing arrays from a 'recently-visited' per-process list... capped at 500 per USER but never globally capped; unique users accumulate. Expose the cardinality-based leak and the lifecycle-aware cap design.
reasoning: Per-key caps don't bound total size when the key-space is unbounded. Cardinality × per-key cap = total footprint. Any unbounded cardinality map in a long-lived process leaks by construction: 14-day cycles = unique-user accumulation rate meeting memory ceilings.
answer: Leak mechanics: 'cap 500 per user' bounds per-value length, not MAP SIZE: unique userIds accumulate forever (each entry holds user ids, timestamps, request paths: small × N grows daily; 14 days × uniques/day × entry-size = threshold where GC pressure + array copies pin CPU: p95 doubles as copying/GC dominates; restart clears). Cardinality classes for any in-memory structure: (1) closed/bounded (tenant feature flags: fine), (2) open-but-high-churn-sessions (session cache: size active-session-count × ttl: still needs cleanup scanning), (3) open-unbounded (user ids forever: yours: MUST have global bound: LRU by count or bytes, or TTL eviction per entry, or off-process entirely); design per structure: name its class explicitly in code comments + review checklists. Lifecycle-aware cap design here: (a) semantic: does 'recently-visited' need to survive per user forever? if product wants last-N per user persistently: it belongs in Redis/DB authored per user (TTL like 30d sliding), not process memory: in-proc copies are disposable accelerators at most; (b) if in-proc is right (hot data): global LRU (size cap total entries) + optionally per-key sub-cap, plus metrics: cache_entries gauge alerted on growth slope (a week-over-week climb without organic traffic climb = regression alarm); (c) memory-pressure hygiene: monitor heap per pod and restart policies cannot be the 'fix' (they are the symptom loop you're in); (d) sweep: grep for every Map/Object-as-dict in long-lived modules with per-key caps and unbounded keyspaces (analytics buffers, rate limiters keyed by user!!: same class: audit them NOW: limiter stores worse because bots mint keys: global caps protect from abuse-driven memory DoS). Conclusion: unbounded keyspace × any structure = leak: global bounds + TTLs + cardinality metrics per map, and per-user persistence moves to stores designed for it.

instruction: An AI assistant is asked to 'fix the login redirect loop' in a 400k-line repo and loads 60 files 'for context': all of auth/, all middleware, two README versions, and the user model. What is the relevance-prioritization failure here, and what evidence selects the minimal working set?
reasoning: Breadth-loading conflates presence with relevance. Loops usually involve very few decision points (redirect guards, callback handler, session writing). Select by symptom-anchored tracing. Reproduce, locate the redirect decision code, and load only files in the loop's causal cycle.
answer: Failure: loading by theme ('everything auth') instead of by causal role burns context on non-participating code (password hashing, OAuth providers rarely in redirect loops) and dilutes attention from the few files that matter. Selection procedure: (1) reproduce and capture the HTTP trace: the alternating 302 locations name the EXACT parties (e.g., /login → /app → /login): two handlers, not sixty files; (2) find each redirect decision site (grep Location writes / res.redirect calls) plus the predicate they evaluate (session present? callback URL validation?): that predicate's data sources (session middleware, one config for allowed origins) are the context set: typically 4-6 files + one config snippet; (3) load action specs with intent: for the predicate lines you need full functions, elsewhere you need signatures (read only what proves/disproves the loop hypothesis: the loop mechanism forms a tense little graph where a cookie isn't set due to SameSite or an always-falsy check); (4) skip docs-first approaches: READMEs about auth 'architecture' describe ideals, while the bug lives in actual code behavior; consult docs after code to sanity-check intended behavior only. Conclusion: minimal working set = the redirect cycle's participants plus their predicate dependencies, discovered from a captured trace: thematic bulk-loading stalls analysis and buries signal.

instruction: Task: upgrade axios across the repo safely. Assistant reads axios docs for an hour, then edits. What does documentation-vs-codebase ratio reasoning look like for dependency upgrade tasks?
reasoning: Upgrade risk lives at usage sites, not in general documentation. Find every call signature, interceptor, and config used by THIS codebase first (grep inventory), then read only the changelog sections affecting those patterns. Doc-first reading is uncoupled from the actual blast radius.
answer: Ratio reasoning: (1) inventory first: grep for axios usage: create() instances with custom configs, interceptor registrations, response-type assumptions (response.data double-unwrap: v1 changed error shapes and removed some transitive deps), timeout/cancel token APIs (CancelToken deprecated in v1 in favor of AbortController: only matters IF used: check); categorize sites by pattern: the risk register is this list, not the changelog's full length; (2) targeted doc reading: only migration-guide sections matching used patterns (error.code strings, qs behavior, proxy env leakage bugs in specific versions); the rest is noise for this task; (3) verification scoped: typecheck catches signature breaks; unit/integration tests around HTTP-adjacent flows (mock servers that emulate both happy/error paths) give the safety the upgrade actually needs; a canary deploy beats more doc hours; (4) time split for a 0.x→1.x class bump in a mid-size repo: most on inventory + tests, some on migration sections, least on generic reading. Common trap: upgrading based on 'it compiles' because types cover little of runtime behavior (error object shape changes break error.classify() helpers without type errors: grep helpers too). Conclusion: usage inventory bounds the doc surface: read the changelog for your patterns, then spend effort on tests at the HTTP boundary.

instruction: A bugfix needs the 'auth middleware'. Repo has middleware/auth.ts, middleware/auth_legacy.ts, and admin/middleware/auth.py (different service). The task's failing request hits the Python admin service's endpoint. Loading the TS middlewares first 'because they matched grep better' wastes the session. What's the selection principle?
reasoning: Name-similarity is not relevance. The executing system under the failing request decides. Identify the serving stack from the request path (route table, gateway routing rules, ports), then the middleware file in that stack, before any source file opens.
answer: Principle: evidence of execution beats lexical match. Procedure: (1) identify the failing endpoint's owner: route prefix (/admin/api/* per gateway/nginx conf routes to the Python service), compose/ports mapping, or simply curl -v the endpoint and inspect Server header/framework fingerprints; (2) then trace auth in THAT service: admin/middleware/auth.py + its registration (app factory, middleware stack ordering: knowing ORDER matters for why auth ran or didn't); (3) the TS files belong to a different failure world: they may share copy-pasted logic (same bug class!), but confirmation requires their executions to be implicated: not here; optionally note them for a follow-up consistency audit after the immediate fix; (4) when the serving system is ambiguous (mixed proxies): capture one failing request with tracing headers (X-Request-Id through gateway) and read the backend log line containing that id: the service logging it is the owner; never 'assume by directory name'. Also: the investigation then reads the legacy vs current candidates WITHIN the python service by import wiring (which module the app factory imports), not by filename freshness. Conclusion: disambiguate by which process serves the broken request and by import wiring inside it; grep similarity is a distraction until execution context is fixed.

instruction: Fix 'billing page loads slowly'. Context options: the entire React tree of the billing page (40 components), the five network calls from the page, the metrics API server code. The symptom: loading spinner for 8s then fine. Where does context effort belong first?
reasoning: Client performance issues split into network-wait and render-block. Spinner-dominated-with-fine-data-afterwards almost always indicates upstream latency (API), making the backend handler + its DB queries the primary context instead of component internals. DevTools waterfall decides before file opening.
answer: Decision procedure: (1) measure before reading: network waterfall for the page: which requests span the 8s (probably one: /usage/summary); performance trace would separate paint-blocking JS from wait-time: here symptom signature says WAIT (spinner until data then instant fine: components aren't the cost); (2) therefore context = the specific API handler chain: express route for /usage/summary, its service, and its queries (pg_stat_statements/EXPLAIN one slow query; N+1 loops fanning out per account id are the classic); plus any cache middleware in front; (3) deliberately leave React component internals OUT of context: 40 components × spinners are theater unless evidence implicates rendering (long tasks in trace, INP metrics bad); if later evidence shows 600ms scripting after data arrival, then a narrow set (the chart component) joins; (4) risk: 'fixing' perceived slowness by optimizing components when the aggregate endpoint recomputes per request is THE common waste pattern; also check the query scoping (tenant filter present? missing index on (tenant_id, month) typical). Deliverable: backend-side fix (query/index/materialized cache) with a benchmark before/after. Conclusion: let the waterfall choose the context: spinner-until-data = handler+query territory: load that, explicitly defer everything downstream.

instruction: An agent solving 'dark mode contrast fails a11y on the pricing page' loads global.css (3000 lines), the design token file, and 12 component stylesheets — then drowns. On a 19-inch monitor, only the pricing page 'Annual' toggle is actually low-contrast. Contrast global-vs-local loading discipline for style issues.
reasoning: Style issues have a computed-value pipeline (specificity → variables → cascade layers) that devtools computes for you. Read the ELEMENT's computed styles and the 2-3 rules that win, then open exactly the files defining those rules instead of the system's surface area.
answer: Discipline: (1) start from the failing element, not the system: devtools shows computed color/background plus the winning selectors with file:line: for the Annual toggle you get e.g. .toggle-annual { background: var(--surface-alt) } from PricingToggle.module.css:45 and --surface-alt defined in themes/dark.css:12: that's the ENTIRE context needed for diagnosis; (2) then check token semantics: is --surface-alt's dark value used elsewhere acceptably? Changing the token has blast radius (find usages); changing the component's var assignment to --surface-elevated is local: the two candidate edits differ in scope: pick per design-system semantics (tokens are the API: prefer fixing the wrong TOKEN choice over patching token values unless the token itself is globally defective in dark mode); (3) validate systematically afterward: run contrast checks (axe/Lighthouse on the page in dark mode) to catch sibling failures on the same page (the user reported one toggle; the rule-change may fix or reveal more); global.css loads only if the cascade layers themselves are misconfigured (specificity wars won't show in computed view): rarely, so it's last; (4) never read 12 stylesheets speculatively: style bugs are reachable by computed-value evidence. Conclusion: compute-first (devtools pipeline) → open only the winning-rule files → reason about token vs local assignment scope → verify page-wide with automated contrast tooling.

instruction: 'Booking email not sent' bug: loads handler code (correct), email template (correct), mail provider config (correct). Actual cause: the booking-CONFIRMATION event emitted by a DIFFERENT handler name mismatch ('booking.confirmed' vs 'booking.confirm'). What's the editor-of-event-edges heuristic for missing-side-effect bugs?
reasoning: When the expected side effect is absent but every inspected component is individually correct, remaining suspects live at the EDGES. Event names, topic subscriptions, feature flags, cron registrations. Cross-reference the producer/consumer name-space before opening more implementation detail.
answer: Heuristic: absent-side-effect → enumerate the edge graph, not deeper reads: (1) producer: find where booking completion publishes (grep emit/publish near the booking service capture actual string literals: 'booking.confirm'); (2) consumer: find email trigger's subscription registration ('booking.confirmed' in the notification worker): compare literal-by-literal: event systems don't typecheck names across files; mismatches fail silently (nothing routes anywhere: no errors: this class hides from logs until dashboards show consumer-idle-vs-producer-active); (3) other edge classes for this symptom family: the consumer's queue binding may exclude the routing key (topic filters '*created' not matching), DLQ may be filling with poison messages (check queue depths), the handler may be feature-flagged off in this env (flags in env config), cron may not be registered on this process type; (4) cheap tooling: emit a test event / turn on 'events delivered' metrics; verify the subscription table at runtime (some buses list subscriptions), grep BOTH strings in the same session so mismatches jump; (5) repair + hardening: centralize event names in a shared constants file (delete string duplication so edits atomically change both edges), add contract test: producer emits X → consumer accepts X (fixture in CI: would have caught this at write time). Conclusion: side-effect-not-happening means edge graphs (emits/subscribes/binds/flags/cron) before internals: mismatch of literals is invisible to type systems and logs.

instruction: Fix a GraphQL error 'Cannot return null for non-nullable field Order.total'. Options to load: the Order type resolver file, the backing SQL query builder, the schema SDL, the frontend query document. The null appears only on archived orders. What is the minimal set and why?
reasoning: Non-null violation localizes to the field resolver and its data source conditional on entity state (archived → rows missing in joined table). The schema SDL defines the contract (non-nullable assertion), the resolver+query reveal why data lacks it. The frontend query usually carries no causal info for nullability.
answer: Minimal set: (1) schema SDL for Order.total: confirms non-null contract (total: Money! or Float!) and its type; (2) Order.total resolver implementation: where does it read (order.total_cents column vs computed via lines join?); (3) the data fetch behind it (SQL/knex/Prisma query): the archived-order-only pattern implicates conditional joins (e.g., INNER JOIN order_totals WHERE deleted_at IS NULL excluding archived rows: join collapses to NULL for archived) or a totals table whose rows are purged/after--archive lacking (archive job deletes computed rows); resolvers then hand null upward in violation; frontend doc is noise (it only selects fields). Then design decision at the contract level: either archived orders legitimately lack totals → schema was wrong (total nullable) + frontend must handle, or total must exist always → data layer must synthesize/preserve totals at archive time (compute & store into archive snapshot: usually the right business answer for financial records: archived order data must remain auditable!). Fix in the data model/archive job + backfill, not by hiding nulls in resolver (a zero/empty fallback for money amount destroys auditability). Also add test: archived order query passes the non-null contract. Conclusion: non-null errors = contract (SDL) vs data-path conditions: resolver+query of that field, where the conditional on entity state explains null: frontend and other types stay unloaded.

instruction: An agent edits a hot path in services/checkout.ts. Expert colleagues debate: should it load services/checkout.repository.test.ts (existing tests, 800 lines) or services/checkout.spec.ts (another suite, stale 2 years)? How do you choose which test file guides the fix, using repo evidence?
reasoning: Guiding tests must be TRUSTED ones. Indicative signals are recent modification aligning with the source file, CI inclusion (config globs that actually run them), and passing-in-CI status. Stale suites mislead the fix toward obsolete behavior. Choose by evidence of liveness, not filename recency.
answer: Evidence hierarchy: (1) liveness: does CI execute it? Check jest/vitest config project globs: *.repository.test.ts matches active patterns while *.spec.ts might be excluded (legacy convention kept only in an old config: verify via package.json test:ci script and workflow runs history); ask: when did it last CHANGE (git log -1 --format=%ci each file): recently touched alongside checkout.ts = maintained contract; 2-year silence on spec = abandoned scaffolding; (2) semantic adjacency: the repository test exercises the exact unit being edited (checkout.ts's repository interactions: mocks DB boundary) while the stale spec may test pre-refactor architecture (mocking modules that no longer exist: run it: does it even pass currently? npm test -- checkout.spec: quickly reveals zombie status: skip-on-presence or import errors betray death); (3) usage mode: load PASSING-and-relevant tests to pin behavior before edits; treat stale tests as historical documents at best (maybe worth salvaging their scenarios into the live suite: a separate hygiene task, not today's fix). Takeaway rule for agents: before loading any artifact as 'the truth', answer 'who would notice if this file were wrong?' CI-running suites have an audience; stale files have nostalgia. Conclusion: select the suite with CI execution + recent co-evolution + passing status; validate liveness empirically by running it before trusting it.

instruction: Feature: add rate limiting to a public API. Context candidates: existing api-gateway.yaml (kong), services' app-level middleware, the Redis wrapper lib, a README on 'rate limiting' from 2022. Which defines the design surface you should load and why?
reasoning: Appropriate enforcement layer depends on where ownership of the resource lives (shared edge vs per-service logic) and what state backend exists. The question is architectural BEFORE it is textual. Load the configs of existing policy (gateway rules), then the minimal middleware precedent in one service to match conventions; READMEs from past years describe aspirations, not the stack.
answer: Selection: (1) api-gateway.yaml: determines if limiting can/should live at the edge (kong rate-limiting plugin exists: per-route policies with redis backed counters: edge is the default home for PUBLIC API budget enforcement: protects ALL services uniformly incl. services without code changes: load the plugin config + how env/secrets inject); (2) evidence of whether gateway enforces anything today (grep file for rate-limiting sections: may exist for some routes: then the task = extend policy table, not build anything); (3) app-level middleware only if rate classes differ per-tenant/per-account with business logic (plan-tier budgets: gateway can't know Stripe plan of API key owner without a call: then the limiter belongs at BFF/service where account lookup exists: load ONE service's existing middleware stack + its redis wrapper pattern to follow conventions (not all services); (4) the 2022 README: skip (aspiration archaeology); the Redis wrapper lib: load ONLY its public API surface (constructor, INCR-with-TTL helpers): never its internals for this task. Decision gate: enumerate limit dimensions first (per key? per plan? per IP?) since the dimension determines the owning layer: that determination precedes any file loading: an hour in gateway docs is wasted if budgets are plan-based. Conclusion: dimension analysis → owning layer → load that layer's existing policy config + one convention-setting implementation: platform-readmes and unrelated libs stay unread.

instruction: One-line task: 'change the session cookie SameSite from Lax to Strict for the admin app.' Where's the single line, given: infra sets a login cookie at SSO callback, an express-session cookie, and a Next.js rewrite proxying /api? What does the hunt teach about seemingly-one-line changes?
reasoning: Cookie attribute changes require locating EVERY Set-Cookie writer and deciding which token(s) the attribute policy covers. Also Strict breaks flows that Lax allowed (cross-site navigation from email links to authenticated pages, auth handshakes that hop domains). One-line edits are never one-line investigations.
answer: Hunt set: (1) enumerate writers by grep 'Set-Cookie', res.cookie(, setCookie, cookie.serialize across the SSO callback handler (identity cookie) and express-session config (session cookie), and the proxy layer (Next rewrites may strip/forward headers but cookies flow: check whether a next.config rewrites cookies attrs via header rules: some platforms rewrite through edge functions adding their own Set-Cookie for region/AB: keep those intact); (2) decide SCOPE: the requirement says 'admin app session': likely the express-session config AND the SSO identity cookie (inconsistent pairs create half-strict behavior: login works but session re-issues Lax: policy illusions); (3) Strict impact analysis (the actual content of the task): Strict blocks cookie on ALL cross-site navigations: users opening password-reset emails (from mail domain to admin domain) land logged-out at first navigate (then client-side fetch may still carry? no: Strict blocks all cross-site sends until same-site context established): choose explicitly: often the answer is Lax+CSRF-token for mutations instead of Strict, or Strict with a documented re-auth interstitial; (4) verification: e2e across the email-link flow and a cross-site POST test asserting rejection; don't ship until flows confirmed. Teaching: 'one-line config' = three writer files + behavioral verification matrix; scoping the cookie set and the cross-site flow list is the real work. Conclusion: locate all writers, confirm attribute consistency scope, then let cross-site flow analysis decide Strict vs Lax-with-tokens: verify in e2e before calling a one-liner done.

instruction: The task: 'find why our Docker image is 2.4GB.' Options: read all apt-install docs, read the Dockerfile once, or run layer analysis (docker history/dive). What does tool-first evidence gathering look like for artifact-composition questions?
reasoning: Composition questions are answered by measurement, not prose. Layer tools attribute bytes to exact instructions. Read the Dockerfile AFTER the tool output, interpreting which instructions to blame (and which are fine), avoiding generic best-practice tinkering.
answer: Tool-first flow: (1) docker history --no-trunc image | sort by size: immediately shows the fat layers (apt-get without cleanup, node_modules dev deps, .git copied, test fixtures, build caches in final stage); dive interactively attributes bytes per layer + wasted-file detections (duplicate copies of same content across layers: COPY . then COPY node_modules again: double-billing!); (2) NOW read the Dockerfile once, matching instructions to layers: targets identified: e.g., a pip install without --no-cache-dir (600MB), apt lists not rm'd (200MB), multi-stage misuse copying whole /app instead of dist; (3) compose the fix list from measured items only, each with expected byte win (dive estimates + verify after rebuild with another history run: byte-verified PR description); (4) guardrail: add CI image-size budget alert (build job prints size, fails if >N-MB regression) so this becomes a watched metric not an annual expedition. Contrast with prose-first: apt best-practices reading would have you 'cleanup lists' everywhere blindly possibly breaking pinned debugging tools, while missing the actual 1GB (.git in build context copied: .dockerignore fix). Judgment: docs reading earns its place when you MODIFY specific instructions (cleanup flags semantics) but AFTER measurement names the instructions. Conclusion: measurement attributes bytes, then prose informs targeted edits: history/dive first, Dockerfile second, docs third, re-measure to close.

instruction: 'Make the import feature handle 1M rows' — context options: the import UI (React), the API endpoint handler, the worker (BullMQ job), the DB schema of staging tables, the queue/dashboard config for memory limits. Old PRs of similar features. Where do you assemble the working set for a scale-class change?
reasoning: Scale-limit changes are bound by the pipeline's slowest stage and its memory/time budgets, not by the request that starts it. The working set spans the whole pipeline. Handler (initiation. Is file fully uploaded/temp-stored), worker (batching strategy), DB (bulk write primitives), infra (memory/visibility timeouts), measured with a staging-sized test before code edits.
answer: Working set by stage with questions: (1) API handler: how does the file arrive (multi-hundred-MB upload is itself a latency bomb: stream to object storage (multer s3/stream) and pass a pointer, never buffer: load handler code for the upload mode); (2) worker job (primary residence of the fix): batch size choice (500/1000-row chunks), transaction scope (per-batch, not per-file: no table locks for 45min), checkpoint/resume design (idempotency key + progress table), backpressure against DB (pool saturation: concurrency 2 not 20), error taxonomy (row-failures isolated + reported vs whole-job abort); (3) DB schema: staging-table pattern (load into unindexed staging, validate, set-based INSERT/UPDATE: indexes on the match keys), COPY vs row-inserts (where supported), bloat/vacuum awareness; (4) infra knobs: worker memory (stream parsers, not readFile), queue visibilityTimeout > p99 batch time, dashboard retries config; (5) old PRs: SKIP unless they named a similar pipeline (CSV import of inventory: patterns reusable; generic 'big feature' PRs add noise); (6) staging test with a synthetic 1.2M-row file BEFORE architecture-signoff: measures stage throughputs so the fix lands where binding. The set is this pipeline's code+configs, chosen by stage topology, and validated by staged measurement. Conclusion: scale tasks context = the full data-flow pipeline stages with throughput evidence: never the trigger surface alone.

instruction: On-call asks you (agent) to diagnose 'login broken in EU only' at 3am. Time-boxed triage: which 5 checks maximize information per minute in an unfamiliar repo?
reasoning: Regional incidents at odd hours call for invariant checks ordered by information gain. Health/synthetic probes by region, edge/CDN config recent changes, regionalized config values (DNS, locale/TZ, legal-gating), deploy timelines, and then targeted logs, before any deep code archaeology.
answer: Five checks: (1) is it actually EU-region or EU-users: synthetic login attempts from EU vantage points (hosted checkers and curl via region-pinned runners) vs EU-users via VPN from other regions: region-INFRAs tructure vs locale-CONFIG differs fundamentally: 2 minutes decides the family; (2) deploy/config timeline in the last 24h touching region-labeled surfaces (cdn rules, geo redirects, middleware IP lists, legal gates: GDPR-banner gating code paths often trigger 'login broken' by looping consent redirects: check recent commits and flag/targeting changes for EU audiences); (3) error identity: what do EU users SEE (hang/loop/4xx/5xx: collect one HAR from support with timestamps+correlation ids): hangs = network/edge; loops = redirects/consent/CSRF cookie attrs across region domains; 4xx/5xx = backend+gwp logs with request-id; (4) backend logs filtered by EU edge-POP or IP ranges + geo-tag: is traffic ARRIVING (no → DNS/CDN path: check DNS resolutions per region, cert validity: regional TLS issues!) or arriving-and-failing (app: then request-ids → trace); (5) dependency regionality: auth provider/IP allow-lists egress-blocked from some EU ranges? EU data-residency routing config shipped recently (a region-pinned session store mis-routed writes: sessions instantly 'unknown' across POPs: sticky-session breakages). Most fixes at this hour: rollback the flagged config/geo change from check (2): root-cause continues at 9am. Conclusion: order triage by branch-cutting checks (region-vs-locale, timeline, error-identity, arrival-logs, external deps), not by code reading depth.

instruction: A junior agent must 'add a second currency to pricing.' It finds money.ts, prices.sql, checkout UI, invoices PDF, Stripe integration, analytics events — and tries to read all deeply in one pass. Teach staged relevance layers for cross-cutting features.
reasoning: Cross-cutting features should be explored in widening rings. The canonical computation core first (where money decisions are made), then the nearest edges (API contracts), then far edges (display/docs), reading far layers only for schema impact, not implementation detail.
answer: Rings discipline: Ring 1 (core, deep-read): the pricing computation authority (likely money.ts + pricing service + the SQL schema of price tables: currency column presence): decide the semantic change (per-price currency + conversion policy: multi-currency is a data-model decision first: amounts become (amount, currency) pairs with an explicit 'no mixing' rule); Ring 2 (contracts, targeted-read): API request/response schemas (checkout payload money fields: serialize Money object?), Stripe integration surface (which calls carry currency today: single hardcoded 'usd' node: locate it), error surfaces (currency mismatch cases); Ring 3 (presentation, scan-only): checkout UI price components (they need Money-aware display but no logic changes: skim to note the formatMoney util), invoices PDF (same), analytics events (add currency field: don't read event internals: note schema registry entry); Ring 4 (go-away unless evidence): unrelated services, historical scripts (backfill is Ring 3b: note need for currency backfill on existing rows as its own work item, not today's edit). Rule per layer: deeper rings get DECISIONS, outer rings get IMPACT LISTS. Typical trap: reading analytics internals burns the budget before the canonical core decision is made (currency-mixing rules: never silently convert: conversion only at explicit boundary with rates ledger: that's the Ring-1 output). Conclusion: explore cross-cutting work in widening rings with per-ring reading depth quotas: decisions core-ward, impact-encountered lists edge-ward.

instruction: Fix 'search suggestions fade-in flickers'. Candidates: SuggestionList.tsx, useDebounce hook, the /suggest API, the CSS transition file, lodash version. All are 'nearby'. Which two files do you open first given the flicker is a visual timing artifact, and why not the API?
reasoning: Timing-artifact bugs are property-shaped. Debounce/transition sequencing visual issues live in the hook and presentation layer; API enters only if evidence shows request frequency, not render sequencing, as the cause. The cheapest discriminator. Log render vs fetch counts on interaction.
answer: Open first: (1) useDebounce hook: verify semantics: leading/trailing configuration and whether it also flashes loading state per keystroke (debounced fn returning new callbacks each render resetting timers: classic: valueStale vs value), and how 'fade-in' interplay: debounce emits → list mounts fresh → fade animation restarts: visible flicker if exit/enter overlap not handled; (2) SuggestionList.tsx: how it renders during transitions (keying! keys changing per result batch remount items → css animation restarts: unconditional class toggles per render: animation-play-state reset; AnimatePresence-like wrappers with exit timings). Explicitly NOT first: /suggest API — network latency may contribute but flicker morphology tells: capture once: devtools network: if responses arrive stable ~150ms with no duplicates, renders jump around anyway: client-sequencing proven: API read unnecessary; open the API only when duplicates/aborts (double fetch, racing responses written out of order: then the fix is abort/previous-response-drop logic: you'd see it in the network log first: which is why the discriminator is the log, not the file read); CSS transition file: third, only if keying/animation-restart isn't the issue (duration/easing per theme: less likely); lodash version is pure noise (nothing here smells versioned-dep). Conclusion: morphology (network log shows stable fetches + render churn) → hook semantics + component keying/mount behavior: two files, evidence-gated.

instruction: Agent task: 'find why weekly digest emails go to spam in Gmail only.' Candidates: mail template HTML, DNS zone file (SPF/DKIM), sending-service config, list-unsubscribe headers, the worker sending code. Order the check-context by how Gmail deliverability actually breaks.
reasoning: Gmail deliverability failures are usually authentication/alignment (SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment with From domain), missing one-click unsubscribe (2024 sender rules), or reputation/complaint rate, not template aesthetics. Check infrastructure headers from actual received mail first (message source), then DNS and sender config. Code and template come last.
answer: Order: (1) REAL EVIDENCE FIRST: get the message source of a spammed digest (support asks a user/test mailbox: 'Show original'): read Authentication-Results: SPF/DKIM pass? DMARC alignment between From: domain and d= in DKIM/SPF? (The classic: provider sends with DKIM d=sendgrid.net while From is company.com: 'pass' but MISALIGNED: DMARC partial fail → spam); ARC chains if forwarded; (2) DNS zone file (repo-managed?) or live dig (dig TXT domain, _dmarc.domain, domainkey selectors): alignment fixes mean set DKIM for the corporate domain selector at the provider or relax From domain (r=relaxed considerations explicitly, eschewed by security policy? read dmarc p= and rua reports address); (3) sender-service config: dedicated vs shared IP (reputation: shared pool poisoning by others: check provider's deliverability dashboard for complaint rates >0.1%: Gmail's threshold), IP warmup age; List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post one-click headers (Gmail requirement for bulk senders since 2024: absence now gets bulk mail spammed: verify headers in the source from step 1: config lives in transport setup: add if missing); (4) template: content triggers are LAST (image-only emails, URL shorteners, tracking-domain mismatch: visible in source: quick scan: usually fine); (5) worker sending code: only to verify it plumbs headers correctly per digest TYPE (digests marketingish vs transactional: separate streams/IPs recommended). Then Gmail Postmaster Tools domain reputation as external confirmation. Conclusion: deliverability: message-source forensics → DNS alignment → provider reputation/headers → content → code: exactly the reverse of naive template-first reading.

instruction: A performance task: 'n+1 queries on the orders admin page.' Options: open the page component, the orders API handler, the ORM models with relations, the query-logging middleware. Where do you verify and where do you fix, and what's the anti-pattern selection that wastes the session?
reasoning: N+1 is diagnosed at the query layer (log the actual statements per request), localized to the data-access path (eager vs lazy loading declarations), fixed there. Anti-pattern. Opening React components and re-structuring them. Presentation shape motivated the call pattern but the fix lives in one include/join at the ORM boundary.
answer: Assign: (1) VERIFY at the query-logging middleware/DB logs: enable per-request query capture (pg log_min_duration, prisma query logging, knex debug) for the admin page's endpoint: count statements: 1 orders list + N per-row price lookups: confirmation shows the repeated shape (orders → items per order): identifies the accessor function issuing per-row queries (repository method order.getItems() called inside a map loop: classic property access triggering lazy load); (2) FIX at the ORM model layer: include/eager-load declaration with the main query ({ include: { items: true }} / .withGraphFetched / joins) per endpoint: write the endpoint-specific resolve to batch (DataLoader for graphql shapes: N queries → 1 WHERE order_id IN (...)); measure again at (1): 1-2 queries; (3) the API handler: read only to understand endpoint semantics and add the include; the page component: do NOT load: presentation arrangement can wait until data-cost is structurally fixed (components re-render frequency is a separate later issue if any); (4) guardrail: add a per-request query-count budget test for this endpoint (integration test asserts <= 5 queries constant vs row count: the regression proof) and query-count telemetry in prod logs. Anti-pattern to avoid: N+1 hunting via guess-edits across components ('maybe memoizing this helps') or blind global eager-loading (eager-everything makes OTHER endpoints slow: fix per endpoint with intent). Conclusion: N+1: measure statements at the DB log, fix at the ORM include/batching boundary by endpoint, guard with query-count tests: UI structure isn't where this class lives.

instruction: 'Legal says the ToS acceptance timestamp must be provable.' Evidence options: frontend click handler, POST /accept body, DB row write, audit log pipeline, email receipt sender. Rank each by evidentiary strength and define which code must change to upgrade the proof to the required level.
reasoning: Proof strength scales with tamper-evidence and independence of the recording layer (server-time + immutable log + signature/hash beats client timestamps and mutable rows). The required change is at persistence/audit layers (time source, immutability, integrity anchoring), rarely at the click handler.
answer: Strength ranking (weak→strong): (1) frontend click handler: client clock, user-tamperable, weak: do not rely (keep only as UX metadata); (2) POST body timestamp: client-asserted transit data: weak for the same reason: useful payload but NOT proof; (3) DB row (created_at server default + tos_version): server-time + row data: meaningful but mutable (update/delete possible by operators: weaker against internal threat model); (4) append-only audit log (WORM storage / restricted writers, structured record: actor, ip, user-agent, ToS version hash, server time with timezone source, request-id): strong in normal audits; (5) integrity-anchored: audit events hash-chained (each event includes prev hash) and/or periodically anchored externally (timestamp to an external notary / signed by HSM): defeats row-rewrite claims retroactively; (6) orthogonal corroboration: email receipt with same acceptance details (user-visible record + provider timestamp: dispute-resistent UX too). Required changes: capture server-time authoritatively at write (DB now() not client payload), persist ToS version text hash (not just version label: version content hash proves WHAT was accepted), route the event into append-only audit with integrity chaining (verify pipeline exists: if audit log table lives mutable in the same admin-writable DB as orders, promote storage class), send corroborating receipt; DEPRECATE trust in client timestamps (ignore field server-side). Load the DB write + audit pipeline first; the click handler needs no change beyond UX. Conclusion: provability is built at server-time persistence + immutable audit + optional integrity anchoring layers: client/front layers inform but never prove.

instruction: You're asked to review a PR that 'improves WebSocket reconnection resilience'. Which artifacts constitute competent review context: the PR diff alone, the reconnect lifecycle code outside the diff (heartbeat/close handlers), and/or incident history about disconnect storms?
reasoning: Competent review of state-machine changes requires the machine's full transition table (diff shows changed lines only). Read adjacent close/open/error handlers and timers, plus the incident record driving the change. So review validates the fix's claimed invariants rather than merely its syntax.
answer: Review context composition: (1) full reconnect lifecycle file(s): open/close/error handlers, heartbeat timers, backoff state, resubscribe logic: changes in send() interact with close() races outside the diff: map invariants first (e.g., 'after close(1006), exactly one reconnect timer pending, socket singleton never doubles': check whether the diff can produce two sockets when open fires after a manual close: the classic double-socket zombie this class of PR introduces BY FIXING THE OBVIOUS PATH only); (2) incident history (the storm postmortem): the fix must address the storm's mechanics: server restarts → all clients reconnect simultaneously without jitter → overload → closes: if the PR adds backoff WITHOUT jitter and no resubscribe-idempotence, review asks for the amplification fixes (reported evidence: the incident doc demanded jitter: diff lacks it: syntactically fine, semantically incomplete); (3) test evidence promised: does the PR include storm-simulation (reconnect flood test with fake timers asserting backoff distribution) and the NO-double-socket invariant test? absence under a 'resilience' claim = request-changes territory; (4) environment configs (LB idle timeout for WS: 60s typical: heartbeat interval must be shorter: read the deploy config constant and CHECK the PR heartbeat number against it: a 45s heartbeat with a 60s LB works; if PR sets 90s it's wrong-by-config-facts beyond the diff). Verdict rule: review-for-invariants supported by adjacent code + incident facts; diff-quality alone approves typos, not resilience. Conclusion: assemble lifecycle machine files + the driving incident + config constants (LB timeouts): review the invariants the diff must preserve, including the pathologies it didn't address.

instruction: 'Then vs Now' task: understand why a migration from redux to zustand is half-done and decide where the boundary is. Options: load all stores, load docs, or trace a couple of feature flows end to end. Which context strategy resolves mixed-paradigm occupancy?
reasoning: Mixed-paradigm states are understood by occupancy mapping. Which domains still live in which store, and what the coupling between them looks like today. A few end-to-end feature traces reveal that faster and more accurately than bulk-reading both universes.
answer: Strategy: (1) census first, shallow: list the redux slices (reducers/index) and zustand stores (grep create( ), then tabulate domains per paradigm (auth in redux, cart in zustand, notifications BOTH?? dual-write zones are where half-migrations hide their pain: flag any domain with producers in both paradigms as 'contested': those are the bugs' home); (2) then trace 2 flows END-TO-END: pick one fully-in-zustand-domain feature (new-write style) and one CONTESTED domain feature: follow events: dispatch → selector → component: in contested zones, look for synchronization shims (useEffect syncing redux→zustand copies: dual-writes with drift windows, and mixed selectors reading inconsistent snapshots mid-UX: these are the actual risks to name); (3) decide boundary-target by coupling evidence, not aesthetics: a principled interim rule like 'new domains → zustand only; redux domains frozen with additions requiring ADR; sync shims allowed at explicitly listed seams, each with a migration ticket and expiry' — then enforcing via lint (no new redux slices; no new imports of redux in zustand files) + tracking domain counts dashboard (burndown of redux domains); (4) read docs last: an RFC stating the migration intent (breadth-first vs domain-by-domain) tells you if half-done is policy or drift: the decision whether to continue, finish, or formally adopt the dual-state as the architecture (rarely right, but honest) depends on that intent plus the cost map you now have. Bulk-reading all stores would bury these answers in detail. Conclusion: census domains by paradigm, trace representative flows (especially contested ones), surface sync-shim risks, then codify an interim boundary with lint + burndown before reading strategy docs.

instruction: Security task: 'audit permission checks on file attachment downloads.' Options: read all controllers, the auth middleware, the attachments service+storage layer, or the IAM policy files. Which forms the correct audit set, and what non-code sources must join?
reasoning: Authorization correctness is verified at ENFORCEMENT points along every path to the object (HTTP handlers, signed-URL issuers, background emailers), not by counting policy docs. Enumerate paths to the resource first, then the check at each, plus infra-level ACs on the storage (bucket policy).
answer: Audit set: (1) enumerate ALL read-paths to attachments, not all controllers: grep for download routes, res.sendFile/redirect-to-storage, signedUrl issuance (search the storage SDK calls: getSignedUrl/presign), inline preview endpoints (images rendered: /attachments/:id/raw with content-type variants), export/zipping jobs (background bundlers that include files!), emails attaching proxies; each is an enforcement opportunity or bypass; (2) per path, the CHECK: centralized policy or inline (download/:id checks can(user, attachment) → good single point; signed-URL issuer: does it verify requester vs object binding? The classic IDOR: /attachments/:id/signed-url returns a presigned S3 link for any id: the URL becomes an unguessable bearer token: policy applied at ISSUANCE is the only control: re-verify per-object); (3) storage layer itself: S3 bucket policy / ACLs (if PublicAccessBlock mis-set or policy allows s3:GetObject on * in some prefix, all app checks are moot: infra evidence from tf files or console export joins the audit: THE non-code source)); other non-code: CDN behaviors caching attachment GETs (private objects cached publicly at edges = leak channel: check cache rules + signed-cookie config), and log pipelines for signed URLs in plaintext (contain the token: access to logs = access to files: flag); (4) IAM policy files: read but as context for the bucket layer, not the app layer. Deliverable: path×check matrix with evidence (test per row: unauthenticated, wrong-user, authorized cases), storage-config appendix. Conclusion: enumerate every path to the object (including jobs, previews, exports), verify checks at each, and audit storage-level ACLs/CDN/logging as equal members of the enforcement surface.

instruction: Task: 'get this repo running locally for a backend dev new to the team.' Which docs matter in order: README, .env.example, docker-compose.yml, package.json scripts, docs/onboarding.md (3 years old), Makefile?
reasoning: Bootstrap truth ordering. Executable config (compose, Makefile, scripts) outranks prose; .env.example is the config contract. Old docs rot (verify against scripts). Walk the dependency-install-run chain with each step's verification before reading history-laden documentation.
answer: Order: (1) package.json scripts + Makefile: enumerate the intended verbs (dev, setup, seed, test): names reveal the workflow the team actually runs (make setup often wraps: install → env → compose up → migrate → seed); Makefile targets' timestamps (recent commits touching them = maintained); (2) docker-compose.yml: the service topology + images/ports + healthchecks: the external-dependency contract (postgres 15, redis, localstack?): start these first (compose up -d) and verify health (compose ps: wait healthy since 'starting' masks failures: the #1 onboarding failure is migrating against an unready DB); (3) .env.example: copy to .env: READ every var (which are critical vs optional: DATABASE_URL consistency with compose's ports: common mismatch: compose exposes 5433 but example says 5432: port collision relabels land here: verify against compose); identify any vars requiring secrets (quasi-optional for dev: mocked?); (4) README: only now: read for project-specific gotchas (monorepo init command, native deps like libvips: platform notes), cross-checking against what you just did (mismatches = note as doc-debt PR); (5) docs/onboarding.md (3 years): treat as archaeology: skim for concepts (what worker vs web means), verify every command against scripts before suggesting it: flag stale blocks with dates in your onboarding report; (6) the SEED step: run migrations+seed: errors now are either env wiring (fix) or actual repo decay (CI green? then likely YOUR env: compare versions node -v vs .nvmrc!). Report: a working run + a diff-list of doc-staleness filed as issues (onboarding debt repaid). Conclusion: execute config-first with verification at each step (prose last, dated docs suspicious), and capture staleness as actionable debt.

instruction: 'Explain the request flow for POST /checkout' to a new agent. Options: read every file in the import tree, or curated trace: router → controller → service → repository → DB plus the async job it enqueues and the webhook consumer it triggers. What makes a good REQUEST-SHAPED context for flow explanation?
reasoning: Request flows are narrative paths, not module inventories. Follow the request object through layers naming the transformations at each boundary, INCLUDING the async edges (queue publish, webhook delivery) that complete the observable behavior. Prune siblings at each layer aggressively.
answer: Curated trace construction: (1) registration evidence: route table/mount chain establishing the actual URL → middlewares (authz? idempotency key middleware? validation schema) → controller: cite files:line for each hop so the reader can verify; (2) per-layer transformation vocabulary: controller unmarshals DTO + calls usecase; service: domain rules (inventory check, pricing) + orchestrates tx; repository: SQL/ORM statements (name them); boundaries of DB txn (what commits when); (3) async completion: the outbox/event published inside the txn (if present), the worker consuming it (payment-intent creation + fulfillment steps), and the inbound webhook from the PSP confirming funds → order state machine transitions: a flow narrative missing these edges misleads ('checkout' silently continues after 200 OK, and the 200 semantics ('accepted') matter); (4) prune: every layer has siblings (auth service internals, other controllers, models catalog): cite contract-only (signature + responsibility + WHERE the reader dives deeper if needed); (5) draw the artifact: a compact diagram or annotated sequence with file:line anchors (renderable in docs), plus a 5-item 'where bugs of class X live' index (validation errors = schema layer; double charges = idempotency middleware/worker; totals = pricing service): intentional reading map built once, reused per feature. Effort split: most effort on async edges and txn boundaries (least documented parts), least on controller boilerplate. Conclusion: build curated flow narratives with per-hop citations and async completion paths, pruning sibling detail into navigable signposts: trees of imports are not flows.

instruction: Manager: 'why does staging occasionally serve prod data?!' You must choose context fast: env var files, proxy configs, the DB resolution code, or analytics code. Given 'occasionally' and cross-environment, what's the highest-signal artifact class to open first, and the reasoning behind the order?
reasoning: Cross-env data bleed in otherwise separate deployments is almost always configuration identity. An env var pointing at the wrong resource (shared DB URL, copy-paste from prod), or layered overrides where one env's file shadows another inconsistently (per-instance drift). The resolution code + the effective env per instance are the signal. Proxies rarely route DB connections.
answer: Highest-signal order: (1) effective config artifacts: this repo's env-loading code (config.ts: how files+env merge) to know where DATABASE_URL could possibly come from, then the deployed instances' actual env (platform dashboard values per service instance: staging has N instances: ONE misconfigured replica explains 'occasionally' perfectly: request lands on prod-pointed instance 1/6th of the time: match symptom shape!): dump and diff each instance: look for DATABASE_URL/REDIS_URL/ES host in staging values; (2) the DB code only insofar as it logs target host at boot (add if missing: one line logging host WITHOUT credentials: future diagnosis becomes grep-level); (3) proxy configs: only if the app reaches DB through a sidecar/proxy (pGBouncer? then the proxy's config per deployment is the identity: check its env feed instead); analytics code irrelevant (it receives, doesn't decide). Root-cause families for 'occasionally': per-instance drift (one canary/old instance not redeployed after rotate), in-app env-file fallback order (a stale .env.production baked into the image used selectively), build-time vs runtime env confusion (staging image built with prod env inlined: serves prod ALWAYS though: not 'occasionally': distinguishes). Fix per finding: normalize instance envs, remove fallback-file mechanisms for secrets (env-only), boot-log targets, and a startup guard: staging builds REFUSE to boot against prod hostnames (allowlist check: cheap config-lint code: the regression vaccine). Conclusion: 'occasionally cross-env' → per-instance effective-config diff + resolution code + boot-logged identity, plus a boot-time guard refusing cross-env hostnames.

instruction: The agent gets: 'our emails render broken in Outlook desktop only (dark button unreadable)'. Email code: React Email components → compiled HTML → provider sends. Which files get attention: React components, compiled output, provider settings, or Outlook-specific conditional markup? WebKit mindset is the trap.
reasoning: Outlook desktop renders via Microsoft Word engine. Subset CSS, no modern features (border-radius limited, margin rules differ, dark-mode auto-inversion mangles colors). The fix zone is email-compiler patterns (conditional MSO markup, VML backgrounds, inline styles, MSO dark-mode meta) — inspect COMPILED OUTPUT against an Outlook capability list, not React elegance.
answer: Attention map: (1) the compiled HTML OUTPUT first: the artifact Outlook consumes: check for Word-engine-incompatible CSS (buttons via div+padding with border-radius: Outlook needs table-based buttons or VML fallback for rounded+background; dark mode: Outlook force-inverts unless meta tags (color-scheme supported) and explicit !important color guards: button text becomes inherited-gray-on-inverted-gray: exactly 'unreadable'); target where the component emitted these constructs; (2) the React Email components then: mapping which produce incompatible output (a Button component with display:inline-block div: swap pattern: use their Outlook-safe components or conditional blocks <!--[if mso]>…<![endif]--> with VML/Table fallback), knowing ANY React-side elegant abstraction is fine ONLY if compiler output passes (3); (3) provider settings: rarely causal for RENDERING (sending infra irrelevant here; exception: provider auto-CSS-inliners sometimes break conditionals: confirm they're not stripping MSO comments: some do!); (4) verification loop: send test to an Outlook-instrumented service (Litmus/Email on Acid or a real Windows+Outlook box: web-preview lies: must be the Word engine): iterate until pass in Outlook dark+light; add rendered screenshot test to CI email-suite per template (currently only web-client snapshots exist: gap named). Conclusion: Outlook = Word engine: read compiled HTML against its capability table, apply MSO conditionals/VML/table-button patterns in components, verify in actual Outlook dark mode, and snapshot-test email templates per engine class.

instruction: 'Reduce cold-start for the checkout lambda from 6s to <1.5s.' Candidates for context: the lambda handler, its import tree, the bundler config, runtime metrics (init duration spans), error monitor. What constitutes the measurement-first toolset for cold-start budgets?
reasoning: Cold-start cost decomposes into load (bundle size/eager imports) and init (top-level side effects). Metrics tracing init phases reveal which dominates BEFORE reading code. Then inspect only the heaviest import subtrees and top-level clients. Speculative import-trimming wastes hours on noise modules.
answer: Measurement-first: (1) runtime data: X-Ray/otel init-phase spans or platform INIT_REPORT logs (the init duration per cold start) + bundle stats (artifact size, largest modules via esbuild visualize/webpack stats): 6s at 6MB bundles usually = init-side effects & SDK clients; 50MB bundles = parse/load dominated: treatment differs (lazy loading vs tree shaking/decision-made differently); (2) import-cost profile: tools (require-so-slow / --cpu-prof on cold boot / lambda-optimize packages) ranking module load times: hits like aws-sdk v2 whole-sdk (500ms), full ORM init at module scope (2s), heavy crypto init: enumerate top 10; (3) inspect only top-offender modules & the handler's module-scope (anything running at import: db.connect() top-level = per-cold-start connection + TLS handshake: solution pattern: lazy + reuse across warm invocations via cached promises; secrets fetched at cold start serially: batched/cached); (4) bundler config: minify/tree-shake status on the deployed artifact (surely unminified? check), externals (aws-sdk v3 provided by runtime: don't bundle), sourcemaps inline?; (5) fixes armed with numbers: convert to lazy init, swap to v3 modular clients, defer non-critical init post-first-response (fire-and-forget warmup), bundle slimming; re-measure INIT_REPORT after each: ship the delta table in the PR. Error monitor: ignore for this task (relevance: zero cold-start info). Conclusion: decompose cold-start by measured phases first; read only the top-cost modules and module-scope side effects; budget-driven fixes verified by before/after init telemetry.

instruction: Marketing asked: 'add UTM capture to signup.' Agents often load the whole analytics pipeline. The signup submit handler, the analytics client wrapper, and how events reach the warehouse. Pick and justify the context envelope for this bounded feature.
reasoning: Bounded features need one path's pipeline, not the whole analytics estate. Capture point (signup form submit. Where params must already be stored before submit), attribution store (session/first-touch persistence), event emission (existing wrapper conventions), and the downstream contract (warehouse schema rows), proving each hop satisfies UTM keys.
