Almost always yes (one comparison operator/page-boundary computation): so the fix ships standalone: minimal diff, regression test asserting count-across-pages, done; (2) assess whether the structural issue AMPLIFIES the symptom's cost: OFFSET at page 4000 makes pages slow (perf complaint exists separately?) vs merely inelegant: cost evidence collected into the escalation doc (query timings at deep pages, total-count query cost, count mismatch examples users see); the escalation sells the rewrite; emotion never does; (3) escalation artifact: a short ADR/proposal: problem (with measured blast), options (cursor pagination design sketch, keyset pagination with the sort-key constraints named, compat strategy: existing clients holding page=N links: hybrid? short URLs?), migration path (dual-read period, code-owners affected, rollout order), risks; (4) review economics: leaving both in one PR: reviewers see 40 changed files flavored as 'off-by-one': review fatigue merges structural bugs under a trivial title: incidents ratify the shortcut ('merged with the pagination fix' becomes archaeology); (5) the anti-pattern avoiding both extremes: don't ship the tiny fix and quietly forget the escalation (rot vanishes into personal memory): the issue must EXIST, ranked; and don't rewrite unrequested (mandate drift). Also note: if the fix itself PROVES internals wrong in ways QA relied on (a test asserting the off-by-one as expected: tests encode the bug: fix those fixtures transparently in the same PR: that IS in-scope). Conclusion: fix the symptom minimally, quiet the bleeding, then escalate structural change via measured ADR literature: rewrite-resistance is scope discipline, not cowardice.

instruction: Agent receives: 'Upgrade React 17 to 18.' Mid-migration: the team's internal component library needs migration too, legacy class components rely on deprecated lifecycles, and the test setup mounts differently. Which parts are legitimately INSIDE the upgrade's blast radius, and which are tempting excursions?
reasoning: A major upgrade's honest blast radius = what the upgrade's contract breaks (cry for help in build/tests), not everything unfashionable adjacent. Inside: concurrent-mode hazards of mounted libraries, test harness mounting, StrictMode double-effects. Outside (usually): aesthetic modernization of class components, state-library re-architecture.
answer: Radius sorting: inside (breakage-driven, not preference): (1) the internal component library: IF it touches APIs with changed semantics (hydration API move, StrictMode double-invoke surfacing its effect bugs, children-prop typing change in TS react 18): then it's in the radius with a checklist as long as the errors, test-failures, and its version-matrix (the library's consumers pin its release: coordinate releases: library 4.x supports React 18: repo updates both atomically?); (2) test setup (mounting utilities: ReactDOM.render→createRoot: adapter updates, act() warnings now fail-loud): required since CI red = upgrade unfinished; (3) TypeScript/react type bumps (children implicit removal) fixing only compile errors mechanically; (4) documented behavior risks specific to react 18: automatic batching altering code that relied on sync-render-after-setState (measure-flashes): audit the handful of setTimeout/read-after-setState sites: target audit is in-radius because behavior silently changed; excursions (outside unless mandated): rewriting class components to hooks 'while we're here' (deprecated lifecycles still work: risk-y rewrites are their own project), adopting suspense architecture, replacing the state library, opportunistic dependency freshening beyond peer-requirement; (5) project shape: upgrade PR = version bumps + compile/test fixes + createRoot + seeded audit fixes with before/after e2e: everything else in follow-ups visible to planning (library-major as its own milestone when independent, 'compat shim' when the repo-side must land first). Budget rule of thumb: the upgrade is DONE when main is green, smoke flows pass, and the audit-list items are resolved-or-explicit-ticketed: not when the codebase feels modern. Conclusion: define the radius by contract-breakage and behavior-change audits; aesthetic neighbors get tickets; timeline honesty beats elegant collapse of distinct risks into 'the upgrade'.

instruction: Code review of YOUR (agent) PR: reviewer asks 'while you're in here, can you also fix the X edge case?' — seductive adjacency. How do agents decide when review-time scope creep acceptance is merited vs. when push-back preserves review integrity?
reasoning: Adjacency requests split by shared-invariant (same property, same tests, same review burden → cheap accept) vs orthogonal-behavior (new requirement in rented clothes → push back with issue+followup). Criteria. Blast-radius union, review burden, and whether deferral harms correctness of THIS PR.
answer: Decision criteria: (1) invariant-overlap: the PR changes input sanitization; the requested edge case is another unsanitized input the SAME function touches: the tests to add sit beside the PR's tests, the reviewer already holds the context, the property 'all inputs sanitized' completes here → accepting is CHEAPER than the motion of a new PR (cognitive piggyback legitimate: scope discipline measures JOINT review burden, not ticket count); (2) correctness-dependence: the requested change is REQUIRED for this PR's promise ('your partial fix breaks X edge case as-is': then X is in-scope by definition: the PR's invariant is unsound without it: either absorb or retract the PR: no third option); (3) when to push back: orthogonal behavior change (X lives in different module/ownership, needs product input or its own QA: 'happy to: filing ISSUE-1234 and prefer a follow-up PR where the X team can own the semantics: keeping this one reviewable'), risk-compounding (PR already large: growing it slows merge of a live bugfix: state the cost explicitly), or standards covert-changes (the request embeds an un-discussed convention shift masked as edge-case fix: surface the convention question instead of implementing its exemplar); (4) etiquette mechanics: whatever the answer, the response NAMES the decision rule used ('same-invariant, same-test-file → accepted' vs 'orthogonal ownership → filing'), netting reviewers a reusable map of your philosophy: subsequent reviews get faster and trustier; (5) the systemic fix when adjacency-requests pile up: the PR template's scope-line ('this PR promises: ...') makes deviations describable: teams with written promises debate promises, not vibes. Conclusion: accept shared-invariant sweets, absorb correctness-blockers, and push back orthogonal work with tickets and named rules: scope integrity is a property of reviewability, not stubbornness.

instruction: Manager non-negotiably bundles: 'While fixing the payment timeout, also make the retries smarter and the logs better.' Three wishes, one ticket. How does an agent handle mandated-bundled scope: sequencing, PR-splitting where possible, and honest pricing of the bundle?
reasoning: Mandated bundles deserve honest decomposition even when they must ship together. Separate the incident-fix from the enhancement pieces (retry policy, observability), sequence them with independent verification, and price each so the cost-accounting survives the merge.
answer: Handling: (1) decomposition table up front (in the ticket reply, respectful): three work items: (a) timeout fix (the bleeding: root cause per the trace + targeted fix + regression test), (b) retry policy (backoff-with-jitter, idempotency guarantees: touches a different module + needs different test harness (failure-injection), a design choice (exponential vs decorrelated-jitter) worth showing), (c) log improvements (structured events, request-id propagation: no behavior change, but reviewers differ (platform team owns logging format): separate reviewer optics); (2) sequencing: (a) ships first and hot (today if possible): incidents outrank enhancements regardless of bundling politics; (b)+(c) ride a normal cycle; if the manager insists on one deploy, the COMMITS stay separated in one PR stack with per-commit verification legible (stacked-diff tools or at least clean commit slicing: archeologists will thank you); (3) risk labeling per piece: retry-policy changes carry thundering-herd class risk (needs the 2-sided capacity arithmetic from the knob-discipline: present it); logs: low-risk but high-diff-noise: call it out so the (a) fix doesn't hide in (c)'s churn; (4) honest pricing: give (a) hours, (b) 2-3 days including failure-injection tests, (c) 1 day + platform-review latency: the sum tells the manager the bundle is a week, not an afternoon: next time bundling happens consciously rather than phonetically; (5) also warn on the coupling pitfall: deploying (b) before understanding whether (a)'s fix changes the failure shape (retry storms might vanish with the real fix: enhancing retries for a world that no longer exists: data after (a) should inform (b)'s urgency). Conclusion: bundles decompose into separately verifiable items with incident-first sequencing, legible commit slicing, per-piece risk labels, and honest day-pricing: the bundle may deploy together, but it must not think together.

instruction: Task: 'Make the README setup instructions actually work for Windows developers.' The README is generally outdated (old logo, dead links, v1 claims). The Windows fixes need only the setup section. What stays in-focus, and how do drive-by doc-fixes differ from drive-by code-fixes in scope ethics?
reasoning: Doc tasks share scope discipline with code but differ. Doc fixes are lower-risk and reviewable almost free, yet a 'README overhaul' balloon buries the promised Windows-verified improvements in noise, and unverified claims (logo aside) rot faster. Keep the promised section verified-and-shipping, issue-file or clearly separate-commit the rest.
answer: Focus plan: (1) the mandate: make setup-verified-for-Windows the PR's backbone: actually RUN the steps in a Windows environment (VM or a teammate's machine: PowerShell vs CMD differences, path separators, core.autocrlf landmines, node-gyp/Visual-Studio-build-tools requirements, WSL2 question answered EXPLICITLY (supported native or only via WSL? say which, with reasons)); every command as pasted must run; record the verification (screenshots/terminal transcript link in PR: doc PRs carrying proof are rare and precious); (2) doc-specific scope ethics: dead links / old logo: technically easy, low-risk, BUT they bloat review attention and mix verification-classes (link-checks are CI-able; the logo is marketing-owned: touching it without asking creates politics): recommend: keep the setup section surgical; open a follow-up issue 'README hygiene sweep' listing link-check output (lychee run: paste results: gift) and brand questions for the owner; (3) the exception class: fixes that are prerequisites to the mandate's promise (setup section references a dead link NOW: then fixing THAT link IS the mandate: entitlement-by-dependency, noted in the PR body); (4) anti-bloat structures if you do bundle small doc fixes: physical separation (distinct commits: 'setup-windows' vs 'readme-hygiene') so reviewers can rubber-stamp hygiene while squinting at the verified section; never let hygiene prose push the verified section out of the PR body's headline; (5) durable asset: add the commands-as-scripts (scripts/setup-windows.ps1) so the README references executable truth + a CI smoke job on windows-latest running the script weekly: Windows-support stops being folklore (this IS scope-adjacent but verify-class-equal: flag it in the PR as the guarantee mechanism). Conclusion: verify-and-ship the promised section with run-evidence, hygienically issue-file the rest, fix-by-dependency only what the promise touches, and prefer executable setup scripts + platform CI so the claims stay alive.

instruction: 'Add a health-check endpoint.' Then someone suggests: also add startup checks, readiness/liveness split, detailed dependency checks, and a dashboard JSON. Kubernetes probes will consume this. What's the minimum viable contract for k8s use, and what's the staged buildout that won't gold-plate v1?
reasoning: Health endpoints for k8s have precise minimal needs (liveness. Process alive. Readiness. Can serve), each with distinct semantics. Gold-plating risk is high because health endpoints look trivial until dependency-checks cause cascading restarts. Stage. Minimal probes first, dependency details cold-pathed separately, dashboards last.
answer: Minimum viable contract (v1): (1) /livez: returns 200 if the event loop/request loop functions (no dependency checks! liveness wired x dependencies = restart cascades when redis hiccups: self-inflicted outage class: reserve liveness for 'am I alive'); (2) /readyz: checks ONLY what readiness-gating requires: DB connectivity essential? (if the app dead-without-DB, readiness false while DB down: k8s holds the pod out of rotation: correct), optional dependencies excluded (no redis? degrade-and-serve rather than unready: traffic-serving ability is the criterion, learned from k8s semantics: readiness about ROUTING, not morality of subsystem completeness); (3) response format: 200/503 + terse reason: no giant JSON yet (probe payload size actually counted in latency at scale); (4) timeout posture: probes must answer fast (< probe timeout seconds: dependency checks with their own 100-300ms timeouts internally, not blocking on a lying socket for minutes). Staged buildout: v2: /healthz/details page (non-probed, for humans/dashboard) carrying per-dependency checks with statuses/latencies (consumed by ops, never by kubelet: prevents restart-cascade regressions) + startupProbe only if cold-start long (JVM-class: k8s startupProbe vs initialDelaySeconds decision: measured cold-start needed to choose); v3: metrics for probe outcomes over time (alerting on readiness-flapping rather than instance-restarts), dashboard JSON if material value shown. Each stage justified by an observed need with the dependency-wiring rule repeated everywhere: kubelet-facing semantics differ from human-facing diagnostics. Conclusion: v1 = minimal livez/readyz respecting routing-vs-alive semantics and dependency-cascade hygiene; details/dashboards/startup probes land in staged versions behind diagnosed needs, never as speculative architecture.

instruction: Feature buildout: 'a CSV export of the users table.' Ambiguity farm: which columns? which users (filtered by current admin view? permissions-scoped?)? size limits? streaming or async? In scope-free tasks, what's the clarification protocol vs the acceptable-defaults protocol?
reasoning: Ambiguous features don't justify interrogation-storms. Use acceptable-defaults for low-cost-reversal choices (columns = visible list columns + documented additions), but REQUIRE decision-owners for irreversible or high-risk choices (PII exposure scope, permission semantics, giant-dataset delivery mode).
answer: Protocols: ask-first (blocking, risk-irreversible): (1) permission semantics: does the export honor the admin's view filters and row-level rights (exporting 'all users' silently bypassing the shared-view scoping = a PII disclosure incident class: spreadsheets escape systems: escalate: 'the export will respect the requesting admin's visible scope — confirm?'); (2) column-level PII inclusion: email/phone/DOB presence: does the use-case legitimately need them (purpose-limitation question: ask the requester 'who consumes the CSV and for what': marketing-import answers differ from finance-reconciliation answers: include minimum necessary: also affects retention guidance); (3) dataset scale: row count upper-bound (query: count(*)): decides sync-stream vs async-with-notification (a 5m-row sync export kills the API: decide from data, not vibes). Acceptable-defaults (ship, document, note as adjustable): columns = the admin table's visible columns + created_at (documented in the export dialog), ordering = id ascending, encoding = UTF-8 with BOM for Excel-friendliness (+ documented), delimiter = comma with proper quoting (RFC 4180), filename = users-export-{date}.csv, limits = hard-cap with clear error (better than silent truncation), format = no styling (CSV not XLSX: XLSX-request becomes its own ticket). Ship-notes listing every default with 'tell us to change any of these' convert post-hoc complaint into cheap configurability; (4) record the decisions in the PR body AS the scope statement: future enhancement requests join a visible list (streaming, column-picker UI, scheduled exports) rather than ballooning v1 in the dark. Conclusion: block only on permission/PII/scale questions (risk-shaped), ship explicit-documented defaults elsewhere with a visible decisions list: ambiguity gets resolved by risk classification, not by per-field polling.

instruction: Bugfix PR for a login error-message typo. Teammate comments: 'this file imports are a mess, please sort them.' Imports are indeed unsorted, and the file has no lint rule enforcing sort order. Drive-by-lint discipline: when do formatting requests become scope abuse, and what's the etiquette both ways?
reasoning: Formatting-without-enforcement requests inflate unrelated diffs, spawn merge conflicts for parallel work, and make review noisy. Etiquette. Rules belong in linters (enforce or stop discussing), reviewers ask formatting via follow-up issues or lint-rule PRs, authors may decline politely citing the no-rule status.
answer: Discipline: (1) classify the request: cosmetic unenforced (import ordering with no eslint-plugin-import sort rule: pure taste) vs enforced-but-lagging (rule exists, this file grandfathered: then fixing is debt-paydown and MAY still not belong in a typo PR: check repo norms on grandfathered-file practices: some repos: 'leave it cleaner than you found' applies to FILES CHANGED SUBSTANTIALLY, not one-line typo targets); (2) cost articulation: in a hot file (frequently edited: login.js likely IS hot: 3 parallel branches conflict constantly), a 40-line import-reorder in a typo PR manufactures conflicts for strangers: name this gently: 'import sorting will conflict with teammate's open branch touching login.js; prefer the lint-rule PR so sorting becomes automatic everywhere at once'; (3) the durable answer (either side may propose): add eslint-plugin-import's order rule (or the repo's formatter choice) as its own PR with auto-fix run across the repo: formatting ceases to be a review topic forever (the only legitimate formatting fix is the one that deletes the conversation); (4) both-ways etiquette: reviewer: phrase as question + offer the rule-PR path ('want a lint rule for this? happy to pair'), avoid blocking approval on taste; author: don't die on the hill either: if the team norm is sort-on-touch in THIS repo (CONTRIBUTING says so), sorting in an isolated commit within your PR is fine (commit-slicing preserves reviewability: 'fix typo' vs 'sort imports (no logic)' commits separately); (5) agent-specific note: models trained on diffs love pleasing reviewers by expanding diffs: resist: the best review-response currency is principled refusals-with-alternatives, not bulk compliance. Conclusion: unenforced formatting in hot files: decline-with-rule-PR offer, or isolate into no-logic commits when repo-norms demand; the system-level outlet for taste is lint config, never typo-PR diff growth.

instruction: The ticket: 'improve error handling in webhook consumer.' The consumer has 6 distinct failure modes (bad signature, schema-violation payload, downstream 429, downstream 5xx, poison payload crashing the handler, ack-ordering bugs). One 'improvement' PR covering all six becomes un-reviewable. What's the fault-message decomposition that lets each failure mode get the review it deserves?
reasoning: Error-handling upgrades decompose by failure MODE because each has distinct semantics (retryable vs not, alertable vs not, DLQ-worthy vs drop) and distinct reviewers/QA. A matrix where each mode gets (detection, classification, action, telemetry) rows reviewed independently prevents mode-conflation bugs.
answer: Decomposition: (1) mode registry first (a markdown table in the PR description of PR #1 or an issue): per mode: detection (sign: signature-verify fail), class (security: NO RETRY, alert on volume spikes: attack signal), action (reject 401 fast, minimal logging of signed-prefix), telemetry (metric+sampled-log); repeat for schema-violation (validation rejects: not retryable: DLQ+report to sender report-card: alert threshold per-source), 429 (retryable honoring Retry-After: bounded, jitter), 5xx (retryable: exponential backoff, circuit-breaker after sustained), poison-crash (crash-loop detection via redelivery-count: DLQ after N with payload-quarantine: never retry infinitely), ack-ordering (ack ONLY after durable write: two-phase discipline: audit the flow, failure-injection tests); (2) PR-per-mode (or per 2 modes max, grouped by shared mechanics: retryable-family 429+5xx share the backoff engine: co-reviewed): each PR: its row of the matrix implemented + mode-specific tests (signature test vectors, malformed payloads fixtures, fault-injection of downstream codes, redelivery-loop simulation): reviewers hold ONE mode's truth at a time; (3) sequencing architecture-first: the first PR adds the CLASSIFICATION layer (error taxonomy enum + dispatcher: each mode currently mapped to its CURRENT best-effort action: behavior-preserving refactor only, green-CI proof, no semantic change): subsequent PRs upgrade one cell at a time: diffs become small and behavior-scoped (this is strangler-fig quality applied to error semantics); (4) the reviewer-map: security-minded reviewer for signature-mode PR, platform-resilience reviewer for backoff-engine PR, data-integrity reviewer for ack-ordering: addressed to expertise instead of one giant review Roulette; (5) end-state: the matrix doc lives in-repo beside the consumer, updated per PR: becomes the failure-mode contract future senders/integrators read. Conclusion: failure modes are separate semantic units: taxonomy-first refactor in isolation, then mode-per-PR upgrades with mode-appropriate reviewers and fault-injection tests: 'improve error handling' arrives as a reviewed fleet, not a blur.

instruction: Agent told: 'Fix the N+1 in the orders list endpoint ONLY: do not touch other endpoints right now' (a staged performance program exists). During the fix, the same N+1 pattern is visible in 5 sibling endpoints. What does 'ONLY' scope-loyalty look like in practice, including how you transfer the knowledge without violating the staging?
reasoning: Explicit scope limits often encode planned rollout (measurement-per-stage, regression attribution). Loyalty. Fix exactly the target endpoint, prove it, and transfer sibling knowledge as a structured issue-map so the program owner schedules the rest with full data.
answer: Loyalty in practice: (1) the mandated endpoint: fix with the endpoint-scoped include/batching approach, plus its query-count regression test (assert the constant-bound explicit: this also becomes the template the other endpoints will copy: in-scope as it guards YOUR fix); (2) sibling knowledge transfer WITHOUT editing: write the issue (or update the program's tracker): per sibling endpoint: file:line of the lazy-load access, observed query-shape (from staged query logs: evidence not rumor), estimated severity (fanout cardinality: orders→items vs orders→items→item→options: differ), and the proposed identical-fix-pattern one-liner referencing your PR as the template: this is the knowledge gift that respects the staging; (3) why loyalty matters here (say it plainly if pushed): the staged program likely measures each endpoint's fix ROI separately (before/after p95 per endpoint: attribution science: bundling 6 endpoints into one unmeasured landing destroys the program's dataset); plus mixed diffs make rollbacks surgical-or-nothing; (4) the exception triage: if a sibling is ACTIVELY the top-3 production-slowest endpoint (check the slow-log over a week), a heads-up message to the program owner ('sibling /orders/export bleeds worst: recommend pulling forward') beats silent compliance-but also beats unilateral heroics: ONE escalation, decided by the owner; (5) resist pattern-smuggling: shared helper extraction ('I extracted a batching utility used only by my endpoint for now') is acceptable IF tiny and used by your fix; pre-migrating siblings 'to the utility' is NOT: the migration wave belongs to later stages where it can be measured per endpoint. Conclusion: fix the one, guard the one, report the many with evidence-per-sibling and offer one measured escalation: scope limits in staged programs protect attribution, which protects engineering honesty.

instruction: Big refactor merged where 'logic shouldn't change, only structure.' Post-merge: subtle behavior DID change (bug). The merge commit is 200 files. What's the bisection-within-refactors strategy, and what refactor-discipline would have made this recoverable?
reasoning: Behavior leaks in pure-refactors happen via semantic ambiguities hiding in structural moves (evaluation order, laziness, scoping). Recovery: git-bisect with behavior-tests over the refactor range, then intra-commit diff analysis of behavior-sensitive classes (short-circuit, ordering, timing). Prevention: incremental verified moves with characterization tests.
answer: Recovery plan: (1) anchor the behavioral delta into a test FIRST: write the test that distinguishes old-vs-new behavior (characterize the buggy observable exactly): this test is the bisect oracle (bisect run <test>: automatable); (2) git bisect across the refactor range (pre-refactor known-good tag → post-merge bad): 8 bisect steps reduce 200 commits: the CAUSAL commit (small or big) is the review unit: if the refactor was one squash-merged mega-commit, bisection ends at 'the whole PR' and you proceed inside it; (3) intra-commit analysis when the commit is monolithic: apply behavior-sensitive pattern search over its diff: moved function CALL positions relative to awaits (evaluation-order shifts), inlining that duplicated side-effects, lazy→eager conversion (default params evaluated at call-time), closure-capture changes (let→var in hoisting-cultural code), export star ambiguities (default vs named collisions), TZ-dependent code moved into different initialization order; these classes account for most 'structural-only' semantic leaks: audit diff hunks against the class-list; (4) prevention-for-next-time (the retro deliverable): (a) characterization tests written BEFORE the refactor over the touched surface (pin behavior: gray-box I/O oracles: for UI components: DOM-contract snapshots; for services: fixture request/response corpora: they run green across every refactor step); (b) move-then-change commit alternation (rename commit: pure, reviewed; then a separate commit for changed files: never both-in-one); (c) refactor-size budget (a PR ceiling with mechanical changes only: bigger = split by directory/module waves); (d) unusual-semantics checklist in the refactor template (the classes above as explicit questions). Conclusion: turn behavior deltas into oracle tests, bisect to the causal commit, audit behavior-sensitive diff classes when commits are monolithic; make refactors recoverable ex-ante via characterization tests and move/change commit alternation.

instruction: 'Implement dark mode.' The repo has: design tokens half-defined, 200 hardcoded colors, a charting lib with its own theme object, third-party widgets (chat, payments) with fixed skins, and email templates. Which segments define dark-mode-done vs. dark-mode-forever? Define scope rings with delivery strategy.
reasoning: Dark mode explodes combinatorially unless ringing. Core surfaces with token plumbing first (owned CSS), third-party/embedded widgets as constraints (config options or deferred), emails as a separate medium entirely. Rings make 'done' definable per ring with a deferred-register.
answer: Ring decomposition: Ring 1 (the owned app shell, in-scope v1): complete the token set (semantic layer: surface/elevated/text-primary etc. — the half-defined tokens finished FIRST as the API the dark palette plugs into), automated codemod for the 200 hardcoded colors (stylelint-plugin-no-hardcoded-colors as the guardrail; codemod references tokens by mapping table: the mapping REVIEW is the design work: codemod runs free), theme switch (prefers-color-scheme default + override persisted via cookie/server pref: FOUC strategy on first paint), gate tests (dark-theme smoke screenshots of the 8 key screens: screenshot-diff suite scope); Ring 2 (third-party/embedded: scoped SEPARATELY, v1.1): chart lib: theme object wiring (documented token-to-chart mapping: moderate), chat widget: vendor theming API exists? (config knobs vs 'no support' → wrap in fixed-shell decision documented to design), payment widget (PCI iframe: often NO theming: explicitly deferred with product sign-off listing it as a known visual seam: writing 'won't fix' visibly STOPs the weekly pings); Ring 3 (out of app scope entirely: email templates): dark-mode email support is its own medium (clients invert, image considerations: a design project: ticket to email-system owner, explicitly not this feature); decisions on ring-borders get LIGHTING from policy: anything not in the rings needs product review against a deferred-register (the list keeps 'done' definable: v1 ships Rings 1 + register for 2/3 with target dates or explicit deferrals). Effort-reporting per ring (v1 effort vs known follow-ups) prevents the 'dark mode took 6 months' narrative while 90% of users had it in month 1. Conclusion: ring the work (owned-core / vendor-constrained / separate-medium), codemod-with-lint-fences the owned ring, register deferrals with owners and reasons: dark-mode-done is a ring decision published, not a vibe.

instruction: 'While you're migrating the DB, also switch from varchar to uuid ids everywhere' — arrives as a casual addendum to a planned Postgres version upgrade. Why is this the canonical dangerous-bundling, and what risk-math separates acceptable small bundlings from forbidden ones?
reasoning: Bundling is forbidden when risk classes multiply rather than add. An upgrade (engine behavior, planner, extensions) × a data-model identity change (every FK, every external integration, every backup assumption) are independently incident-worthy. Combined, rollback stories collapse and root-cause windows overlap invisibly.
answer: Risk-math framing: (1) independence test: 'if the bundle incidents, can we attribute?': version-upgrade failure signatures (plan regressions, extension incompat, replication-protocol issues) vs id-type-migration signatures (FK integrity breaks, ORM type-mismatch at boundaries, external-webhook id-format parsers dying, reports joining by cached ids): attribution feasible only because signatures differ: BUT: (2) rollback multiplication: the uuid rewrite is effectively irreversible once downstream systems ingest new ids (rollback of the bundle = engine downgrade + id re-conversion: double jeopardy where the safe move exists on neither axis: you're stuck-forward in TWO dimensions simultaneously: the actual forbidden property); (3) blast-radius product: upgrade touches ~every query indirectly (low-depth, wide-surface risk), id-change touches every table directly (high-depth, wide-surface): the Cartesian of the two surfaces = outage-space near-total; (4) acceptable-bundlings math (for contrast): same risk-class, same rollback-unit, additive-not-multiplicative surface: upgrading minor version + bumping the same-day backup retention setting (one rollback verb); renovating one module + its tests (one directory of blast); (5) the professional no: respond with a paragraph of respect: 'uuid migration is valuable and should lead its own quarter with dual-write phases, external-id-compat shims, and bi-directional rollback; riding the engine upgrade denies it the engineering it deserves and hands us a two-dimensional stuck-forward if anything goes sideways: sequencing proposal: upgrade first (with its own rollback drills), id migration next quarter as a designed program': convert refusal into sequencing leadership, not negativism. Conclusion: bundle calculus = independence of attribution × reversibility per axis × blast-radius product: forbid irreversible multi-axis bundles, allow same-class additive ones, and always answer bundling pressure with sequencing proposals instead of just no.

instruction: Mandate: 'Reduce CI pipeline time.' Broad like fog. You have ONE sprint. Decompose into scope-values that make 'done' demonstrable: target metrics, exclusions, and the demonstrable-end-state contract with stakeholders.
reasoning: Fog mandates become demonstrable via measurement-first scope. Pick the target pipeline and percentile-metric (p50/p95 of pr-verify), decompose to find top-2 items fitting a sprint, and define done numerically with baseline→target deltas on a stated cohort, exclusions named.
answer: Contract construction: (1) metric & cohort pinning: 'CI time' = wall-clock of the pr-verify workflow, p50 AND p95 (p50 for median-momentum, p95 for the anger-driver), measured over the 20 most recent weekday runs on main-repo PRs (a dashboard URL the whole team watches); the alternative pipelines (nightly, release) explicitly EXCLUDED from sprint scope (named, parked, and dated: scope rage happens at unwritten exclusion boundaries); (2) decomposition reality: one day of measurement (per-step timestamps: queue wait vs setup vs test vs report: from the earlier discipline: get the top-3 items predicated on data; if queue-wait dominates (capacity classes), the sprint is a platform/negotiation sprint not engineering: say it honestly; stakeholders accept truths with graphs over promises); (3) sprint-scoping to top-2 items with savings arithmetic per item ('cache-key fix: predicted -4m p50, -6m p95 based on miss-rate math': predictions REVIEWED by a skeptical peer before being promised upward); (4) done-state contract: 'post-sprint: dashboard shows p50 from 18→≤12m and p95 27→≤18m on a 20-run cohort post-merge; items shipped listed; unfixed top-items become the next-sprint proposal document; regression monitors on (new flakes? cache-correctness incidents=0)'; the contract's survival rules: measurements by the same dashboard, same metric definitions, over comparable cohorts (no timezone/season swaps); (5) integrity insurance: pre-declare the failure-story protocol ('if -30% not reached, report what the curve says, what was learned, no spin': the scope contract includes honest-failure terms upfront, which is exactly what lets aggressive targets stay aggressive without career-risk backing off them mid-flight); (6) anti-fog extra: the 'what-we-won't-do' list (no rewriting the test suite, no runner-migration, no monorepo-split: the three seductive universe-sized items). Conclusion: turn fog into (metric, cohort, top-2 items, numeric done-state, exclusions, honesty-terms): a scope contract you can be measured against is what 'reduce CI time' always wanted to be.

instruction: Requirement: 'improve accessibility of the checkout.' Infinite-rabbit-hole potential (WCAG AA across 40 screens vs checkout's 6). Formalize scoping via conformance-target and audit-based inventory, so the mandate becomes sprintable without becoming hollow.
reasoning: Accessibility mandates scope by (surface × conformance level × assistive-tech matrix). Checkout's 6 screens against WCAG 2.2 AA with the AT matrix actually used by your customers, inventory by audit (automated + manual keyboard/screen-reader scripts), quantify item count to price sprints honestly.
answer: Scoping mechanics: (1) surface ring: the checkout funnel screens enumerated (cart, shipping, payment, confirm, receipt, error states: + the modals/toasts they spawn: infinite-surface risk through dialogs: list them physically); out-of-ring: marketing pages, settings, emails (registered for later programs); (2) conformance target: WCAG 2.2 AA (state the version+level: company legal exposure docs often mandate: if unknown, AA 2.2 is the defensible default), PLUS explicit AT-matrix (NVDA+Chrome, VoiceOver+Safari/iOS, keyboard-only, 200% zoom: each sampled, not exhaustive: matrices exist because 'full coverage' is a fantasy: sample-based honesty beats coverage-theater); (3) inventory pass to price reality: automated scan (axe per screen: expect dozens of mechanical issues: color-contrast counts, labels: hour-cheap, high-yield), manual audit scripts (keyboard walkthrough of each screen against tab-order/visible-focus/nothing-trapped, SR script for form-error-announcement patterns & dynamic updates aria-live-ness, zoom/reflow check): the audit OUTPUT table (screen × issue × severity × est-effort) IS the scope: count items (say: 41 findings: 12 quick (2h), 20 medium (1d), 9 hard (3d)) → sprint sizing proposal: two sprints cover quick+medium+critical-hard; (4) acceptable-risk register for the residue (some hard items need design-system changes: registered with dates, not silently deferred; legal references risk-register artifacts later: they're professionally protective); (5) regression-proofing within scope: axe-core CI rules for the 6 screens (merges blocked on new violations in-ring) + a quarterly manual audit calendar entry: scope closed, guardrails remain. Hollow-ness avoided because ring+level+matrix+register all exist in writing and the report shows item-counts delivered vs inventory. Conclusion: access-scope = ring × WCAG-level × AT-sample-matrix, priced off a real audit inventory (auto+manual), hardened with CI automation and a named residue register: infinite work turns into priced sprints with defensible done.

instruction: Found during a small bugfix: the entire logging module violates PII policy (request bodies with emails dumped at debug level in prod-configs-that-drift). Bugfix mandate is narrow; the finding is severe. What escalation classes exist for discovered-severity surprises, and when does an agent legitimately break its mandate boundary?
reasoning: Severity-of-discovery outranks mandate-scope. Incidents (active PII exposure in prod) justify immediate containment actions (config flip disabling debug-in-prod) with heightened communication, distinct from optional improvements which keep flowing through issues. Classify. Active-harm → contain+notify now. Latent-severe → same-day escalation. Chronic-priority → issue-track.
answer: Severity classes: (1) ACTIVE-HARM (PII currently written to logs/queryable): this class authorizes mandate-break with discipline: containment-first minimal action (disable debug-level in prod config NOW: lowest-risk one-line deploy via standard hot-path procedure), because the exposure compounds per minute; notification-next: security/privacy owner + the directing manager + a record (incident or security-ticket per org taxonomy: data-residency decisions (who queries logs? access review) are NOT yours to improvise: escalate those with evidence: sample log-lines (redacted screenshots!), affected timeframe via config-history); then return to your bugfix with the incident separated (your PR body doesn't absorb it: contamination-avoidance: incident work rides its own trail); (2) LATENT-SEVERE (would-harm conditions present but dormant: debug-on-flag exists anywhere-reachable, log-retention-long, bodies-logged also at info-level in error paths): same-day escalation document (evidence + exploitability-ish narrative + recommended containment timeline), offer to own the remediation or hand it cleanly: latency is not optional: dormant-PII-rivers wake during every future debugging incident; (3) CHRONIC-PRIORITY (stack smells: no PII-scrub helper: the missing utility enabling the above): normal issue + proposal, referenced from the episode so the fix-list includes root-tooling; (4) agent-discipline for staying-credible: the escalation message distinguishes YOUR evidence from inference (sample-dates, config-lines, code-refs vs your model of consequences); pre-written severity-ladder in your head avoiding both crying-wolf (everything severe = nothing heard) and anchoring-calm (a PII fire deserves raised volume); (5) after-action: if the org's response shows the policy was theater (ticket ignored quarterly), the professional record of escalations (dated, evidence) is your duty performed: you can't force compliance, you can make ignoring it a recorded decision. Conclusion: discoveries triage into active (contain + notify immediately), latent-severe (same-day documented escalation), chronic (issue-flow): mandate-bends only for active-harm with containment-minimalism and separated audit trails.

instruction: 'Make the settings page better.' Zero spec. As an agent: how do you keep vague-improvement mandates from becoming design-by-author fiat, using bounded-discovery outputs that force the requester to express taste as decisions?
reasoning: Vague UX mandates convert into bounded-discovery outputs. A prioritized critique (heuristic audit), quick user-evidence (session replays, support themes), and a decision-menu with 2-3 framed options per decision-point. The author proposes. The requester decides. Both are on the record.
answer: Bounded-discovery flow (timebox: 2-4 hours producing artifacts, no code): (1) audit-artifact: heuristic pass over the settings page (Nielsen-ish checklist × the page's actual content: information-architecture flatness (37 toggles unsorted), naming ambiguity ('Enable notifications' vs 'Email me'), destructive-action patterns (Delete-account next to Save: misclick class), inconsistent save-model (auto-save in one section, button-save in another: the classic settings-page incoherence), a11y quick-scan): output = numbered issue-list with screenshots, each issue SEVERITY-tagged; (2) evidence-artifact: 30 minutes mining: support tickets mentioning settings (themes: 'can't find X', 'didn't save'), session-replay sampling (rage-clicks on toggle groups? exit-rates from settings), analytics (which sections get visited vs dead-weight: rename-or-hide candidates); (3) decision-menu construction: distill to 3-5 decision-points, each with 2-3 options framed with cost/UX-fidelity: e.g., save-model: (a) all-button-save consistent 1d, (b) auto-save everywhere with undo-toast 3d, (c) leave-mixed documented 0d; grouping: (a) thematic sections 2d, (b) search-filter flat list 2d; destructive-actions: (a) separate danger-zone page 1d, (b) confirm-dialogs-only 0.5d; the menu turns taste into checkboxes: the requester replies in minutes; (4) scope-lock record: the reply + the picked options + estimated days become the ticket's spec: implementation references it: no drift accusations later (decisions attributed to deciders, safely); (5) anti-fi generalizable: for any vague mandate, the deliverable shape is always (numbered findings + evidence + options-with-prices + explicit request-for-decisions with a deadline-gentle nudge): speed bonus: including your RECOMMENDED option per decision lets lazy approval be rational approval; (6) if no decisions come back: implement nothing-or-recommended with the written record that defaults-to-recommended were signaled: never silently canonize your taste. Conclusion: vague-UX mandates get debugged by bounded discovery: findings, evidence, priced options, recorded decisions: taste by deciders, construction by agents.

instruction: 'Clean up dead code' mandate. You find: unused functions (easy), a whole legacy feature (moderately used by 2 enterprise tenants), and old migration files. Each has wildly different cleanup semantics. Build the taxonomy of deletability and the differing evidence bars per class.
reasoning: Deadness is class-relative. Unreachable code (no live call graph paths) needs static evidence. Still-used-but-legacy features need business decisions + deprecation programs. Historical migrations need preservation-policies (bootstrap from scratch paths vs audit archives), not deletion reflexes.
answer: Taxonomy with evidence bars: (1) unreachable-by-graph (functions/branches with zero call paths from entry surfaces: static analysis + grep + DI-container string-dispatch checks (runtime 'getService(name)' string names hide call edges: unreferenced classes still reachable by strings: bar = graph + string sweep + framework-convention sweep (route registries, template auto-discovery)): safe to delete with CI green; (2) runtime-gated zombies (code reachable only behind dead flags/experiments: bar = flag-service shows flag fully-off all-environments for N days + the flag's removal PR removes code+flag-together (separate them and the code re-zombifies)); (3) enterprise-legacy feature (the 2 tenants): NOT dead: used-by-human-money: class transfers from engineering to business: deprecation program artifact (usage telemetry, tenant contact window by AM/CSM, migration-offer or LTS policy with date, removal only after contract review: 'dead code' deletions here become legal events: evidence bar includes product sign-off doc); (4) migrations history: never just-delete (they're the bootstrap path for new environments AND the audit trail): options-men: squashed-baseline migrations (create-table snapshots as new baseline + archive the chain: frameworks support squash: preserves bootstrap + removes drag) or archive-directory moves; bar = fresh-database-bootstrap still works (CI job 'migrate from scratch' exists and runs green post-change); (5) reported-dead-by-tooling classes needing suspicion: test-only entry-points (kept deliberately), feature-loaded plugins (plugin-loader conventions invisible to statics: convention-list review before deleting 'unimported' plugin modules); (6) the deliverable PRs SEPARATE by class: unreachable-sweep PR (big, mechanical, CI-trusted), flag-removals (per-flag with evidence lines), enterprise-deprecation (tracker + program, no code yet), migration-baseline (its own carefully-reviewed PR: database tooling risks): review-budgets differ per class; one mega 'cleanup' PR blends trust-classes and gets rubber-stamped into an incident. Conclusion: deletability classes (graph-dead, flag-zombies, business-alive-legacy, historical migrations, convention-hidden) carry different evidence bars and separate PRs: cleanup mandates are taxonomies before they're deletions.

instruction: Emergency scope question mid-incident: during the 2am fix, you notice a quick-hardening change (add missing timeout) near the fixed code. Add it now or hold? Incident-time scope decisions have special rules: what are they?
reasoning: Incident-time changes compete with verification bandwidth and attribution. Extra changes dilute the incident's controlled variable (the fix), complicate rollback, and bypass review normally guarding them. Rule. Restore-first, harden-after, unless the hardening is required to stop the bleeding safely.
answer: Incident rules: (1) restore-first discipline: the deploy that ends the incident should contain the minimal-diff fix only, so mitigation-verification measures ONE variable (did error-rate fall? by how much? anything else moved?) and rollback stays mechanically one-step; (2) the exception window, narrowly drawn: hardening joins THE SAME deploy only when (a) the incident is still bleeding AND the hardening directly reduces ongoing harm (a missing timeout is letting requests pile into the sick dependency: adding the timeout IS mitigation, not hygiene), OR (b) fixing-without-hardening would re-break within hours predictably (the race-window fix with retries still un-agented will retrigger at next peak: include the co-mitigation but say so on the incident channel); (3) midnight-attribution formalism: whatever ships, log each semantic change separately in the incident timeline ('deploy 03:12 contained: connection-lease fix + 5s client timeout (defensive)': postmortem reviewers shouldn't archaeology your bundle); (4) review-at-incident-time: two-person rule for anything beyond the one-line (even at 2am: a second pair of eyes oncall: 'quick hardenings' at 2am produce the 4am incident-classic); risk-ask inverted at night: 'what if MY NEW LINE is wrong while the system is already sick' (sober-incident algebra beats daytime momentum); (5) release-note discipline: post-incident, the hardening-without-bleed items get PRd through normal reviews with daylight-speed (often the next day: 12 hours later with tests written caffeinated-free: the timeout test with fake clocks never gets written at 3am properly); (6) cultural note: heroes love soldering extra wires mid-crash; professionals leave the patient on ONE anesthetic at a time. Conclusion: incident-time: restore-first minimal experiments with logged semantics; hardening rides along only if it stops present bleeding, and everything else waits for daylight reviews with tests.

instruction: Ticket: 'Fix the bug where admins can be demoted by other admins' — authorization bug. The obvious fix (permission-check addition) is small. Adjacent: no audit trail for role changes, no notification to the demoted admin. The mandate says fix. What belongs to THIS fix, and what belongs to the governance followups it should spawn?
reasoning: Security-adjacent fixes must close the vulnerability class within the mandate (the demotion path + symmetric paths). While governance features (audit, notifications) are explicitly registered followups with owners. Conflating them delays the security fix behind feature-building.
answer: Split: inside the security fix PR: (1) close the CLASS within this codepath family: the permission predicate (canDemote(actor, target): rules like self-demotion-block, last-owner-protection, role-hierarchy comparisons) implemented ONCE centrally (policy module), applied to the demotion endpoint; the symmetric audit of sibling authorization decisions reachable in the SAME module (promotion, role-edit endpoints suffer identical missing checks ONE file over: authorization bugs live in swarms: fixing one check while six sibling-mutations remain open is half-a-vuln: the 'class' argument legitimately extends scope to the sibling endpoints' predicates: still small, same review); (2) regression tests: matrix of actor×target×expected-result (admins-demote-admin = 403, owner-demote-admin = 204, self = 403, LAST-owner-demotion = 403 with specific error): the test-matrix IS the receipt the security fix actually happened; outside (governance followups, filed with owner + priority): audit trail for role-changes (append-only log row: actor/target/old/new/ts: notify security-data owners: retention rules theirs), notification-to-demoted (product-flavored: comms copy, rate limits), session-invalidation-on-role-drop (security-relevant! escalate to security owner promptly: privileges lingering in live sessions post-demotion = the fix's shadow needing its own deliberate handling: mention in the fix PR body explicitly), periodic access-review report (governance program matter); (3) sequencing communication: 'vuln closed today (attached test matrix), governance items filed SEC-123..125 with suggested owners+sprints' : the PM sees speed on the vuln, governance boards see trail, no scope-blur in any PR; (4) watch for mandate-creep excuses: 'while fixing authz let me also cleanup the role-model' = the session-invalidation finding is different from role-model-refactor smells: the latter enters the chronic-issue flow, never this PR. Conclusion: close the vulnerability CLASS in the module (sibling predicates + test matrix), file governance features (audit, notify, session-invalidation) with owners and cite them in the PR body: security speed and governance completeness via different tracks.

instruction: 'Modernize our frontend to a framework' — the vaguest-yet-largest scope class. No target named (React? Vue? Svelte?), no driver stated (dev velocity? hiring? performance?), no constraint list. What's the discovery-block that such mandates legally require before any code, and the decision-record template?
reasoning: Framework-adoption mandates are decisions-first projects. The discovery block captures drivers (ranked), constraints (team skills, ecosystem needs, migration surfaces), option-analysis with scored criteria, and a pilot plan with measurable exit criteria — all in an ADR before a line of app code moves.
answer: Discovery block contents (the ADR template): (1) drivers, ranked by the requester (force the ranking: dev-velocity / hiring-market / performance / ecosystem-access / seo-needs: each framework argument collapses without knowing which driver paid for the meeting: a 'performance' driver pointing at a content-site implies islands/SSR-first candidates (Astro/Next), a 'complex-app-state' driver implies rich-client candidates: driver-shapes select shortlists BEFORE brand wars start); (2) constraint inventory: team expertise (retraining-cost = real budget: name weeks), existing-investment (component library porting surface: estimate files/LOC), integration-must-keeps (auth SDK, analytics, design-token pipeline), deployment-targets (edge? mobile-wrapper? SEO-static for marketing?), risk-appetite (bleeding-edge vs LTS); (3) options matrix with evidence-based criteria: score candidates per driver+constraint (evidence per cell: bundle-size benchmarks for content-paths, ecosystem-solution coverage for needs (i18n, forms), maintenance-vitality (release cadence, governance), hiring-market size local pool, migration-path exists (incremental adoption mechanisms: islands? microfrontend seams? full-replace?); attach the source per claim, no vibes); (4) pilot + exit criteria: one bounded surface (one route/one admin section), success-defined (TTFB deltas, dev-velocity on two real tickets timed, bundle budget), failure-cost-defined (revert to status-quo is a real, written option: sunk-cost trap-door kept open); (5) decision-gate: the ADR reviewed by architecture owners + EM + the dissent-collector (someone assigned to argue the strongest 'stay' case: decisions without documented dissent calcify into religion): then and only then migration-program planning (phased strangler-figs, per-phase budgets, per-phase abort-criteria); (6) anti-pattern warnings embedded: resume-driven-development sniff-test, two-frameworks-forever risk (the partial-migration purgatory: the ADR must answer 'how do we ensure completion'), big-bang prohibition. Conclusion: framework mandates get ADR-first shapes (drivers ranked, constraints listed, scored options, pilot criteria, dissent recorded) — code waits until the record exists, because in this class the record IS the engineering.

instruction: 'Fix all the TypeScript errors' — repo has 3,000 of them, accumulated after strict-mode flip. The mandate is bulk-clean. But mechanical fixes (as-casts everywhere) create WORSE debt than the errors. What's the graded-fix taxonomy for error-debt programs, keeping the mandate but refusing the mechanical destruction?
reasoning: Bulk-error programs need fix-class taxonomy. Provably-safe mechanical fixes (inferable types, dead-suppressions-removal) vs judgment classes (domain-nullability, API-boundary validation) vs suppress-then-ticket (legacy islands). Quality metrics (casts-added-count) guard the program against dishonest-zero outcomes.
answer: Taxonomy with tooling: (1) class A: provably-mechanical (missing return-types, implicit-any solvable by inference, unused-import removal, lib-type upgrades with deterministic codemods (React 18 types, node-fetch→undici)): codemods + ts-morph scripts: runs produce PRs that CI+tests adjudicate: ~60-70% of the 3,000 often falls here: zero judgment per instance by design (the codemod's correctness is reviewed ONCE); (2) class B: judgment-required (domain-model nullability: 'user.email possibly undefined' demands domain decisions (email optional in the model? or guaranteed post-verification?): per-module OWNER-time required: reserved for scheduled sweeps with module owners: tracked by error-count-per-module board: these are architecture conversations, budgeted as such); (3) class C: suppress-with-ticket (legacy islands scheduled for deletion/refactor this year: @ts-expect-error + link to the island's exit-ticket: honest accounting: suppressions expire-with-ticket so they don't fossilize: lint-rule requiring ticket-link in every suppression comment keeps the registry alive); (4) anti-destruction guardrails (the mandate's quality-gate): track CAST-DELTA per PR (added 'as any'/'@ts-ignore' counts: a week where casts-added > errors-fixed is net-debt-positive-backwards: the dashboard shames mechanical-fixers: zero-errors-via-casts is debt-relabeling, call it what it is); review-notes demanding cast-justifications for any new suppression (why is this not fixable at the boundary?); (5) pacing & prioritization: errors-per-directory burn-down orders by module criticality (payments first: type-safety is a risk-tool, not aesthetics: the mandate inherits prioritization-logic instead of alphabetical folders); (6) end-state definition: strict-errors == 0 measured by CI gate PLUS suppression-registry size ≤ N and trending down, PLUS no-new-casts budget on diffs (max-lines-touched-rule: ratchets): 'all fixed' becomes a gate others can trust. Conclusion: bulk-error mandates survive via A-mechanical / B-judgment / C-ticketed-suppression classes with cast-delta telemetry and criticality-ordered burn-down: honesty-metrics prevent the zero-errors-scam.

instruction: 'Can you also make it faster?' tacked onto a delivered feature-PR. No slowness complaint on record. Fast-talk is scope-creeps favorite costume: what response-protocol prices performance requests properly when no baseline problem exists?
reasoning: Performance-without-evidence requests invite speculative optimization (worst debt class). Protocol. Ask for the target metric and baseline problem, offer a cheap measurement pass as the legitimate bounded response, and refuse speculative surgery with the reasoning on record.
answer: Protocol: (1) the redirect questions (polite, one message): 'faster per which metric for which flow? (cold-start TTFB? interaction latency on X? bundle-bytes?): do we have a baseline or a user complaint?': requests that can't name a metric usually dissolve here, which is the desired outcome most of the time; (2) the bounded legitimate response when they insist: a MEASUREMENT pass (1-2 hours): quick synthetic profile of the flow (dev-tools waterfall, bundle-analyzer screenshot, one APM trace-sample): produces the one-page 'performance state' note with top-3 actual costs observed: reality replaces vibes: if the note shows a real outsized item (a 3MB hero image, an un-memoized 5000-row render), THAT becomes a ticket with evidence and sized separately; (3) refuse speculative surgery explicitly: 'without an observed cost, code-level optimizations here are guess-shaped: they tax reviews, add complexity, sometimes regress the median for tail-gains: opt instead for a perf-review of the flow as its own ticket when a metric hurts'; put the principle on record (premature-optimization ethics + review-economy math); (4) leave the door institutionalized: a performance-budget (bundle-bytes CI check, route-level TTFB budgets, web-vitals dashboards) converts future 'also faster?' into budget-compliance checks: requests route through 'the budget says X, this PR moves it by Y, fine-or-not': the budget answers faster-talks forever, automatically; (5) note the exception-class: obscene-in-face costs discovered during your own work (you profiled; the 800ms blocking JSON.parse on a 9MB payload IS on-screen during measurements you ran for the feature's own verification: then fixing-or-ticketing with your measured evidence is professional hygiene, not creep: evidence is the dividing line, always). Conclusion: metric-naming redirect → bounded measurement-pass offer → measured-item tickets → polite refusal-with-principles for speculation → institutional budgets as the permanent deflection surface.

instruction: 'Delete the legacy v1 API end of this quarter' — deprecation mandate receiving pushback from integrators who still call it (12% of traffic). What does a deprecation-scope program look like: telemetry truth, migration mechanics, hard deadlines vs graduated pressure, and the scope of YOUR engineering role vs. customer-success functions?
reasoning: Deprecation programs scope by evidence (who calls what, how much, from which versions), migration pressure mechanics (docs, warnings, sunset headers, graduated error injection), and role-boundaries. Engineering owns enforcement mechanisms and telemetry. Customer-facing negotiation belongs to AM/CSM. Dates become binding only with exec-signposted escalation paths.
answer: Program anatomy: (1) truth-baselines: per-integrator call-inventory from gateway logs (api-key × endpoint × volume × last-seen): the 12% isn't abstract: it's 41 integrators, Pareto'd (top-6 = 9%: name them: the program's real surface); also version-usage (mobile app old-builds calling v1: deprecation-date ties to app-store update-forcing mechanics: different constituency with different pressure-tools); (2) migration mechanics owned by engineering: migration-guide with per-endpoint v1→v2 mapping (measured against actual v1-usage shapes from (1): the guide covers observed usage, not the resource catalogue), dual-run window with identical-responses-diff tooling (give integrators the diff-harness: 'run both, diff, migrate when silent'), sunset-headers (RFC 8594 Sunset + Deprecation headers on v1 responses: machine-readable pressure, dashboards pick it up), support-cost telemetry (the v1 maintenance-hours/mo number made visible: justifies the program all by itself); (3) pressure graduation: docs-banner → sunset headers → interstitial warnings (API response warning-fields) → scheduled brownouts (v1 returns 503 during announced windows: the honest escalator: scheduled weekly 10-min blackouts teach faster than any email: with alert-channels pre-notified and a self-serve extension-request form) → final cutoff (with break-glass paid-support path for genuine stranded cases: the exec-blessed exception-lane that keeps the deadline credible); (4) role-boundaries: negotiation with the top-6 = CSM/AM-led with engineering supplying per-account usage-summaries and migration-effort estimates; you do NOT email integrators directly about dates (mixed-message-class risk), but you attend the two gnarliest technical calls as the expert; (5) date-honesty: if quarter-end arrives with 2% stranded, the-decision-document (exec signs: hard cut vs 30-day extension with published FINAL date) matters more than the date itself: deprecation programs die of date-that-cried-wolf, not of extensions-granted-gracefully. Conclusion: deprecations are evidence-led pressure-funnels with role-clean engineering/CSM split, graduated enforcement (headers → brownouts → cutoff), and exec-owned exception-lanes keeping deadlines real.

instruction: New repo, first task in 5 minutes: 'find where HTTP requests to /api/users are handled.' What is the fastest reliable navigation sequence an agent should run before opening any file?
reasoning: Fast navigation anchors on executable wiring, not folder names. Search the route-path string first, then the router registration that mounts it, then follow the handler reference. Framework convention files (routes/index) constrain the search space immediately.
answer: Sequence: (1) string-anchor grep for the literal path fragment: rg "api/users" or the segment "users" quoted within route definitions (narrows to route-declaration sites directly); expect hits in a routes/ module or controller decorators; (2) if the path is composed (prefix /api mounted separately): search the mounting side: rg 'use(' in the app bootstrap (app.ts/server.ts) to find app.use('/api', apiRouter) then within apiRouter for '/users': composition chains (mount prefixes) are resolved by reading each mount level exactly once: no need to open unrelated controllers; (3) framework-convention shortcuts: Django: urls.py chain (include() nesting); Laravel: routes/api.php; Next.js: it IS the filesystem (app/api/users/route.ts): recognize the convention from config files (package.json deps, framework files at root) BEFORE grep conventions; (4) then open the handler file at the resolved site, noting the middleware chain attached at mount level (auth attached app-level vs route-level: recorded from the mount line, not guessed); (5) sanity-confirm execution: if ambiguity remains (two candidates), the runtime wins: hit the endpoint in dev watching logs, or check which router the bootstrap actually imports (an old router file may exist unwired: import-graph settles it). Conclusion: path-literal grep → mount-chain resolution → framework-convention shortcuts → handler + attached-middleware notation → runtime confirmation when two candidates survive: seconds-to-the-line, no folder tourism.

instruction: A large repo has both src/ and lib/, both app/ and application/, both test/ and tests/. Task: add a field to the user profile API response. Which layout-ambiguity resolution protocol tells you which of each pair is live code vs. vestigial?
reasoning: Duplicate-convention directories resolve by wiring evidence. Which the entry points import, which the build config compiles, which CI runs, and recent-modification density. Vestigial dirs show stale imports and no config references.
answer: Resolution protocol per pair: (1) config-first: tsconfig paths / include arrays, package.json main/exports pointing at dist built FROM which source dir (build scripts read src/ or lib/?), jest roots/testMatch globs (test/ vs tests/: which pattern matches which); config files are the repo's own answer key and outrank vibes; (2) entry-point import graph: from the application's main file (identified via package.json scripts: start→node dist/index.js←built from src/), walk imports shallowly: which of app/ vs application/ appears in the import graph of the live entry (a one-level rg 'from \'../app' style search answers fast); (3) recency-density check: git log --format=%ad -3 -- each candidate dir: a directory whose latest change is 14 months old beside a sibling with yesterday's commits = vestigial-with-high-probability: confirm by still failing the wiring test (nothing imports it: note the imports of IT exist at all? unreferenced tree = dead even if importable); (4) check for symlinks/aliases (lib might be a symlink or a tsconfig path-alias for src: ls -la + paths mapping: pairs sometimes are the same tree twice); (5) act + protect: use the live tree; then, because vestigial directories are comprehension traps for the next human: file (or PR) the removal-rename of the dead tree with your evidence inline: navigation-debt deletion is cheap hygiene when evidence is fresh; (6) worst case (both live: legit monorepo with package-boundaries): each is live for its own audience: task's blast-radius determines which you edit: the API-response field belongs to the package serving the API, per the wiring test. Conclusion: config paths + entry-import-graph + recency density + symlink check resolve twin-directory layouts; unreferenced trees deserve evidence-backed removal proposals, and runtime serving-path always crown the winner.

instruction: You need 'the logic that sends password-reset emails' but grep 'password' floods 400 hits. What query-refinement ladder gets from flood to the 3 relevant files, using email-context, provider-calls, and template references instead of keyword luck?
reasoning: Keyword-floods drain via semantic-anchored secondary terms. Narrow by the non-generic sibling concepts (reset token, email template names, provider SDK calls), then intersect result sets. Each ladder rung should cut hits by an order of magnitude.
answer: Ladder: (1) rung 1 — type the real noun: the flow's own vocabulary: 'resetToken', 'reset_token', 'passwordReset', 'forgot': rg 'resetToken|reset-token|forgotPassword' (400→30); (2) rung 2 — anchor on the mail machinery: provider SDKs have rare names: rg 'sendgrid|ses.sendEmail|nodemailer|resend.emails|postmark' -l: intersect mentally with files from rung 1 (30→8); (3) rung 3 — template artifacts: email templates live as files with distinctive names: fd or rg -g '*reset*' for templates (reset-password.hbs / ResetPasswordEmail.tsx): the sender references the template by import or string: find references of the template id string (rg 'reset-password' --type-add yields the composing call-site: 8→3); (4) rung 4 — direction-grep within candidates: the actual sender: find where the token is GENERATED (crypto.randomBytes near 'reset') vs CONSUMED (verify): sender-side cluster = generation + template render + provider call in one request handler: you now own the 3 files (route/service, template, maybe a token-repo); (5) trajectories learned: flood-managing greps always search for the SIBLING of the generic word (the mechanism the flow uniquely touches: provider SDK, template id, token column): generic words describe the domain, siblings describe the mechanism: mechanisms are rare strings; (6) bonus: commit-history vocabulary: git log --grep='reset' may surface the original PR touching precisely these files (fast curriculum). Conclusion: ladder = flow-vocabulary → provider-SDK anchors → template-artifact references → generation-vs-consumption partitioning: each rung an order of magnitude, bypassing keyword-luck entirely.

instruction: The function you must change is defined in packages/shared/src/date.ts and imported by 9 packages. Before editing, what usage-mapping queries show the semantic contracts callers rely on (not just symbol-existence), so your change doesn't compile-clean and behavior-break 9 ways?
reasoning: Reference-finding lists call-sites but not their contract assumptions. For shared utilities, classify call-sites by argument shapes and output usage (what downstream operations the result feeds), because behavioral compatibility is per-call-pattern, not per-symbol.
answer: Usage-mapping: (1) enumerate call-sites per package (IDE references or rg 'functionName' + import-source filter to exclude same-name accidents: same-named functions across libs: filter by import path in the import lines: rg --context around the import); (2) contract-classification pass over the 9×N call-sites: record per call: (a) argument-varieties: which optional params exercised (callers passing locale? DST-sensitive timestamps at midnight? string-vs-Date inputs), (b) output-sensitivity: the result feeds comparisons (subtraction of two outputs: relative-diff-safe even if absolute shifts), serialization (API payloads: ISO-format-reliant: behavior-breaks leak to clients!), DB queries (format-driven predicates: index-use ties to exact string formats), or display-only (locale-format-safe-zone); (3) identify the DISAGREEING contracts ahead: half the callers want UTC-normalized, half want local-tz (a shared date util accumulating both because 'it mostly works': your fix to one semantics breaks the other: detect BEFORE choosing: map it on the call-site list: a 2-column table suffices); (4) then design the change as contract-explicit: new explicit param or a new function name for changed semantics (formatUtc vs formatLocal as separate functions while old name survives delegating to the dominant behavior + deprecate): codemod migrates the minority call-sites explicitly; (5) verification plan per class: package-level contract tests run per consumer package (if the repo is a monorepo with per-package tests: run all 9 test suites: their pin behavior); for API-payload classes, snapshot tests exist per boundary?; (6) briefing: PR body lists the call-site contract-classes found and the migration chosen per class: reviewers from affected packages see their reliance named: shared-utility edits are diplomacy by table. Conclusion: map call-sites by argument-shapes and output-usage-classes, pre-detect contract conflicts among consumers, then change via explicit-semantics APIs + codemods with per-package verification: compile-clean is the floor, not the treaty.

instruction: 'Who calls this endpoint?' — /api/reports/quarterly, an internal endpoint. Static route-analysis shows nothing in the repo. Before declaring it dead: enumerate the out-of-repo caller classes that static analysis cannot see, and the runtime evidence available to consult.
reasoning: Endpoints with no in-repo callers may be consumed by external systems (mobile builds, other repos, cron workers, integrators, browser bookmarks with hardcoded URLs in emails). Liveness verdicts need runtime logs (gateway access logs by path), not symbol search.
answer: Out-of-repo caller survey: (1) gateway/ingress access logs: THE primary evidence: query 90 days of logs for the exact path (count per week + user-agents + sourceIPs + api-key identities): zero-hits over long windows with several request-classes excluded = evidence-backed dead; low-but-steady hits = alive-with-consumers-to-identify (UA strings: okHttp = old android builds; python-requests = someone's script; UA-less from datacenter IPs = another internal service); (2) api-gateway route config: an explicit route registered at the gateway (kong/tyk config) suggests planned-external use (ask the registering commit's author: PR metadata lives); (3) other repos in the org (code-search across org: the path string in other repos' codebases: monorepo-external consumers live: mobile app repo, data-pipeline repo, ops-scripts repo: org-wide search for the literal path fragment); (4) secrets: consumers-with-cookies: browser bookmarks and emails with hardlinks (users startling at 'endpoint removed' via 404s on old emailed links: check redirect-policy needs if it's a GET viewed by humans); (5) infrastructure-as-code: cron entries (k8s CronJob manifests across repos, airflow DAGs) referencing the URL: rg the path in infra repos; (6) monitoring probes: uptime checks hitting it (synthetic monitors configured externally: removing the endpoint pages nobody but breaks the check: listing matters); (7) decision: with the traffic+log evidence in hand: deprecation-program path (from the deprecation discipline: headers, notices, brownouts) vs delete (only zero-evidence): navigation verdicts about 'dead endpoints' are operational conclusions, not repo conclusions. Conclusion: out-of-repo callers surface via access logs, gateway configs, org-wide code search, IaC cron manifests, and monitor configs: liveness is a runtime-log property; symbol-absence in one repo proves nothing.

instruction: Task: 'understand the search feature' in a next-generation monorepo: apps/web (Next), services/search-api (Nest), packages/search-core (shared lib), infra/opensearch (terraform). What's the navigation order that assembles a features cross-repo mental model on rails, registering layer-of-truth per aspect?
reasoning: Feature-shaped navigation follows the feature's data path across layers, registering which layer owns which aspect (query building. Search-core. Transport/auth. Search-api; UX/state. Web. Index topology. Terraform), rather than reading layers wholesale.
answer: Rails order: (1) entry rail (apps/web): locate the search view/route + its hook calls hitting the API (which endpoint, which params, which state-shape: the UX contract: user's observable semantics live at this rail: synonyms visible? instant vs submit); (2) transport rail (services/search-api): controller for the endpoint: validation/auth/rate caps at this layer: then the service delegating into search-core: note the request-shape crossing the boundary (what the web can ask vs what core supports: contract gaps = feature-gaps or tech-debt); (3) capability rail (packages/search-core): the query-DSL assembly: analyzers usage, fuzziness config, permission-filter logic (tenant filters: SECURITY-sensitive: read closely: cross-tenant search bleed = incident-class: who appends the filter and is it un-bypassable from the API layer: cite it); (4) topology rail (infra/opensearch): index mappings (field analyzers per language), shard counts, alias strategy (blue-green reindex aliases: how reindexing works without downtime: you'll need this knowledge the first time a mapping changes); (5) registration output: a small ownership-table in your session notes or the team's docs: aspect → layer → file:line (synonyms: search-core synonyms.ts; boosting: core; auth-filter: search-api middleware calling core with tenant id; UI empty-state: web): the table converts future 'search questions' into O(1) lookups; (6) cross-edges beware-belt: types generated between web and api (shared zod schemas? drift source), feature-flags touching search (flag evaluated on WEB but modifying API-call-params = split-brain configs: note them). Conclusion: navigate features along UX→transport→capability→topology rails, producing an aspect-ownership table with citations: future questions on the feature route to owners instantly, and contract edges (flags, shared-schemas) get flagged as drift-zones.

instruction: The bug-report points at the settings screen, but the settings UI code is trivial rendering. The actual decision logic lives in a 'policy' package 2 hops away consumed via a hook. Multi-hop abstraction navigation: what discipline keeps agents following the DECISION SITE instead of drowning near the symptom site?
reasoning: Symptom-sites vs decision-sites diverge in layered code. Discipline = trace the returned VALUE's construction backwards (the hook's return, into the policy call, into the rule inputs), tagging each hop with file:line and stopping when the decision predicate is found.
answer: Trace discipline: (1) name the observable precisely (toggle disabled: its disabled prop = hook return value canX): open the hook: return shape: canX = policy.allows(actor, action, resource): the hook is plumbing: hop-1 tagged (file:line) and left behind quickly; (2) into the policy package: find allows(): it composes rules (rule-arrays per action: which rule evaluates this resource-type: read the rule SET REGISTRATION to know which rules apply (a missing rule registration for settings-entities = allow-by-default bug-class: common: decision semantics hide in registration files, not rule bodies): hop-2 tagged; (3) read only the matching rule bodies + their INPUTS (what resource attributes feed it: resource.ownerId? tenant.plan?): then where inputs come from (loader fetch? stale-cache? serialization error making plan undefined → default-deny): the bug's root may hide in input-plumbing rather than rule-logic: tag the loader (hop-3) with its data-source; (4) symptom-context completion: the UI shows non-trivial cases (spinner-vs-disabled distinctions inform WHICH policy path went silent: read the component's branches once to learn the UI contract: then return to decision-site work); (5) anti-drowning tools: a scratch trace-list (numbered hops, each one line: hop, fact learned, next-question: enforced discipline when hops exceed 3; beware helper-chains (utility-wrapped-utility: collapse mentally by behavior not by name); markers of rabbit-holes: docs-free generated clients mid-chain: legitimately note and skip-their-internals); (6) fix + test at the decision site (unit the rule / registration, not the button: regression targeted where semantics live). Conclusion: trace observable→hook→policy-call→rule-registration→rule+inputs→input-plumbing with hop tags and depth-limits, fixing semantics at the decision site with tests: symptom-site tourism is the failure mode this discipline deletes.

instruction: You keep finding config values that are 'just there' (constants.ts replicas with different values per service).
