So a misspelled or missing key silently propagates into SDKs and auth headers — surfacing only as downstream 401s. Loud-failure habits. Schema validation at boot, centralised config access, and boot-time connectivity checks.
answer: Why silent: process.env.X for a missing X is plain undefined; template strings render it as 'undefined' and HTTP clients happily send 'Authorization: Bearer undefined' — the failure detonates far from the cause, at the vendor's 401, under load or at 3am. Habits: (1) validate config at boot with a schema — parse process.env through zod/envalid at app start: required keys missing => throw immediately with a message naming the key ('SENDGRID_API_KEY is required') — the app refuses to boot rather than limps: failures happen in deploy pipelines and logs, not in vendor dashboards weeks later; (2) single config module — all env reads go through one config.ts exporting typed constants; nothing else in the codebase touches process.env (lint rule can enforce: no-restricted-syntax on process.env outside config) — a typo then exists in exactly one auditable place, and .env.example is trivially kept in sync because there's a canonical list; (3) smoke the dependency at boot where practical — a cheap startup check (list one SendGrid template or call the vendor's auth test endpoint) turns wrong-key problems into deploy-time failures; where vendors charge per call, at least log which key *name lengths* were loaded (never values — log 'SENDGRID_API_KEY: loaded (12 chars)' or 'missing'). The .env.example / config-schema pair is the living contract: PRs adding a required var must update both — CI can diff them.

instruction: Docs folder contains architecture.md (2019), a README at root updated last week, and a wiki with setup steps from 2022. Before following ANY instructions, what cheap metadata check orders these by trustworthiness, and what does it not tell you?
reasoning: Documentation decays monotonically. Last-modified evidence (git log on the file, wiki page history) is a fast trust-ranking proxy. Recently maintained prose usually tracks reality. While untouched multi-year docs are read for concepts and verified step-by-step before use.
answer: Check: git log -1 --format='%ci %an' -- <file> per document (last commit date and author), the root README's recent activity, and the wiki's page history (most platforms show 'last edited'); also count how many files reference the doc (a linked-from-README doc is more maintained than an orphan). Order by recency + referenced-ness: last-week README first (executable-verifiable sections like scripts can be trusted most), then 2022 wiki (use with verification per step), 2019 architecture last — read it for vocabulary and intended structure rather than procedures ('auth flows through gateway X' is still useful as a hypothesis to verify in code). What recency does NOT tell you: (1) correctness now — a doc updated yesterday may have restructured around a feature that then reverted; recent edits prove attention, not accuracy; (2) which parts changed — a 2023 touch may have fixed one link while the design section remained 2019-stale (git log -p shows which sections moved; per-section recency is the finer signal); (3) authoritativeness — the CONFLUENCE page may be someone's draft notebook while the 2019 doc was the approved ADR. So: use the ordering to decide reading sequence and verification depth, and verify the steps you actually attempt as you execute them (every command runs, every path exists — copy evidence into your notes); mark or fix the specific stale lines you hit rather than declaring whole documents dead: dated, partial precision beats wholesale rewrites.

instruction: A license header check must run on every PR. There's already a GitHub Actions workflow linting files. What's the 60-second orientation that tells you WHERE in the workflow file your new check's job should be added, without breaking existing jobs?
reasoning: Workflow files have a simple grammar. Named jobs under 'jobs:', each with runs-on, needs (dependencies), and steps. Adding a job means inserting a new top-level job id alongside siblings — no nesting inside another job — and watching the trigger and path-filter context.
answer: Read the workflow top-down: (1) 'on:' triggers — confirm it fires on pull_request for the branches you need (if it only triggers on push to main, add pull_request or create a separate workflow for PRs; checks required by branch protection must run on pull_request events); (2) 'permissions:' if present — your check probably needs only contents: read; (3) the 'jobs:' map: existing job ids (lint, test, build) with their needs chains — your new job is a SIBLING key at jobs: level, not a step unless it's trivially fast (prefer a step only if it reuses the same checkout/setup; a standalone job is cleaner when it has different needs or should report as its own check name); (4) steps grammar for your job: actions/checkout, then the check script (npx license-checker or a custom script), with the job-level 'name' set — that name becomes the required-check label in branch protection. Insert, run yamllint or the repo's CI config validator if present (actionlint is the standard catch for workflow typos), then open a throwaway test PR to watch the check report correctly (fails on a bad header, passes after) — the proof PR is the fastest end-to-end verification. Two gotchas to check in the same minute: paths/paths-ignore filters on the triggering workflow (if the workflow ignores *.md pushes, required checks will stall pending on doc-only PRs — either scope the filter or keep required checks on unfiltered workflows), and 'concurrency' groups that might cancel your job on rapid pushes (usually fine; cancel-in-progress applies per group).

instruction: In a Docker-less repo, how do you discover the production runtime's Node version without asking anyone, using files committed in the repo?
reasoning: Version declarations hide in CI matrices, package.json engines, .nvmrc, and hosting-platform config (vercel.json, render.yaml, fly.toml, app.yaml). Cross-check at least two, because drift between them is common and production truth comes from the deploy config.
answer: Search order: (1) hosting/deploy manifests: vercel.json (now rarely pins node), render.yaml / fly.toml / app.yaml (engine fields), Procfile+any buildpack configs, serverless.yml/provider.runtime (e.g., 'nodejs20.x' — very explicit for Lambda), Elastic Beanstalk .ebextensions, Azure config — wherever the deploy target defines runtime, that's production truth; (2) package.json 'engines.node' — the project's declared constraint, enforced at install time only (and then only optionally); (3) .nvmrc/.node-version — developer-side agreement; (4) CI workflow (actions/setup-node node-version or a matrix) — what tests ran against; ideally engines, .nvmrc, CI, and deploy config all agree. When they disagree: rank deploy config > engines > CI > .nvmrc for what's running in production today, then report/fix the drift (a .nvmrc saying 18 with the deploy on 20 is a ticket waiting to become 'works on my machine, broken in prod'). If nothing pins a version anywhere (deploy setting absent, no engines), the runtime follows the host's default — which CAN silently bump (platform upgrades): then your deliverable includes adding an engines entry + aligning CI to the actual current production runtime as the cheapest hazard fix. Verify where the app actually runs when accessible: a status endpoint that prints process.version (if it exists) trumps all files.

instruction: After 'npm install' a fresh clone fails to start with a peer dependency warning escalated to an error about React versions. What exactly is a peer dependency conflict, and what are the three legitimate resolutions ranked?
reasoning: Peer dependencies declare what the consumer must provide. A plugin saying 'react: ^17' while the app installs react 18 is a contract conflict — npm (v7+) refuses to install mismatched trees. The resolutions, ranked. Align the peer with reality, swap versions deliberately, or selectively relax the check — never blind --force.
answer: Mechanism: peerDependencies in a library declare 'I need React provided by my host app at this range'; if your app pins react@18 and a library demands react@^17, npm v7+ treats the tree as unsatisfiable and errors (older npm merely warned and installed a subtly broken tree — runtime explosions later). Resolutions ranked: (1) upgrade/fix the actual constraint — a newer version of the library supporting React 18 usually exists; upgrading it is the correct path when available (a five-minute check in its changelog saves the hack below); (2) adjust YOUR app version when appropriate — if a critical plugin truly caps at React 17 and you're mid-migration, stay pinned deliberately (with a comment + ticket link in package.json explaining the constraint) rather than silencing the checker; (3) LAST RESORT: install with --legacy-peer-deps (restores old-npm leniency) or --force, only after confirming the peer range is aspirational rather than real (library uses no removed APIs — verify by grepping its source for the affected APIs or its issue tracker confirming compatibility) — and always: a teammate-visible PR note + post-install smoke of the plugin's feature + a TODO ticket to remove the override. What never to do: silently commit lockfiles generated under --force without noting it (next clean CI install will explode differently), or pin exact library versions forever as a hiding strategy. Resolution quality is judged by whether the mismatch's ROOT moved, not whether the error text disappeared.

instruction: You must decide which of two duplicate-looking utility functions (utils/date.ts and helpers/dates.ts) to use for your new feature. What's the 3-signal decider when neither is clearly newer?
reasoning: When duplicates compete, the living one is the one more code actually uses (import counts), more recently touched (git log), and better specified (tests). The decider makes adoption evidence-based instead of alphabetical.
answer: Signals: (1) usage census: count importers via rg 'from.*utils/date' versus rg 'from.*helpers/dates' (include re-export barrels in both counts — a barrel index can redirect most uses through one path) — the widely-used one is the de-facto standard and matching it keeps the codebase converging rather than forking; (2) maintenance signal: git log --oneline -5 --each file — the one with recent commits tracks changing requirements (locale handling, DST fixes); a file untouched for years may be stale-but-used (still prefer used) or simply dead; (3) specification signal: which has tests pinning behavior (dates.test.ts with timezone/DST cases = the safer base for your feature)? Compare their behaviors directly for YOUR use-case: run both against your inputs in a scratch REPL/test (or read their implementations: are they actually duplicates or subtly different — one returning UTC-normalized, the other local time? Choosing wrong here silently exports the difference into your feature's data). Decision rule of thumb: use the imported-most/recent/tested one for new code, note the duplicate pair in an issue (consolidation proposal with migration path — roadmap work, not your feature PR), and never 'improve' the loser while touching it only because you're nearby (scope control). If signals split evenly (both used, both stale), prefer the one with tests for safety, and now consolidation deserves a real ticket since the split is knowledge debt — your feature just measured it.

instruction: While reading auth code you find localStorage.setItem('token', jwt) and httpOnly cookies used elsewhere in the same app. For session tokens specifically, which storage is preferred and what's the one-sentence security rationale plus one compatibility caveat?
reasoning: localStorage is reachable by any JavaScript on the page — one XSS payload exfiltrates tokens. HttpOnly cookies are invisible to JS, closing the theft channel. Caveat. Cookie flows need CSRF protection that bearer-token headers don't.
answer: Prefer httpOnly Secure cookies for session tokens: the rationale in one sentence — XSS (the most common web breach class) cannot read httpOnly cookies with JavaScript, while anything in localStorage is one injected script away from theft (localStorage exfiltration is the standard explain-why line). Compatibility caveat: cookie-based auth attaches cookies automatically to requests (that's the point), so every state-changing endpoint needs CSRF defense (SameSite=Lax/Strict attribute on the cookie plus a CSRF token or Fetch Metadata checks for mutations) — token-in-header designs skip CSRF by construction but pay by being JS-readable; also cross-domain/native clients can't use the cookie easily, so mixed estates often run cookies for browser + bearer tokens for native apps as sibling schemes. When auditing the codebase: session tokens in localStorage are a finding (class: sensitive data exposed to XSS), while preferences/draft UI state there is fine — the audit question is 'what does a script reading localStorage get?', not 'is localStorage used?'. Migration traps if you move: rolling logout for existing sessions (plan dual-accept windows), third-party cookie blocking in iframes (embedded widgets scenario breaks cookie flows — that environment plus Safari ITP requires measuring first), and remember to set Secure and a tight SameSite when creating the cookie — defaults vary across frameworks.

instruction: A route works in dev but 404s in production builds (Next.js App Router). Before deeper debugging, what are the two most common structural mistakes that produce exactly this symptom?
reasoning: App Router routing derives from the filesystem with strict conventions. Route handlers/pages must follow naming and export rules, and any dynamic segment or case mismatch between dev filesystems (case-insensitive) and Linux build servers (case-sensitive) breaks only in production.
answer: Mistake 1 — convention violation: a file exists but doesn't satisfy App Router's requirements: page must be page.tsx (not Page.tsx, not index.tsx), and route handlers must be route.ts with HTTP-method exports (export async function GET/POST — an old pages-style default export inside app/ quietly never matches); similarly a 'use client'/server-component violation can surface only at build time. Mistake 2 — case-sensitivity: on macOS/Windows dev (case-insensitive filesystems) app/Dashboard/page.tsx resolves /dashboard imports happily; Linux CI/containers treat them as different paths and the route never materializes in the build output — inspect the build log's route listing (next build prints the route tree: missing lines = structural issue) and git ls-files for casing drift. Cheap disambiguators: locally run a production build (npm run build && npm start) — if it reproduces, the cause is structural (convention or case) not environmental; compare the printed route tree to expectation; check git mv for filename case fixes since OS-level renames don't register in git case-changes without it (git config core.ignorecase interactions). Also note genuinely separate causes with the same symptom (don't conflate): middleware rewrites blocking paths in prod-only matcher configs, route groups (folder) not creating URL segments as expected, and output: 'export' static mode lacking the dynamic route — verify mode set in next.config.js. Repair pattern: fix the structure/name/case, re-run the production build locally, confirm the route prints in the tree, then add a CI smoke test asserting the built app serves the expected route.

instruction: Your express app behaves differently behind the new nginx reverse proxy: req.ip is now the proxy's address and secure cookies are rejected. What two classic trust-boundary misconfigurations cause this pair of symptoms?
reasoning: Proxies terminate the client connection. The app must be told to trust the proxy's forwarded headers for client IP and protocol — missing 'trust proxy' (IP/log/rate-limit wrong) and missing X-Forwarded-Proto handling (secure-cookie rejection on http-looking requests) are the classic pair.
answer: Root cause: Express defaults to treating the direct TCP peer (nginx) as the client and the connection's scheme as http. Behaviors that depend on client ip (logging, geo, **rate limiter keys** — a very real security issue: all users share one bucket or a single miscreant DOSes everyone) read the proxy's address, and secure cookies (cookie-session with secure: true, or csrf/https checks) refuse on requests that look non-HTTPS because nginx terminated TLS and forwarded plain HTTP. Fixes: (1) app.set('trust proxy', setting) — enable with the correct SCOPE: 'trust proxy', 1 (or a subnet/loopback list) so req.ip/req.protocol come from X-Forwarded-* ONLY when the peer is your known proxy — 'trust proxy', true from any address lets strangers spoof client IPs (security regression if the app is ever directly exposed); (2) ensure nginx actually sets the headers: proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; (and Host $host when the app builds absolute URLs); (3) for https-only behaviors, either trust the forwarded proto or redirect http→https at nginx so the app sees consistent semantics. Verification: curl -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4' -H 'X-Forwarded-Proto: https' to the app THROUGH nginx and log req.ip/req.secure — expect the spoofed remote peer ignored unless the trust hop chain matches; then check rate-limiter keys no longer collapse to one IP and secure cookies set in responses. Watch out when CHANGING proxy layers (Cloudflare + nginx + app): count hops deliberately (trust proxy setting must cover the whole chain) — misjudged hop counts re-create the same class after a CDN addition, which is why this config belongs in a comment-documented env-gated setting.

instruction: An API returns 500 for /users/123 but 200 for /users/456. You have ids and timestamps. What's the fastest evidence plan that distinguishes 'bad data row' from 'buggy code path on specific input' without reading the whole handler first?
reasoning: Id-dependent 500s split into data-shape (a specific row breaks otherwise-fine code — a null field, unexpected array length, encoding edge) and logic-shape (the input's value takes a rare branch — non-USD currency, deleted-relation). The cheap discriminator. Diff the two users' data and capture the failing request's actual error.
answer: Step 1 (30 seconds): read the exact 500 response — modern stacks return an error id or a message even in prod; otherwise pull the two request-ids into log search and get the stack trace line that threw. The frame that threw tells you which code ran (serializer? mapper? email formatter?) and the exception TYPE (TypeError cannot read property X of undefined vs RangeError vs database error) already classifies the bug family. Step 2: diff the two entities cheaply — a SQL/ORM query dumping both user rows (plus their direct relations the endpoint touches) side by side; what differs beyond the id: null phone vs set, 0 orders vs N orders, currency code, unicode in the name. The differing field that aligns with the throwing frame is nearly always the cause: TypeError reading 'length' of undefined in the addresses serializer + user 123 has zero addresses rows while 456 has two = data-shape bug (code assumed at least one address). Step 3: name it precisely: if ANY row with that field shape fails (confirm by finding a third row with the same shape and requesting it — cheap falsification), it's a code bug exposed by data (fix the code to handle empty collections — data is legal, code was wrong); if only this one row carries a truly invalid state (currency EXX that violates the CHECK constraint semantics), it's a data-integrity case (fix the row and find its writer). Never jump straight into reading the handler top-to-bottom: the stack frame plus the row diff shrink the suspect surface to one function and one field first. Afterwards: the regression test is 'endpoint returns 200 for an entity with zero addresses', and check whether the error was swallowed without the error id — surfacing correlation ids in 500 bodies is the small observability fix that makes the next such report a 30-second answer.

instruction: A dev-network-tab shows your browser calling POST https://api.acme.com/v1/invites with a 422. What does copying the request as cURL from DevTools buy you over re-clicking the UI while you debug?
reasoning: DevTools' 'Copy as cURL' captures the exact request (path, headers, auth, body, content-type) as a replayable, editable command. This decouples the API's behavior from the UI so each side can be debugged in isolation.
answer: What it buys: (1) reproducibility — the identical request on demand, without form-filling; 422 work means iterating the boundary (which field? which value?), and clicking through the UI for each iteration is slow and inconsistent; (2) editability — drop or change ONE variable per run (remove the optional 'role' field; switch email to a plus-address; drop the custom header) to bisect which property the validator objects to — this is the cheapest experiment harness for 4xx debugging; (3) layer separation — if the curl replay also 422s, the UI (JavaScript state, form serialization) is exonerated: the API contract itself rejects that payload, so read the API's validation; if curl succeeds while the UI 422s, the difference is what the browser adds or mangles (serialization bugs, empty-string vs null fields, content-type differences) and the network tab's RAW tab is where you diff byte-level bodies. Practical notes: cookies in the copied command expire (re-copy later or substitute a fresh token), redact authorization headers before pasting the command into tickets/chats (a copied curl is a live credential), and use your own API client (httpie/postman import) if you want persistent collections. Same-discipline variants: 'Copy as fetch' for quick console replays, HAR export for whole-session evidence attached to a bug report. The meta-skill: isolate the server contract from the client experience at the earliest moment — most 'frontend bug or backend bug?' debates end with one curl replay.

instruction: A form POST sends 'companySize' but the server keeps logging 'undefined'. Before blaming the handler, what three tiny places in the form-to-request path sabotage field arrival, ranked by how often each is the culprit?
reasoning: Form-to-server field loss is almost always mechanical. The input's name attribute (not its id) defines the submitted key, disabled/unchecked controls submit nothing, and body-parsing middleware mismatches the content-type (multipart vs urlencoded vs JSON).
answer: Culprit 1 — the name attribute: HTML submits use the input's NAME, not the id you styled with: '<input id="companySize">' without name='companySize' sends nothing; in React controlled forms people also destructure state keys differently than they initialized (company_size vs companySize mismatch). Check DevTools Network → the request's Form Data section for the actual keys on the wire: if the key is absent there, the problem is fully client-side. Culprit 2 — input state rules: disabled inputs are not submitted by browsers (readonly IS submitted — the common fix), unchecked checkboxes send nothing at all (so 'false' never arrives — handlers must default missing to false), and a select with no default may send nothing until touched; file inputs require the form's enctype to be multipart/form-data. Culprit 3 — content-type/parser mismatch: fetch with JSON.stringify(body) but no 'Content-Type: application/json' header makes Express's bodyParser.json() skip it (req.body is {} behind urlencoded-only middleware), while a real HTML form posts urlencoded (json parser skips). The network tab's Content-Type header versus the server's parser stack resolves this in one look. Extra gremlin: a proxy/edge rule that strips unknown body fields (rare, but exists in some WAF configs) — suspect it only when the wire (Network tab) PROVES the field left the browser but server logs still lack it. Fix the one the evidence names; never 'fix' by renaming things until they match by accident — then nobody knows which of the three it was.

instruction: You want a 30-second bird's-eye-model of a repo that has a README with an architecture diagram, a docker-compose.yml, and a docs/arch folder. In what order do you read them, and what do you cross-check beneath the diagram?
reasoning: Diagrams show intended architecture. Compose shows executable runtime truth. Docs add rationale. Reading diagram-first then verifying it against compose catches drift between the picture and reality before it shapes your model.
answer: Order: (1) README diagram/description for the intended boxes-and-arrows (what talks to what, sync/async hints) — fastest possible overview, but treat as a hypothesis; (2) docker-compose.yml for the executable truth: service list = real runtime processes; note every box in the diagram that has NO compose service (external SaaS? deployed elsewhere? dead diagram?), and every compose service missing from the diagram (added after the diagram was drawn — drift evidence worth noting); check depends_on edges against diagram arrows — a redraw-worthy mismatch is a find on day one; (3) docs/arch selectively: ADRs/decision records explain WHY (alternatives rejected), which prevents redoing settled debates; skim titles and read only decisions touching your upcoming work. Cross-checks beneath the diagram: ports the services expose (the diagram's 'API' box becomes api:4001 concrete), environment wiring (which URLs point where: the web's API_BASE pointing to the api service name proves the edge), volumes/queues (a rabbitmq service means events exist even if the diagram shows only request-response arrows). Write the resulting 5-line model in your notes with file citations (boxes, arrows, ports, datastores, external calls) — this tiny artifact drives every later navigation decision and is updated when you find drift. Timebox: 30-60 seconds per file; the point is orientation metadata (what kinds of things exist), not full mechanism yet.
